subs.name: Atomic structure and the Periodic Table
Relative masses of atoms and molecules
The mole and the Avogadro constant
The characteristic properties of acids and bases

questions.q: Which statement describes the particles in a gas?
options: They are far apart, in a regular pattern and vibrate about fixed positions.
They are close together, randomly arranged and move quickly in all directions.
They are far apart, randomly arranged and move quickly in all directions.
They are far apart, randomly arranged and vibrate about fixed positions.
questions.explain: Gas particles have large separations, no pattern and fast random motion in all directions.

questions.q: A diagram shows particles touching each other in neat rows and columns. Which state of matter does it show?
options: A mixture of liquid and gas
questions.explain: Touching particles in a regular pattern are a solid.

questions.q: On a heating curve, the horizontal section for boiling is much longer than the one for melting. Why?
options: There are more particles in the sample when it boils.
The temperature rises faster during boiling.
Boiling releases energy that slows down the heating.
More energy is needed to completely separate the particles when boiling than to free them from fixed positions when melting.
questions.explain: During boiling the attractions between particles are completely overcome, which needs far more energy than loosening them in melting.

questions.q: A sealed syringe contains air. The plunger is pushed in slowly and the temperature stays the same. What happens to the volume and the pressure of the air?
options: The volume decreases and the pressure decreases.
The volume increases and the pressure increases.
The volume and the pressure stay the same.
The volume decreases and the pressure increases.
questions.explain: Squeezing the same amount of gas into a smaller space makes the pressure rise.

questions.q: A gas in a cylinder with a movable piston is heated at constant external pressure. Which explanation of the increase in volume is correct?
options: The forces of attraction between the particles increase.
The particles move faster and hit the piston harder, so the gas expands until the pressure matches the external pressure.
questions.explain: Faster particles push the piston out, and the gas expands until the collisions per unit area fall back to match the external pressure.

questions.q: Which list contains only changes of state in which the substance gains energy?
questions.explain: Melting, boiling and evaporating all need an energy input. Freezing and condensing release energy.

questions.q: A diagram shows a few particles that are widely spaced and not touching. Which state of matter does it show?
options: A mixture of solid and liquid
questions.explain: Widely spaced particles that do not touch are a gas.

questions.q: Why can a liquid evaporate below its boiling point?
options: All the particles in the liquid have enough energy to escape.
Some particles at the surface have enough energy to escape from the liquid.
The covalent bonds in the molecules break.
The pressure at the surface is zero.
questions.explain: Particles in a liquid have a range of energies, so a few at the surface have enough energy to overcome the attractions and leave.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid melts at 17 °C and boils at 118 °C. In which state is it at 10 °C?
options: A mixture of solid and gas
questions.explain: 10 °C is below the melting point of 17 °C, so the substance is solid.

questions.q: Which statement about temperature is correct?
options: It is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles.
It is a measure of the number of particles.
It is a measure of the mass of the particles.
It is a measure of the size of the particles.
questions.explain: A higher temperature means that the particles have a higher average kinetic energy.

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from solid to liquid?
questions.explain: A solid turns into a liquid by melting. Freezing is the reverse change.

questions.q: Which statement about a solid is correct?
options: It has a fixed shape but its volume changes to fill its container.
It has a fixed shape and a fixed volume.
It has no fixed shape but it has a fixed volume.
It has no fixed shape and no fixed volume.
questions.explain: The particles in a solid are held in fixed positions, so both its shape and its volume are fixed.

questions.q: Nitrogen melts at −210 °C and boils at −196 °C. In which state is nitrogen at −150 °C?
options: A mixture of liquid and solid
questions.explain: −150 °C is above the boiling point of −196 °C, so nitrogen is a gas.

questions.q: Which explanation of the properties of a liquid is correct?
options: The forces between particles hold them in fixed positions, so the shape is fixed.
The forces between particles are negligible, so the liquid fills its container.
The forces between particles keep them close, so the volume is fixed, but they are too weak to hold the particles in fixed positions, so the shape changes.
The particles are far apart, so the liquid can be compressed easily.
questions.explain: Moderate attractions in a liquid keep particles touching but allow them to move past one another.

questions.q: The heating curve of a pure solid has two horizontal sections. What is happening in the first horizontal section?
questions.explain: The first flat section is at the melting point, where solid and liquid are present together. The second flat section is boiling.

questions.q: Which change of state occurs when energy is removed from a liquid?
questions.explain: Taking energy away from a liquid makes its particles move more slowly until they are held in fixed positions, which is freezing.

questions.q: Why can a liquid flow?
options: Its particles can slide past one another.
Its particles are held in a regular lattice.
Its particles are far apart and move freely.
Its particles only vibrate about fixed positions.
questions.explain: Liquid particles are close together but not held in fixed positions, so they can move past each other.

questions.q:
The temperature of a pure substance is recorded as it is heated at a steady rate.
0–2 minutes: rises from −20 °C to 0 °C
2–6 minutes: stays at 0 °C
6–14 minutes: rises from 0 °C to 100 °C
14–26 minutes: stays at 100 °C
What is present after 4 minutes?
questions.explain: The temperature is constant at 0 °C between 2 and 6 minutes, which is the melting point, so solid and liquid are both present.

questions.q: Why can a gas be compressed but a solid cannot?
options: Gas particles are much smaller than solid particles.
Solid particles move too fast to be pushed together.
Gas particles are far apart with much empty space, but solid particles are already touching.
questions.explain: Compression reduces the spaces between particles. There is a lot of space in a gas but almost none in a solid.

questions.q:
Four substances have these melting points and boiling points.
P: −219 °C and −188 °C
Q: −7 °C and 59 °C
R: 801 °C and 1413 °C
S: 0 °C and 100 °C
Which substance is a gas at 25 °C?
questions.explain: Only P has a boiling point below 25 °C, so only P is a gas at 25 °C. Q and S are liquids, and R is a solid.

questions.q: A hot gas is cooled steadily and its temperature is recorded. The cooling curve has a horizontal section at 78 °C. Which change of state is happening in this section?
questions.explain: A flat section on a cooling curve at a substance's boiling point (the same temperature as for condensing) shows the gas changing to liquid.

questions.q: A balloon filled with air at room temperature is placed in a freezer. What happens to the balloon?
questions.explain: Cooling a gas lowers the speed of its particles, so the volume decreases at constant pressure.

questions.q: A substance melts at 30 °C and boils at 250 °C. Over which temperature range is it a liquid?
questions.explain: A substance is liquid between its melting point and its boiling point.

questions.q: A gas fills a flask of volume 1 dm³. All of the gas is moved to an empty 2 dm³ flask at the same temperature. What volume does the gas occupy?
questions.explain: Gas particles spread out to fill all the space available, so the gas occupies the whole 2 dm³ flask.

questions.q: Mercury melts at −39 °C and boils at 357 °C. In which state is mercury at 20 °C?
options: A mixture of solid and liquid
questions.explain: 20 °C is above the melting point (−39 °C) and below the boiling point (357 °C), so mercury is a liquid.

questions.q: A diagram shows particles touching each other in a jumbled arrangement with no pattern. Which state of matter does it show?
options: A mixture of solid and liquid
questions.explain: Touching particles with no regular arrangement are a liquid.

questions.q: What happens to the particles when steam condenses to water?
options: They gain energy and move closer together.
They lose energy and move further apart.
They lose energy and move closer together.
questions.explain: Cooling removes energy, so the particles slow down and are pulled close together to form a liquid.

questions.q: Which statement about the forces between particles in a gas is correct?
options: They are very strong, so the particles stay in fixed positions.
They are strong enough to keep the particles in a regular pattern.
They are strong enough to give the gas a fixed shape.
They are very weak, so the particles move independently of each other.
questions.explain: The forces of attraction between gas particles are negligible because the particles are so far apart, so they move almost independently.

questions.q: A pan of pure water is boiling at normal atmospheric pressure. What is the temperature of the water?
questions.explain: Pure water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure, and its temperature stays constant while it boils.

questions.q: The volume of a fixed mass of gas is reduced at constant temperature. Why does the pressure increase?
options: The same number of particles hit the walls more often because they are in a smaller space.
Each particle hits the walls with greater force.
More particles are added to the gas.
questions.explain: The speed of the particles is unchanged, but in a smaller volume they reach the walls more often, so the force per unit area rises.

questions.q: What happens to the particles during the horizontal section of a heating curve at the boiling point?
options: The average kinetic energy stays the same and the energy supplied separates the particles.
The average kinetic energy increases and the particles stay close together.
The average kinetic energy decreases as the particles separate.
Energy is released as the particles move apart.
questions.explain: At the boiling point the supplied energy overcomes the forces of attraction between particles, so the temperature is constant.

questions.q: Which pair of properties both apply to solids?
options: They flow easily and cannot be compressed.
They have a fixed shape and cannot easily be compressed.
They have a fixed shape and are easily compressed.
They flow easily and are easily compressed.
questions.explain: Solid particles are fixed in a pattern and already touching, so solids keep their shape and are not easily compressed.

questions.q: A weather balloon rises into air where the pressure is lower. The temperature stays the same. What happens to the volume of gas in the balloon?
questions.explain: At constant temperature, a lower external pressure lets the gas expand.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes a liquid?
options: Takes the shape of its container | Fixed | Yes
Takes the shape of its container | Fixed | No
Takes the shape of its container | Not fixed | Yes
questions.explain: A liquid flows to take the shape of its container, but its particles are close together so its volume is fixed and it is very hard to compress.

questions.q: Two flasks contain the same number of gas particles at the same temperature. One has a volume of 1 dm³ and the other 2 dm³. Which statement about the gas pressure is correct?
options: The pressure is higher in the 1 dm³ flask because the particles hit the walls more often.
The pressure is higher in the 2 dm³ flask because the particles move faster.
The pressure is the same in both flasks.
questions.explain: The speeds are the same, but particles in the smaller flask collide with the walls more frequently.

questions.q: Wet washing dries on a line on a day when the air temperature is 20 °C. Which change of state takes place?
questions.explain: Water leaves the surface as vapour at a temperature well below its boiling point, which is evaporation. Boiling needs the liquid to reach its boiling point.

questions.q: Ice, liquid water and steam all contain H₂O. Which statement is correct?
options: The molecules in steam are larger than the molecules in ice.
The molecules in ice are different from the molecules in water.
Steam contains separate hydrogen and oxygen gases.
The molecules are the same in all three states, but their arrangement and movement are different.
questions.explain: A change of state does not change the particles themselves. Only their separation, arrangement and movement change.

questions.q: Drops of water form on the outside of a cold can of drink. Where does the water come from?
options: Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold surface.
Liquid from the drink seeps through the wall of the can.
Oxygen in the air changes into water.
Water in the air freezes and then melts.
questions.explain: Warm air contains water vapour, which loses energy and condenses on the cold can.

questions.q: Steam and liquid water are both at 100 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: Steam particles have a lower average kinetic energy.
The particles have the same average kinetic energy, but steam particles are much further apart.
Steam particles have a higher average kinetic energy because it is a gas.
Water particles have a higher average kinetic energy because they are closer together.
questions.explain: Temperature measures average kinetic energy, so it is the same in both. The extra energy supplied to turn water into steam went into separating the particles.

questions.q: Which statement about particles in a solid is correct?
options: They move freely in all directions.
They cannot move from place to place, but they do vibrate.
questions.explain: Solid particles have energy, so they vibrate, but the forces holding them keep them in fixed positions.

questions.q: What happens to the particles when a solid melts?
options: They lose energy and move further apart.
They move far apart and become gas particles.
They gain energy and begin to slide past one another.
questions.explain: Melting supplies energy so the particles can leave their fixed positions and move around, while staying close together.

questions.q: How do the forces of attraction between particles in a gas compare with those in a liquid?
options: They are strong in a gas and very weak in a liquid.
They are very weak in both.
They are very weak in a gas and strong in a liquid.
questions.explain: Gas particles are far apart so the attractions are negligible, whereas in a liquid the particles are close enough to be held together.

questions.q: Which statement describes the particles in a solid?
options: They are close together in a regular pattern and slide past one another.
They are close together in an irregular arrangement and move randomly.
They are close together in a regular pattern and vibrate about fixed positions.
They are far apart in a regular pattern and vibrate about fixed positions.
questions.explain: Solid particles are touching, arranged in a regular pattern, and can only vibrate about fixed positions.

questions.q: A gas is in a sealed rigid container. It is heated. Why does the pressure of the gas increase?
options: The particles expand and take up more space.
The particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often and with greater force.
The particles hit the walls less often but harder.
questions.explain: Faster particles collide with the walls more frequently and with more force, so the pressure increases at constant volume.

questions.q: A pure liquid with a freezing point of 50 °C is cooled steadily from 90 °C to 10 °C. Which description of its cooling curve is correct?
options: It falls steadily with no flat sections.
It is flat at 90 °C and then falls.
It falls to 50 °C and then rises.
It falls, is flat at 50 °C while freezing, then falls again.
questions.explain: The liquid cools until it reaches its freezing point. While it freezes, energy is released at the same rate as it is lost, so the temperature stays constant. The solid then cools further.

questions.q: Which change of state is the reverse of melting?
questions.explain: Melting is solid to liquid and freezing is liquid to solid.

questions.q: Which statement describes the particles in a liquid?
options: They are close together, in a regular pattern and vibrate in fixed positions.
They are close together, randomly arranged and slide past one another.
They are far apart, randomly arranged and move quickly in straight lines.
They are far apart, arranged in layers and slide past one another.
questions.explain: Liquid particles touch but have no regular pattern, and they can move past each other, which is why liquids flow.

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from gas to liquid?
questions.explain: Cooling a gas turns it into a liquid by condensing. Evaporating is liquid to gas.

questions.q: Sulfur melts at 115 °C. A sample of solid sulfur is heated slowly from 100 °C to 130 °C. What happens to it?
options: It changes from a solid to a liquid.
It changes from a liquid to a gas.
It changes from a gas to a liquid.
questions.explain: The temperature passes the melting point of 115 °C, so the solid melts to a liquid.

questions.q: A gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. Which row compares the gas after compression with the gas before?
questions.explain: The temperature is unchanged, so the average speed is unchanged. The particles are in a smaller space, so they hit the walls more often.

questions.q: A pure liquid is heated, and its temperature rises steadily from just above its melting point to just below its boiling point. What happens to the particles in this section of the heating curve?
options: The forces between particles are completely overcome.
The particles move into a regular pattern.
The average kinetic energy of the particles increases.
questions.explain: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy, so a rising temperature means the particles move faster.

questions.q: A sealed bag contains 36 g of ice. The ice melts completely. What is the mass of water in the bag?
questions.explain: Changing state does not change the number of particles, so the mass stays the same at 36 g.

questions.q: Which pair of properties both apply to gases?
options: They have a fixed volume and are easily compressed.
They fill any container and cannot be compressed.
They fill any container and are easily compressed.
They have a fixed shape and cannot be compressed.
questions.explain: Gas particles are far apart and move freely, so a gas spreads out to fill its container and can be squeezed into a smaller volume.

questions.q:
The temperature of a pure substance is recorded as it is heated at a steady rate.
0–2 minutes: rises from −20 °C to 0 °C
2–6 minutes: stays at 0 °C
6–14 minutes: rises from 0 °C to 100 °C
14–26 minutes: stays at 100 °C
What is the melting point of the substance?
questions.explain: The melting point is the temperature at the first flat section of the heating curve, which is 0 °C.

questions.q: Some water is poured from a beaker into a measuring cylinder. Which statement is correct?
options: The shape and the volume both change.
The shape stays the same but the volume changes.
The shape of the water changes but its volume stays the same.
Neither the shape nor the volume changes.
questions.explain: A liquid takes the shape of its container, but its volume is fixed.

questions.q: Which statement about a liquid is correct?
options: It has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
It has a fixed shape but no fixed volume.
It has no fixed volume and can be compressed easily.
It always fills its container completely.
questions.explain: Liquid particles are close together, which gives a fixed volume, but they can move past each other, so the liquid takes the shape of the container.

questions.q: Which statement about gas pressure is correct?
options: It is caused by gas particles attracting one another.
It is caused only by the weight of the gas pushing down.
It is caused by gas particles colliding with the walls of the container.
It is caused by gas particles vibrating in fixed positions.
questions.explain: Many particles hit the container walls every second, and the force of these collisions per unit area is the pressure.

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from liquid to solid?
questions.explain: A liquid becomes a solid by freezing. Melting is the reverse change.

questions.q: A pure solid is heated steadily. Its temperature stays constant while it melts. Why?
options: The particles stop moving while the solid melts.
The energy supplied is used to overcome the forces between particles, not to raise their average kinetic energy.
The energy supplied makes the particles vibrate faster.
The solid gives out energy as it melts.
questions.explain: During melting the energy goes into separating the particles from their fixed positions, so the average kinetic energy, and hence the temperature, does not change.

questions.q: Ammonia has a boiling point of −33 °C. In which state is ammonia at 25 °C?
options: A mixture of liquid and solid
questions.explain: 25 °C is far above the boiling point of −33 °C, so ammonia is a gas.

questions.q: A student heats some ice in a beaker over a Bunsen burner. Which change of state occurs first as the ice warms up?
questions.explain: Ice first reaches its melting point and turns into liquid water. Boiling occurs later at 100 °C.

questions.q: Why does evaporation cool the liquid that remains?
options: The particles with the most energy escape, so the average kinetic energy of the rest falls.
The particles with the least energy escape, so the average kinetic energy of the rest falls.
The particles that escape lose some of their mass.
Energy is absorbed from the surrounding air only.
questions.explain: The fastest, most energetic particles are the ones that leave, so the average energy of the remaining particles is lower.

questions.q: In which state of matter are the particles furthest apart?
questions.explain: Gas particles are widely separated, whereas particles in liquids and solids are touching.

questions.q: A sealed syringe containing a gas is cooled with the plunger free to move at constant external pressure. Which explanation of the decrease in volume is correct?
options: The particles move more slowly, so they hit the plunger less often and with less force, and the plunger moves in until the pressure balances.
questions.explain: Slower particles exert less pressure, so the external pressure pushes the plunger in until the pressures are equal again, giving a smaller volume.

questions.q: Which statement about the particles in a gas at a fixed temperature is correct?
options: They all move at exactly the same speed.
They all stop moving when they collide.
They move more slowly than the particles in a liquid at the same temperature.
They have a range of speeds, and the average kinetic energy depends on the temperature.
questions.explain: Collisions constantly change the speeds of individual particles, so there is always a range, but the average kinetic energy is set by the temperature.

questions.q: A syringe containing air is sealed at the tip and warmed. The plunger can move freely and the pressure outside stays constant. What happens to the volume of air?
questions.explain: At constant pressure, a gas expands when it is heated because its particles move faster.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the change of state?
questions.explain: Condensing is gas to liquid. Freezing is liquid to solid, melting is solid to liquid and evaporating is liquid to gas.

questions.q: Which state of matter can be compressed easily?
questions.explain: Gas particles are far apart with a lot of empty space between them, so they can be pushed closer together. Particles in solids and liquids are already touching.

questions.q: The air pressure in a car tyre rises after a long journey. Which is the correct explanation?
options: The air particles gain kinetic energy, so they hit the walls of the tyre more often and with greater force.
Friction creates more air particles inside the tyre.
The air particles stick to the inside wall of the tyre.
questions.explain: A warmer gas has faster particles, and at constant volume this raises the pressure.

questions.q: Which change of state is the reverse of condensing?
questions.explain: Condensing is gas to liquid, so the reverse is liquid to gas, which is evaporating (or boiling).

questions.q:
Four substances have these melting points and boiling points.
W: −95 °C and 69 °C
X: 98 °C and 883 °C
Y: −182 °C and −162 °C
Z: 1085 °C and 2562 °C
Which substance is a liquid at 25 °C?
questions.explain: W has a melting point below 25 °C and a boiling point above 25 °C. X and Z are solids and Y is a gas at 25 °C.

questions.q: The pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature is increased from 1 atm to 3 atm. Which statement about the volume of the gas is correct?
options: It becomes three times the original volume.
It becomes the same as the original volume.
It becomes one third of the original volume.
It becomes half of the original volume.
questions.explain: At constant temperature, volume is inversely proportional to pressure, so tripling the pressure reduces the volume to one third.

questions.q: Oxygen melts at −218 °C and boils at −183 °C. In which state is oxygen at −200 °C?
options: A mixture of liquid and gas
questions.explain: −200 °C is higher than the melting point (−218 °C) but lower than the boiling point (−183 °C), so oxygen is a liquid.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes boiling from evaporating?
options: Boiling happens throughout the liquid at its boiling point, but evaporating happens only at the surface and at any temperature.
Boiling happens only at the surface, but evaporating happens throughout the liquid.
Boiling happens at any temperature, but evaporating happens only at the boiling point.
Boiling happens only below the boiling point, but evaporating happens only above it.
questions.explain: Bubbles of vapour form inside the liquid during boiling at the boiling point, whereas evaporation is a surface process that occurs at all temperatures.

questions.q: The same mass of a substance is in each of its three states. In which state does it occupy the largest volume?
options: The volume is the same in all three states
questions.explain: The particles in a gas are far apart, so the gas takes up much more space than the same number of particles in a solid or liquid.

questions.q: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 120 cm³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. The pressure is doubled at constant temperature. What is the new volume of the gas?
questions.explain: At constant temperature, volume is inversely proportional to pressure, so doubling the pressure halves the volume: 120 ÷ 2 = 60 cm³.

questions.q: Which statement about a gas is correct?
options: It has a fixed shape but no fixed volume.
It has a fixed volume and cannot be compressed.
It keeps the same volume when moved to a larger container.
It has no fixed shape and fills the container it is in.
questions.explain: Gas particles move freely in all directions, so the gas spreads out to fill any container.

questions.q:
The temperature of a pure substance is recorded as it is heated at a steady rate.
0–2 minutes: rises from −20 °C to 0 °C
2–6 minutes: stays at 0 °C
6–14 minutes: rises from 0 °C to 100 °C
14–26 minutes: stays at 100 °C
What is present after 20 minutes?
questions.explain: The temperature is constant at 100 °C between 14 and 26 minutes, which is the boiling point, so liquid and gas are both present.

questions.q: A tyre pump is used with its outlet blocked. The air inside is compressed to a smaller volume at constant temperature. What happens to the spaces between the air particles?
questions.explain: Compression pushes the gas particles closer together, but they never completely touch while it is still a gas.

questions.q: A sealed rigid flask of gas is placed in boiling water. Which row shows what happens to the gas?
questions.explain: The flask is sealed, so the number of particles is unchanged. Heating makes the particles faster, so they hit the walls harder and more often and the pressure rises.

questions.q: Why does a puddle dry faster on a hot day than on a cool day?
options: The water boils on the surface of the puddle.
A greater proportion of the surface particles have enough energy to escape.
The air particles push the water particles out.
questions.explain: At a higher temperature more water particles have enough energy to escape from the surface, so the rate of evaporation is higher.

questions.q: Which statement about the change from liquid to gas is correct?
options: The covalent bonds inside the molecules break.
The energy overcomes the forces between particles, so they move far apart and move independently.
questions.explain: Boiling separates whole particles from one another. The bonds within each molecule stay intact.

questions.q: Chlorine melts at −101 °C and boils at −35 °C. In which state is chlorine at −50 °C?
options: A mixture of solid and gas
questions.explain: −50 °C is above the melting point (−101 °C) and below the boiling point (−35 °C), so chlorine is a liquid.

questions.q: Drops of water form on a cold window when warm, damp air touches it. Which change of state is this?
questions.explain: Water vapour in the air is cooled by the window and changes from gas to liquid, which is condensing.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the particles in the state shown?
options: Liquid | Regular pattern | Slide past one another
Gas | Random | Vibrate about fixed positions
Solid | Random | Vibrate about fixed positions
Solid | Regular pattern | Vibrate about fixed positions
questions.explain: A solid has a regular pattern and its particles vibrate about fixed positions. Liquids are random and slide past each other, while gases are random and move freely.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes a change of state of a pure substance?
questions.explain: Melting and boiling absorb energy, condensing and freezing release energy, and the temperature of a pure substance stays constant during each change of state.

questions.q: In which state of matter does diffusion happen fastest?
options: It happens at the same rate in all three states
questions.explain: Gas particles move fastest and furthest between collisions, so gases diffuse quickest.

questions.q: The relative molecular masses of four gases are CH₄ = 16, NH₃ = 17, HCl = 36.5 and Cl₂ = 71. Which list shows the order of rate of diffusion from fastest to slowest?
questions.explain: The lower the relative molecular mass, the faster the diffusion, so the order of rate follows increasing Mr.

questions.q: Hydrogen has Mr = 2 and oxygen has Mr = 32. Which row correctly compares their diffusion at the same temperature?
questions.explain: Hydrogen diffuses faster because its relative molecular mass is lower.

questions.q: Which gas diffuses fastest at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explain: Helium has the smallest relative mass (Ar = 4, compared with Mr = 16, 28 and 44 for the others), so it diffuses fastest.

questions.q: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride are placed at opposite ends of a tube. They take several minutes to meet in the tube, although the particles move very fast. Why?
options: The particles are too heavy to move.
The particles collide with air particles, which change their direction.
The particles only move when the tube is shaken.
questions.explain: Many collisions with the air in the tube make the movement of each particle a random zigzag, so the net progress is slow.

questions.q: Which gas diffuses fastest at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explain: Neon has the smallest relative mass of the four gases, so it diffuses fastest.

questions.q: Which gas diffuses most slowly at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explain: HCl has the largest relative molecular mass (Mr = 36.5, compared with 17, 16 and 28), so it diffuses slowest.

questions.q: In which situation does diffusion take place?
options: A fan blows smoke across a room.
A spoon stirs sugar into tea.
A pump moves water through a pipe.
The smell of cooking spreads through a house with no draughts.
questions.explain: In the others the movement is caused by a fan, a spoon or a pump. Diffusion happens because of random particle motion alone.

questions.q: Which observation is an example of diffusion in a liquid?
options: Bubbles rise to the surface of a fizzy drink.
A puddle gets smaller on a sunny day.
An ice cube floats in a glass of water.
A purple crystal is placed in still water and the purple colour gradually spreads through the water.
questions.explain: The purple particles from the crystal spread through the water by random motion.

questions.q: Gas X diffuses more slowly than gas Y at the same temperature and pressure. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Gas X has a greater relative molecular mass than gas Y.
Gas X has a smaller relative molecular mass than gas Y.
Gas X is at a higher temperature than gas Y.
Gas X has a lower density than gas Y.
questions.explain: A slower rate of diffusion under the same conditions means heavier particles, so a greater relative molecular mass.

questions.q: Which statement about particles during diffusion is correct?
options: Particles only move from a region of low concentration to a region of high concentration.
Particles stop moving when the concentration is the same everywhere.
Particles move in both directions, but more particles move from the region of high concentration to the region of low concentration.
Particles only move when they are heated.
questions.explain: Random motion takes particles both ways, but there are more particles to move out of the high-concentration region, giving a net movement down the concentration gradient.

questions.q: A helium-filled balloon deflates faster than an identical air-filled balloon. Which statement explains this?
options: Helium atoms are bigger than the molecules in air.
Helium atoms have a much lower mass than the molecules in air, so they diffuse out through the tiny holes in the rubber faster.
Helium reacts with the rubber of the balloon.
Helium atoms move more slowly than the molecules in air.
questions.explain: The lighter the particles, the faster they move at a given temperature and the faster they escape through the rubber.

questions.q: A small amount of perfume vapour is released in a sealed jar and left for a long time. How is the vapour distributed in the jar at the end?
options: It is concentrated at the top of the jar.
It is concentrated at the bottom of the jar.
It is spread evenly throughout the jar.
It stays near where it was released.
questions.explain: Diffusion continues until the particles are evenly distributed.

questions.q: Which statement about diffusion in solids is correct?
options: It is fastest in solids because the particles are close together.
It happens at the same rate as in gases.
It occurs only if the solid is stirred.
It is extremely slow because the particles only vibrate about fixed positions.
questions.explain: Solid particles cannot move around, so diffusion in solids is negligible compared with liquids and gases.

questions.q: Carbon monoxide, CO, and nitrogen, N₂, both have a relative molecular mass of 28. Which statement about their diffusion at the same temperature and pressure is correct?
options: Carbon monoxide diffuses faster because it is a compound.
They diffuse at the same rate.
Nitrogen diffuses faster because it is an element.
Carbon monoxide diffuses faster because it contains oxygen.
questions.explain: Rate of diffusion depends on relative molecular mass, and both have a value of 28.

questions.q: Gas X diffuses faster than methane, CH₄, at the same temperature and pressure. Which could be gas X?
questions.explain: A gas that diffuses faster than methane (Mr = 16) must have a smaller relative mass. Only helium qualifies.

questions.q: A drop of coloured dye is added to still water and the colour slowly spreads out. Which explanation is correct?
options: The dye and water particles move randomly and mix.
Gravity pulls the dye through the water.
The water particles push the dye particles in straight lines.
The dye particles are attracted to the sides of the beaker.
questions.explain: Both kinds of particle are in constant random motion, so they gradually mix, which is diffusion.

questions.q: Ammonia (Mr = 17) and hydrogen chloride (Mr = 36.5) are released at opposite ends of a long glass tube. A white ring forms nearer the hydrogen chloride end. Which statement explains this?
options: Hydrogen chloride is a stronger acid, so it reacts faster.
Ammonia particles have a lower mass, so they move faster and travel further.
Ammonia particles are attracted to hydrogen chloride particles.
Hydrogen chloride dissolves in the air.
questions.explain: At the same temperature, particles with lower mass move faster, so ammonia covers more distance in the same time.

questions.q: Which factor does not affect the rate of diffusion of a gas?
questions.explain: The rate depends on how fast the particles move and on the concentration gradient. The colour has no effect.

questions.q: The relative molecular masses of four alkanes are CH₄ = 16, C₂H₆ = 30, C₃H₈ = 44 and C₄H₁₀ = 58. Which diffuses fastest under the same conditions?
questions.explain: The gas with the smallest relative molecular mass diffuses fastest, which is CH₄.

questions.q: Cotton wool soaked in ammonia solution is placed at one end of a long glass tube and cotton wool soaked in hydrobromic acid (giving off hydrogen bromide, Mr = 81) at the other end. A white solid ring forms. Where does the ring form?
options: Closer to the hydrogen bromide end
Exactly in the middle of the tube
questions.explain: Ammonia (Mr = 17) is much lighter than hydrogen bromide (Mr = 81), so it diffuses faster and travels further before the gases meet.

questions.q: Which statement about the particles in a gas is correct?
options: At the same temperature, lighter particles move faster on average than heavier particles.
At the same temperature, heavier particles move faster than lighter particles.
At the same temperature, all gas particles move at the same speed.
At the same temperature, lighter particles move slower than heavier particles.
questions.explain: Particles at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy, so the lighter ones must move faster.

questions.q: Why is diffusion in liquids slower than diffusion in gases?
options: Liquid particles are packed more closely, so they collide more often and spread more slowly.
Liquid particles are heavier than gas particles of the same substance.
Liquid particles are held in fixed positions.
questions.explain: Liquid particles can move, but they are close together and so collide very often, which slows their net movement.

questions.q: Two gases are at the same temperature and have the same average kinetic energy. Why does the lighter gas diffuse faster?
options: Lighter particles have more kinetic energy.
For the same kinetic energy, lighter particles must move at a higher speed.
Lighter particles are attracted less to the container walls.
Lighter particles do not collide with other particles.
questions.explain: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed, so a particle with less mass needs a greater speed to have the same kinetic energy.

questions.q: A drop of food colouring is added to a beaker of hot water and to a beaker of cold water. Which observation is correct?
options: The colour spreads faster in the cold water.
The colour spreads faster in the hot water because the particles have more energy and move faster.
The colour spreads at the same rate in both.
The colour spreads faster in the hot water because the dye particles become smaller.
questions.explain: A higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so diffusion is faster.

questions.q: A gas jar of brown bromine vapour is placed under a gas jar of air with a lid between them. The lid is removed and the brown colour spreads upwards into the top jar, even though bromine is denser than air. What does this show?
options: Bromine reacts with air to form a brown gas.
Bromine is less dense than air.
The particles move randomly and spread out by diffusion.
questions.explain: The brown colour moves upwards against gravity because the particles move randomly, which is diffusion.

questions.q: Which gas diffuses most slowly at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explain: Cl₂ has the largest Mr (71, compared with 64, 44 and 28), so it diffuses slowest.

questions.q: The smell of perfume takes several seconds to reach the other side of a still room, even though perfume particles move very fast. Why?
options: The perfume particles move very slowly.
The perfume particles keep colliding with air particles and changing direction.
The air particles push the perfume particles back to the start.
The perfume particles need to be heated first.
questions.explain: Frequent collisions with air particles make the path of each particle a zigzag, so the net spread is slow.

questions.q: Which change makes the smell of a gas spread faster through a room?
options: Decreasing the temperature of the room
Increasing the temperature of the room
Putting the gas in a larger container
questions.explain: Warmer particles move faster, so diffusion is faster.

questions.q: Which noble gas diffuses most slowly at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explain: Krypton has the largest relative atomic mass, so its atoms move the most slowly at a given temperature.

questions.q: Ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas meet inside a glass tube and form a white ring. Which equation represents the reaction?
questions.explain: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride react in a 1 : 1 ratio to form the white solid ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes diffusion?
options: Liquid | Vibrate in fixed positions | Slow
Solid | Move freely and randomly | Fast
Gas | Slide past one another | Slow
Gas | Move freely and randomly | Fast
questions.explain: Gas particles move freely and randomly, so diffusion is fast. Liquid particles slide past each other, and solid particles only vibrate.

questions.q:
The time taken for 100 cm³ of each gas to diffuse through a porous pot is measured at the same temperature.
Gas R: 20 s
Gas S: 35 s
Gas T: 50 s
Which gas has the greatest relative molecular mass?
options: They have the same relative molecular mass
questions.explain: The gas with the longest diffusion time diffuses slowest, so it has the greatest relative molecular mass.

questions.q: Which statement is the best description of diffusion?
options: The movement of particles from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration.
The movement of particles caused only by stirring.
The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, caused by their random motion.
The breaking up of particles into smaller particles.
questions.explain: Particles move randomly, and overall more move from the area where they are more concentrated into the area where they are less concentrated.

questions.q: Which statement about the components of a mixture is correct?
options: They are joined by chemical bonds in a fixed ratio
They always lose their own properties
They can only be separated by a chemical reaction
They keep their own properties and can be separated by physical methods
questions.explain: The parts of a mixture are not chemically combined, so each keeps its own properties and can be separated by physical methods such as filtration or distillation.

questions.q: Which formula represents a compound?
questions.explain: CO contains two different elements, carbon and oxygen, chemically bonded. The others each contain only one element.

questions.q: Which statement describes a compound?
options: Two or more elements mixed together in any proportions
A substance made of only one type of atom
Two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio
A substance that can be separated by filtration
questions.explain: A compound has atoms of different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio; a mixture has no chemical bonding between its parts.

questions.q: Which row correctly classifies each substance?
questions.explain: Sodium contains one type of atom (element), carbon dioxide has carbon and oxygen chemically bonded (compound) and seawater is salt dissolved in water (mixture).

questions.q: Iron filings and sulfur powder are stirred together, giving a mixture. The mixture is then heated strongly and iron(II) sulfide forms. Which statement is correct?
options: Iron(II) sulfide is a mixture, because it contains iron and sulfur
Iron(II) sulfide is a compound, and iron can be removed from the mixture with a magnet but not from the compound
Iron(II) sulfide is an element, because it is a single solid
Iron can be removed from iron(II) sulfide with a magnet, as in the mixture
questions.explain: In the compound the iron is chemically bonded to sulfur, so it loses its magnetic behaviour; in the mixture the iron keeps its properties and can be pulled out by a magnet.

questions.q: Bronze is made by melting copper and tin together. Which statement about bronze is correct?
options: It is a mixture, because the copper and tin are not chemically combined in a fixed ratio
It is a compound, because it is made by heating
It is an element, because it looks like a single metal
It is a compound, because it has a higher melting point than tin
questions.explain: Bronze (an alloy) is a mixture of metals; its composition can vary and the metals are not chemically bonded to form a compound.

questions.q: Which method can be used to break a compound down into its elements?
options: Passing an electric current through it when molten (electrolysis)
questions.explain: The elements in a compound are chemically bonded, so a chemical change such as electrolysis is needed; physical methods separate only mixtures.

questions.q: Which of these is a mixture?
questions.explain: Air contains nitrogen, oxygen and other gases that are not chemically joined, so it is a mixture. The others are pure compounds.

questions.q: A student draws a substance in which every particle is a pair of different atoms joined together, and all the pairs are identical. How should this substance be classified?
questions.explain: Identical particles each containing different atoms chemically joined represent a compound. An element would have only one kind of atom.

questions.q: Chlorine has proton number 17. Which statement about chlorine is correct?
options: Its electronic configuration is 2,8,7 and it is in Group VII
Its electronic configuration is 2,8,7 and it is in Group III
Its electronic configuration is 2,7,8 and it is in Group VII
Its electronic configuration is 2,8,7 and it is in Period 7
questions.explain: 17 electrons give 2,8,7. Seven outer electrons means Group VII, and three occupied shells means Period 3.

questions.q: Which electronic configuration belongs to a noble gas?
questions.explain: 2,8,8 is argon, with a full outer shell. The others have incomplete outer shells.

questions.q: Which particle contains 18 electrons?
questions.explain: K⁺ has 19 − 1 = 18 electrons. Na⁺ has 10, a chlorine atom has 17 and a calcium atom has 20.

questions.q: Which statement about the proton number (atomic number) is correct?
options: It is the number of protons and neutrons in an atom
It is the number of neutrons in an atom
It is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom
It is the number of outer shell electrons
questions.explain: Proton number is defined as the number of protons in the nucleus, and it identifies the element.

questions.q: What is the mass number (nucleon number) of an atom?
options: The total number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus
The total number of protons and electrons
questions.explain: Mass number counts the particles in the nucleus: protons plus neutrons.

questions.q: A particle has 17 protons and 18 electrons. Which is correct?
options: It is a positive ion with a charge of 1+
It is a negative ion with a charge of 1−
It is a negative ion with a charge of 2−
questions.explain: One more electron than protons gives a net charge of −1, so the particle is an anion (Cl⁻).

questions.q: Which particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explain: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons; electrons are found in shells outside the nucleus.

questions.q: What is the electronic configuration of a chloride ion, Cl⁻ (chlorine has proton number 17)?
questions.explain: The chlorine atom (2,8,7) gains one electron, giving 18 electrons arranged 2,8,8.

questions.q: An atom has proton number 11 and mass number 23. How many neutrons does it contain?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number − proton number = 23 − 11 = 12.

questions.q: What is the electronic configuration of a magnesium atom (proton number 12)?
questions.explain: 12 electrons fill the first shell with 2, the second with 8, leaving 2 in the third shell.

questions.q: An element has the electronic configuration 2,8,3. In which group and period is it found?
questions.explain: Three outer electrons give Group III and three occupied shells give Period 3 (this element is aluminium).

questions.q: Calcium has proton number 20. Which statement about a calcium atom is correct?
options: It has 2 occupied shells and 4 outer electrons, so it is in Period 2, Group IV
It has 4 occupied shells and 8 outer electrons, so it is in Period 4, Group VIII
It has 2 occupied shells and 2 outer electrons, so it is in Period 2, Group II
It has 4 occupied shells and 2 outer electrons, so it is in Period 4, Group II
questions.explain: Calcium is 2,8,8,2: four shells give Period 4 and two outer electrons give Group II.

questions.q: What is the relative charge of an electron?
questions.explain: An electron has a relative charge of −1. Its relative mass is very small (about 1/1840), which is separate from its charge.

questions.q: Compared with a proton, how does the mass of an electron compare?
options: It is much smaller, about 1/1840 of the mass
It is about twice as large
questions.explain: An electron has a very small mass, about 1/1840 of a proton, so it is negligible when calculating mass number.

questions.q: Why are the Group VIII noble gases very unreactive?
options: Their atoms have only one outer electron
Their atoms have a full outer shell of electrons
Their atoms have empty outer shells
questions.explain: A full outer shell is a stable arrangement, so noble gas atoms do not need to gain, lose or share electrons.

questions.q: What is the electronic configuration of a sodium ion, Na⁺ (sodium has proton number 11)?
questions.explain: The sodium atom (2,8,1) loses one electron to form Na⁺, leaving 10 electrons arranged 2,8.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives the relative charge and relative mass of the particles?
questions.explain: A proton has charge +1 and relative mass 1. A neutron is neutral with mass 1; an electron has charge −1 and negligible mass.

questions.q: An element is in Group V and Period 2. What is its electronic configuration?
questions.explain: Period 2 means two occupied shells and Group V means five outer electrons: 2,5 (nitrogen).

questions.q: A neutral atom has a proton number of 19. How many electrons does it have?
questions.explain: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so 19 protons means 19 electrons.

questions.q: An atom has the electronic configuration 2,8,6. How many protons does it have in its nucleus?
questions.explain: A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons: 2 + 8 + 6 = 16 (sulfur).

questions.q: What is the electronic configuration of an oxide ion, O²⁻ (oxygen has proton number 8)?
questions.explain: The oxygen atom (2,6) gains two electrons, giving 10 electrons arranged 2,8.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives the numbers of particles in the ion ³⁹₁₉K⁺?
questions.explain: Protons = 19, neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20, and the 1+ charge means one electron fewer than the protons: 18.

questions.q: The symbol ¹⁴₇N represents an atom. Which statement is correct?
options: The atom has 7 protons and 7 neutrons
The atom has 14 protons and 7 neutrons
The atom has 7 protons and 14 neutrons
The atom has 7 protons and 21 neutrons
questions.explain: The lower number is the proton number (7). Neutrons = 14 − 7 = 7.

questions.q: Which pair of atoms are isotopes of each other?
questions.explain: Both carbon atoms have 6 protons but different mass numbers (12 and 14), so they differ in neutron number only.

questions.q: How many protons and neutrons are in an atom of ¹²₆C (the number 12 is the mass number, 6 is the proton number)?
questions.explain: Protons = 6; neutrons = 12 − 6 = 6.

questions.q: Magnesium has three isotopes: ²⁴Mg (79%), ²⁵Mg (10%) and ²⁶Mg (11%). What is its relative atomic mass, to one decimal place?
Element X has two isotopes, ²⁰X and ²²X, and a relative atomic mass of 20.2. What is the percentage abundance of ²⁰X?
questions.explain: Let x be the fraction of ²⁰X: 20x + 22(1 − x) = 20.2, so 22 − 2x = 20.2 and x = 0.90, i.e. 90%.

questions.q: Which property is different for two isotopes of the same element?
questions.explain: Different neutron numbers change the mass, so physical properties such as density differ, while electrons and chemistry stay the same.

questions.q: Boron has two isotopes: ¹⁰B (20%) and ¹¹B (80%). What is the relative atomic mass of boron?
Which atom has the greatest number of neutrons?
questions.explain: Neutrons: Cl-37 has 20, Cl-35 has 18, Al-27 has 14 and Mg-24 has 12.

questions.q: How many electrons and neutrons are in the ion ³⁵₁₇Cl⁻?
questions.explain: The ion has 17 protons plus one extra electron = 18 electrons. Neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18.

questions.q: Carbon-14 is an isotope of carbon with proton number 6. How many neutrons does an atom of carbon-14 have?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number − proton number = 14 − 6 = 8.

questions.q: Why do isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties?
options: They have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration
They have the same number of neutrons
They have the same mass number
They have the same relative atomic mass
questions.explain: Chemical reactions involve the electrons, and isotopes have identical electron arrangements, so they react in the same way.

questions.q: Copper has two isotopes: ⁶³Cu (69%) and ⁶⁵Cu (31%). What is the relative atomic mass of copper, to one decimal place?
Which statement defines isotopes?
options: Atoms of different elements with the same number of neutrons
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of protons
Atoms with the same mass number but different proton numbers
questions.explain: Isotopes have the same proton number, so they are the same element, but different neutron numbers give different mass numbers.

questions.q: Chlorine consists of 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl. What is the relative atomic mass of chlorine?
What is the formula of potassium bromide?
questions.explain: Potassium forms K⁺ and bromine forms Br⁻; equal charges mean one of each ion.

questions.q: Which formula is correct for lithium oxide, made of Li⁺ and O²⁻ ions?
questions.explain: Two Li⁺ ions (+2) balance one O²⁻ ion (−2).

questions.q: An oxygen atom (2,6) forms an ion. What is the ion?
questions.explain: Oxygen gains two electrons to complete its outer shell, giving 2,8 and a charge of 2−.

questions.q: Which sample of sodium chloride conducts electricity?
options: A pressed pellet of solid sodium chloride
questions.explain: Ions are free to move only when the compound is molten or dissolved in water; they are fixed in position in the solid.

questions.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
options: Much energy is needed to break covalent bonds within the ions
The ions are very small and light
The compounds contain strong bonds between separate molecules
Much energy is needed to overcome the many strong electrostatic attractions between ions in the lattice
questions.explain: The giant lattice has strong attractions between oppositely charged ions throughout, so a lot of energy is needed to separate them.

questions.q: Why does an aqueous solution of an ionic compound conduct electricity?
options: The ions are free to move through the solution
Electrons flow freely through the water
The ions are held in a regular lattice
The compound forms molecules in water
questions.explain: When dissolved, the lattice breaks apart and the ions move freely, carrying the current.

questions.q: What happens when an atom forms a negative ion (anion)?
options: It loses one or more electrons
It gains one or more protons
It gains one or more electrons
It loses one or more neutrons
questions.explain: An anion has more electrons than protons because the atom has gained electrons.

questions.q: Which compound contains ionic bonds?
questions.explain: Potassium (metal) transfers an electron to bromine (non-metal), forming ions. The others contain only non-metals joined by covalent bonds.

questions.q: Which pair of properties is typical of ionic compounds?
options: High melting point and conduct electricity when molten
Low melting point and conduct electricity when solid
High melting point and conduct electricity when solid
Low melting point and conduct electricity when molten
questions.explain: Strong bonds give a high melting point; the ions can move when molten, but cannot when fixed in the solid.

questions.q: Which is the best description of an ionic bond?
options: A strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
An attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
A weak attraction between neutral molecules
questions.explain: Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions. Sharing electrons is covalent bonding.

questions.q: A magnesium atom (2,8,2) forms an ion. Which ion is formed?
questions.explain: Losing the 2 outer electrons gives the stable configuration 2,8 and a charge of 2+.

questions.q: What happens when an atom forms a positive ion (cation)?
options: It loses one or more electrons
It gains one or more electrons
It loses one or more protons
It gains one or more protons
questions.explain: A cation has more protons than electrons because the atom has lost electrons; the number of protons never changes in ion formation.

questions.q: Which row correctly shows whether sodium chloride conducts electricity?
options: does not conduct | does not conduct | conducts
conducts | does not conduct | does not conduct
questions.explain: Solid NaCl has fixed ions and does not conduct; molten and aqueous NaCl have mobile ions and conduct.

questions.q: Which description of the formation of magnesium oxide is correct?
options: Each magnesium atom shares two electrons with an oxygen atom
Each oxygen atom transfers two electrons to a magnesium atom
Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to an oxygen atom, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻
Each magnesium atom transfers one electron to an oxygen atom
questions.explain: Magnesium (2,8,2) loses two electrons and oxygen (2,6) gains two, so both ions have the configuration 2,8.

questions.q: What is the formula of the ionic compound formed from Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions?
questions.explain: Two Al³⁺ give +6 and three O²⁻ give −6, so the ratio is 2 : 3.

questions.q: A sodium atom has 11 protons. How many electrons does the Na⁺ ion contain?
questions.explain: The ion has lost one electron from the neutral atom, so 11 − 1 = 10.

questions.q: In lithium fluoride, how many electrons are in the outer shell of the fluoride ion, F⁻?
questions.explain: The fluorine atom (2,7) gains one electron from lithium, giving 2,8 with 8 outer electrons.

questions.q: In a sodium chloride lattice, how is each ion surrounded?
options: By ions of the same charge
By ions of the opposite charge
questions.explain: The lattice alternates positive and negative ions so that attractions between opposite charges are maximised.

questions.q: Which describes what happens when sodium reacts with chlorine to form sodium chloride?
options: Each chlorine atom transfers one electron to a sodium atom
A sodium atom and a chlorine atom share a pair of electrons
Each sodium atom transfers two electrons to a chlorine atom
Each sodium atom transfers one electron to a chlorine atom
questions.explain: Sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to become Na⁺, and chlorine (2,8,7) gains it to become Cl⁻.

questions.q: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?
options: Its ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move
Its electrons are delocalised but cannot move
Its ions are too small to carry charge
questions.explain: Conduction needs charged particles that are free to move; ions in the solid lattice only vibrate in place.

questions.q: Which type of element atoms tend to form positive ions?
questions.explain: Metal atoms lose their outer electrons to form positive ions; non-metals usually gain electrons.

questions.q: Which is the formula of calcium chloride?
questions.explain: Ca²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ ions to balance charge: one calcium atom loses two electrons and each of two chlorine atoms gains one.

questions.q: Which statement describes the structure of an ionic compound such as sodium chloride?
options: Separate molecules of NaCl held by weak forces
A giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions in a regular arrangement
A giant lattice of positive ions in a sea of electrons
Pairs of atoms joined by shared electrons
questions.explain: Ionic compounds form a regular three-dimensional lattice in which each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge.

questions.q: Which statement about the carbon atom in a molecule of CO₂ is correct?
options: It shares two pairs of electrons and has two non-bonding pairs
It shares four pairs of electrons and has no non-bonding pairs
It shares four pairs of electrons and has two non-bonding pairs
It shares two pairs of electrons and has no non-bonding pairs
questions.explain: Carbon forms two double bonds, so it shares 4 pairs, using all of its 4 outer electrons; no non-bonding pairs remain.

questions.q: How many non-bonding pairs of electrons are in the outer shell of nitrogen in ammonia, NH₃?
questions.explain: Nitrogen has 5 outer electrons: 3 are shared with hydrogens and the other 2 form one non-bonding pair.

questions.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared in a molecule of methane, CH₄?
questions.explain: Carbon forms four single bonds, one with each hydrogen atom, so four pairs are shared.

questions.q: How many covalent bonds are in one molecule of water, H₂O?
questions.explain: The oxygen atom shares one pair of electrons with each of the two hydrogen atoms.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes pure liquid hydrogen chloride (HCl)?
questions.explain: Hydrogen and chlorine share electrons (covalent bonding); the HCl molecules are uncharged so the liquid does not conduct.

questions.q: Which compound consists of simple molecules?
questions.explain: Methane has carbon and hydrogen atoms joined by covalent bonds into small molecules. The others are ionic.

questions.q: How many hydrogen atoms are covalently bonded to the nitrogen atom in one molecule of ammonia?
questions.explain: Nitrogen needs three more electrons for a full outer shell, so it forms three bonds, one to each of three hydrogen atoms.

questions.q: Which molecule contains a triple bond?
questions.explain: Nitrogen shares three pairs of electrons. O₂, CO₂ and C₂H₄ each contain double bonds only.

questions.q: In a molecule of methanol, CH₃OH, how many pairs of electrons are shared in total?
questions.explain: Three C–H bonds, one C–O bond and one O–H bond are all single bonds, giving 5 shared pairs.

questions.q: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points?
options: The forces between the molecules are weak and need little energy to overcome
The covalent bonds within each molecule are weak
The molecules are held in a lattice by strong ionic attractions
questions.explain: Melting separates whole molecules, which needs little energy because the intermolecular forces are weak.

questions.q: What happens when liquid methane boils?
options: The covalent bonds within molecules break
The ions separate from one another
The molecules split into carbon and hydrogen atoms
The weak forces between molecules are overcome
questions.explain: Methane has a low boiling point because only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome; the covalent bonds stay intact.

questions.q: Which pair of properties is typical of a simple molecular compound?
options: High melting point and conducts electricity when molten
Low melting point and does not conduct electricity
Low melting point and conducts electricity when solid
High melting point and does not conduct electricity
questions.explain: Simple molecular compounds have weak forces between molecules and no ions or free electrons to carry charge.

questions.q: In a molecule of carbon dioxide, CO₂, how many pairs of electrons are shared in total?
questions.explain: Each carbon–oxygen bond is a double bond (two shared pairs), and there are two of them.

questions.q: Which pair of elements forms a covalent compound?
questions.explain: Covalent bonds form between non-metal atoms. The other pairs each contain a metal and a non-metal.

questions.q: In a molecule of ethene, C₂H₄, how many pairs of electrons are shared in total?
questions.explain: There are four C–H single bonds (4 pairs) and a C=C double bond (2 pairs), giving 6 shared pairs.

questions.q: In a molecule of chlorine, Cl₂, what is shared between the two atoms?
questions.explain: Each chlorine atom has 7 outer electrons and needs one more, so they share one pair.

questions.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared between the two nitrogen atoms in N₂?
questions.explain: Each nitrogen atom needs three electrons to complete its outer shell, so a triple bond with three shared pairs forms.

questions.q: How many non-bonding electrons are on each nitrogen atom in a molecule of N₂?
questions.explain: Each nitrogen atom has 5 outer electrons: 3 are in the triple bond, leaving 2 as a non-bonding pair.

questions.q: What is a covalent bond?
options: A transfer of electrons from one atom to another
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
An attraction between oppositely charged ions
An attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
questions.explain: In a covalent bond two atoms share a pair of electrons so that each reaches a noble gas configuration.

questions.q: A hydrogen atom shares its electron in a covalent bond. How many electrons does it then have in its outer shell?
questions.explain: Hydrogen has one shell, which is full with two electrons, the noble gas configuration of helium.

questions.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared between the two oxygen atoms in an oxygen molecule, O₂?
questions.explain: Each oxygen atom needs two more electrons, so two pairs are shared, forming a double bond.

questions.q: Why do simple molecular substances not conduct electricity?
options: They contain positive ions fixed in a lattice
They contain no ions or free electrons to carry the charge
questions.explain: Molecules are uncharged and have no mobile charged particles, so no current can flow.

questions.q: In a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl, how many non-bonding pairs of electrons are in the outer shell of the chlorine atom?
questions.explain: Chlorine has 7 outer electrons: one is shared with hydrogen and the other 6 form 3 non-bonding pairs.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the electrical conductivity of the two forms of carbon?
options: does not conduct | does not conduct
questions.explain: All the outer electrons in diamond are used in bonding; graphite has delocalised electrons between its layers.

questions.q: Which substance has a structure most similar to silicon(IV) oxide?
questions.explain: Both diamond and SiO₂ are giant covalent structures in which each atom is bonded to four others.

questions.q: Why is diamond used in cutting tools?
options: It is soft and easily shaped
It is very hard because of its strong covalent bonds in all directions
questions.explain: Each carbon atom is held by four strong covalent bonds in a rigid structure, making diamond extremely hard.

questions.q: Diamond has a very high melting point. What is the reason?
options: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it
Weak forces between molecules must be overcome
Strong ionic attractions must be overcome
The bonds between layers are very strong
questions.explain: Diamond is a giant covalent structure, so melting requires breaking large numbers of strong covalent bonds.

questions.q: Why is graphite used as a lubricant?
options: Its layers can slide over each other easily
It has very strong covalent bonds between layers
It has a very low melting point
questions.explain: The forces between layers are weak, so the layers slide past each other.

questions.q: Which statement describes the structure of silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂?
options: Separate SiO₂ molecules held by weak forces
A lattice of Si⁴⁺ and O²⁻ ions
Layers of silicon and oxygen atoms with delocalised electrons
A giant covalent lattice in which each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms
questions.explain: SiO₂ is a giant lattice; each Si bonds to four O atoms and each O to two Si atoms, giving the ratio 1 : 2.

questions.q: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
options: It contains ions that are fixed in position
It is too hard for charge to flow
It has no free electrons because all outer electrons are used in bonds
Its electrons are delocalised but cannot move
questions.explain: Each carbon atom uses all four outer electrons in covalent bonds, so no mobile charged particles exist.

questions.q: Which statement describes the structure of graphite?
options: Layers of carbon atoms, each atom bonded to three others, with weak forces between the layers
A lattice in which each carbon atom is bonded to four others
Small molecules of carbon held by weak forces
A lattice of carbon ions in a sea of electrons
questions.explain: Graphite has hexagonal layers of covalently bonded carbon atoms; the layers are held together only weakly.

questions.q: How many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom bonded to in diamond?
questions.explain: In diamond each carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds in a tetrahedral arrangement.

questions.q: Why is graphite used for the electrodes in electrolysis?
options: It conducts electricity because it contains ions
It conducts electricity because it has delocalised electrons
It has a low melting point
questions.explain: Each carbon atom in graphite uses only three outer electrons for bonding, leaving one delocalised electron that carries charge.

questions.q: Why is silicon(IV) oxide hard and has a high melting point?
options: It has strong forces between separate molecules
It has a lattice of positive ions in a sea of electrons
It has layers that slide over each other
It has a giant structure of strong covalent bonds, like diamond
questions.explain: Its giant covalent lattice means a very large number of strong bonds have to be broken to melt it.

questions.q: Which statement explains why the formula of silicon(IV) oxide is SiO₂?
options: Each silicon atom is bonded to two oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom to one silicon atom
Silicon ions Si²⁺ combine with oxide ions O²⁻
Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom is shared between two silicon atoms
Each oxygen atom is bonded to four silicon atoms
questions.explain: Four Si–O bonds per silicon, with each oxygen forming two bonds, gives two oxygen atoms for each silicon atom.

questions.q: Which pair of properties do both diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have?
options: Low melting point and conduct electricity
Very high melting point and do not conduct electricity
Very high melting point and conduct electricity
Low melting point and do not conduct electricity
questions.explain: Both are giant covalent structures with strong bonds and no mobile charged particles.

questions.q: Diamond and graphite are both forms of which element?
questions.explain: Diamond and graphite are two structures made of carbon atoms only.

questions.q: Which is the best description of metallic bonding?
options: The attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice
The sharing of pairs of electrons between atoms
The electrostatic attraction between positive ions in a lattice and a sea of delocalised electrons
The weak attraction between neutral atoms
questions.explain: A metal is a giant lattice of positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons that are free to move.

questions.q: Why are metals malleable?
options: Layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the electrons keep them bonded
Their atoms are held in separate molecules
Their ions repel each other when forced
The bonds between atoms break and re-form with the same partners
questions.explain: The sea of electrons holds the ions together even when layers move, so the metal changes shape without breaking.

questions.q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
options: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice
Positive ions are free to move through the lattice
Metals contain molecules that carry charge
questions.explain: Metal ions are fixed in the lattice, but the delocalised electrons carry charge when a voltage is applied.

questions.q: Sodium atoms each have one outer electron. How many delocalised electrons does solid sodium have for each sodium atom?
questions.explain: Each atom contributes its one outer electron to the sea, forming Na⁺ ions in the lattice.

questions.q: Does molten metal conduct electricity?
options: No, because the lattice has broken down
No, because the ions are fixed
Yes, but only because the ions carry the current
Yes, because delocalised electrons can still move
questions.explain: Metallic bonding persists in the liquid, so delocalised electrons still carry the current.

questions.q: Why does a hammered ionic crystal shatter while a hammered metal bends?
options: Metals have weaker bonds than ionic compounds
In an ionic crystal like ions are forced next to each other and repel, but in a metal the electrons keep the ions bonded
Ionic crystals have no bonds between ions
Metals have fewer particles than ionic crystals
questions.explain: Moving layers in an ionic lattice line up like charges, which repel and split the crystal; in metals the sea of electrons maintains bonding.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes a metal?
options: positive ions and negative ions | conducts when solid
positive ions and delocalised electrons | conducts when solid
positive ions and delocalised electrons | does not conduct when solid
questions.explain: A metal lattice contains positive ions and delocalised electrons, which allow it to conduct even as a solid.

questions.q: What is the nature of the force that holds a metallic lattice together?
options: Attraction between shared pairs of electrons and nuclei only
Attraction between positive ions and negative delocalised electrons
Attraction between metal ions and non-metal ions
questions.explain: Oppositely charged ions and electrons attract each other electrostatically; this is stronger than the repulsion between ions.

questions.q: What does the word delocalised mean in the term delocalised electrons?
options: Fixed in the shell of one atom
Not fixed to one atom and free to move throughout the structure
Shared in a pair between exactly two atoms
questions.explain: Delocalised electrons belong to the whole lattice, not to any single atom.

questions.q: What does the term ductile mean?
options: Can be hammered into thin sheets
Can be drawn out into a wire
questions.explain: Ductile describes the ability to be stretched into wires; malleable means able to be hammered into shape.

questions.q: A magnesium atom has two outer electrons. In solid magnesium, what happens to these electrons?
options: They are transferred to chlorine atoms
They stay fixed on each magnesium atom
They become delocalised and move through the lattice of Mg²⁺ ions
They are shared in pairs between two atoms
questions.explain: Each atom releases its outer electrons into the shared sea, leaving Mg²⁺ ions in the lattice.

questions.q: Which diagram description represents a metal?
options: A regular arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions
Pairs of atoms each joined by a shared pair of electrons
A regular arrangement of positive ions surrounded by a sea of free electrons
Layers of atoms with weak forces between the layers
questions.explain: Metals have lattices of positive ions in a sea of electrons; the second option is an ionic lattice and the third a molecule.

questions.q: Which statement about the electrons in a metal is correct?
options: The electrons are only attracted to the ion they came from
The electrons are repelled by all the positive ions
The electrons are shared in fixed pairs between two ions
The delocalised electrons are attracted to all of the positive ions in the lattice
questions.explain: The sea of electrons is attracted to many ions at once, which holds the lattice together and allows movement without breaking it.

questions.q: Which particles are present in a metal lattice?
questions.explain: A metal consists of positive metal ions in a regular arrangement with a sea of electrons around them.

questions.q: Why does solid copper conduct electricity but solid sodium chloride does not?
options: Copper has mobile ions in the solid, but sodium chloride has none
Copper has molecules but sodium chloride has a lattice
Sodium chloride has delocalised electrons that cannot move
Copper has delocalised electrons that can move, but sodium chloride's ions are fixed
questions.explain: Metals have mobile electrons even when solid, whereas ionic solids have charged particles that cannot move.

questions.q: Iron(III) ions are Fe³⁺ and sulfate ions are SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of iron(III) sulfate?
questions.explain: The lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6: two Fe³⁺ (+6) balance three SO₄²⁻ (−6).

questions.q: A model of a molecule shows one carbon atom joined to four hydrogen atoms. What is the formula of the compound?
questions.explain: The model has 1 carbon atom and 4 hydrogen atoms, so the formula is CH₄ (methane).

questions.q: Which statement describes the molecular formula of a compound?
options: The number and type of different atoms in one molecule of the compound
The simplest whole number ratio of the atoms in the compound
The total number of atoms in one mole of the compound
The number of molecules in one gram of the compound
