questions.explain: A molecular formula shows the actual number of each type of atom in one molecule, for example C₂H₆ for ethane. The simplest ratio is the empirical formula.

questions.q: Which row gives the correct name and formula?
questions.explain: Ammonia is NH₃. Carbon dioxide is CO₂ (CO is carbon monoxide), water is H₂O and methane is CH₄.

questions.q: Aqueous calcium hydroxide neutralises aqueous nitric acid, forming aqueous calcium nitrate and water. Which is the correct balanced equation?
questions.explain: Two OH⁻ ions need two H⁺ ions, and calcium nitrate is Ca(NO₃)₂, giving 2H₂O in total.

questions.q: Copper(II) carbonate is heated and decomposes. Which word equation is correct?
options: copper(II) carbonate → copper(II) oxide + carbon dioxide
copper(II) carbonate → copper + carbon dioxide + oxygen
copper(II) carbonate → copper(II) oxide + carbon monoxide
questions.explain: Metal carbonates such as copper(II) carbonate decompose on heating to the metal oxide and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: A model of an ionic lattice shows alternating calcium ions (Ca²⁺) and fluoride ions (F⁻), with twice as many fluoride ions as calcium ions. What is the formula of the compound?
questions.explain: The ions are in the ratio 1 Ca²⁺ : 2 F⁻, which balances the charge, giving CaF₂.

questions.q: Fe₂O₃(s) + ?CO(g) → ?Fe(l) + ?CO₂(g). What are the numbers in front of CO, Fe and CO₂ in the balanced equation?
questions.explain: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ has 2 Fe, 3 C and 6 O on each side.

questions.q: Which word equation shows sodium hydroxide being neutralised by hydrochloric acid?
options: sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + hydrogen
sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium oxide + water
sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium + chlorine + water
sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water
questions.explain: An alkali and an acid react to form a salt and water. The salt from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide is sodium chloride.

questions.q: A clean iron nail is placed in blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Solid copper forms and a pale green solution of iron(II) sulfate remains. Which equation has the correct state symbols?
questions.explain: The iron nail and the copper formed are solids (s), while both salts are dissolved in water, (aq).

questions.q: Which row correctly gives the ions present and the formula of the compound?
questions.explain: Ca²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ to balance charge. The correct formulae of the others are Na₂O, AlCl₃ and K₂SO₄.

questions.q: Glucose has the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆. What is its empirical formula?
questions.explain: Divide the numbers of atoms by their highest common factor, 6, to give C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1.

questions.q: What is the formula of sulfuric acid?
questions.explain: Sulfuric acid contains two hydrogen atoms, one sulfur atom and four oxygen atoms: H₂SO₄. H₂SO₃ is sulfurous acid and H₂S is hydrogen sulfide.

questions.q: A model of a compound shows one calcium atom, one carbon atom and three oxygen atoms bonded together. What is the formula of the compound?
questions.explain: The numbers of atoms are Ca 1, C 1 and O 3, so the formula is CaCO₃.

questions.q: Aluminium forms Al³⁺ ions and oxygen forms O²⁻ ions. What is the formula of aluminium oxide?
questions.explain: The charges must balance: 2 × (+3) = +6 and 3 × (−2) = −6, so the ratio is Al : O = 2 : 3.

questions.q: Which ionic equation is balanced for both atoms and charge?
questions.explain: The left side has charge +2 and 2 H atoms; the right side has Mg²⁺ (+2) and H₂ (2 H atoms). The other equations have unequal charge or atoms.

questions.q: Which word equation shows the complete combustion of methane?
questions.explain: Methane is a hydrocarbon. Burning it in plenty of oxygen forms carbon dioxide and water.

questions.q: Which statement defines the empirical formula of a compound?
options: The number and type of different atoms in one molecule
The simplest whole number ratio of the different atoms or ions in the compound
The mass of each element in 100 g of the compound
The total relative mass of all the atoms in the compound
questions.explain: The empirical formula gives only the simplest whole number ratio of atoms or ions, for example CH₂ for C₄H₈ or Na₂O for the ionic compound with ions in a 2:1 ratio.

questions.q: Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ ions and nitrate is NO₃⁻. What is the formula of magnesium nitrate?
questions.explain: One Mg²⁺ (+2) needs two NO₃⁻ (−1 each), and the nitrate group goes in brackets: Mg(NO₃)₂.

questions.q: Aqueous silver nitrate is mixed with aqueous sodium chloride and a white precipitate forms. Which ionic equation represents the reaction?
questions.explain: Only silver ions and chloride ions combine to make the solid silver chloride. Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ stay in solution and are not included.

questions.q: Aqueous silver nitrate reacts with aqueous sodium chloride. Which ions are spectator ions?
questions.explain: Spectator ions are present but do not change. Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ form the AgCl precipitate, but Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ stay dissolved.

questions.q: Sodium reacts with water: Na(s) + H₂O(l) → NaOH(aq) + H₂(g). What are the numbers in front of Na, H₂O, NaOH and H₂ in the balanced equation?
questions.explain: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ has 2 Na, 4 H and 2 O on each side.

questions.q: How many oxygen atoms are shown in 2Mg(NO₃)₂?
questions.explain: Each Mg(NO₃)₂ has 2 × 3 = 6 oxygen atoms. Two of them have 2 × 6 = 12.

questions.q: Which word equation is correct for calcium carbonate reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + hydrogen
calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide
calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water
questions.explain: Acids react with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which compound contains three different elements?
questions.explain: NaOH contains sodium, oxygen and hydrogen. The other three each contain two elements.

questions.q: Which equation for the burning of methane is correctly balanced?
questions.explain: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O has 1 C, 4 H and 4 O on each side. The other equations are unbalanced in oxygen or hydrogen.

questions.q: A model of a molecule shows one sulfur atom joined to two oxygen atoms. What is its formula?
questions.explain: One S atom and two O atoms give SO₂, sulfur dioxide.

questions.q: Aqueous sodium carbonate reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form aqueous sodium sulfate, water and carbon dioxide gas. Which is the balanced equation with state symbols?
questions.explain: The formulae Na₂CO₃ and Na₂SO₄ are needed to balance the charges, and the equation is already balanced with 1 H₂O. Sodium carbonate is aqueous and carbon dioxide is a gas.

questions.q: How many different elements are present in ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄?
questions.explain: The elements are nitrogen, hydrogen, sulfur and oxygen: 4 different elements.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali?
questions.explain: Hydrogen ions from the acid react with hydroxide ions from the alkali to form water.

questions.q: Which row gives the correct name and formula?
questions.explain: Sodium hydroxide is NaOH. The others should be Ca(OH)₂, K₂CO₃ and Mg(NO₃)₂.

questions.q: Which word equation correctly shows zinc reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen
zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + water
zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc oxide + hydrogen chloride
zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc hydroxide + hydrogen
questions.explain: A metal reacting with a dilute acid forms a salt and hydrogen gas. The salt from hydrochloric acid is a chloride.

questions.q: What is the formula of carbon monoxide?
questions.explain: The prefix mono means one oxygen atom, so carbon monoxide is CO. CO₂ is carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Why must a symbol equation be balanced?
options: The number of molecules never changes in a chemical reaction
The reactants and products must be in the same state
Atoms are not created or destroyed in a chemical reaction
The volume of the products must equal the volume of the reactants
questions.explain: Atoms are only rearranged, so each element must have the same number of atoms before and after the reaction. The number of molecules and the volume can change.

questions.q: Which word equation shows the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate?
options: calcium carbonate → calcium + carbon dioxide + oxygen
calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon monoxide
calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide
calcium carbonate → calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Heating a metal carbonate gives the metal oxide and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: In a chemical equation, what does the state symbol (aq) mean?
options: The substance is a pure liquid
The substance is a solid that has formed in water
The substance is dissolved in water
questions.explain: (aq) stands for aqueous: the substance is dissolved in water. Pure liquids are (l), solids (s) and gases (g).

questions.q: How many atoms are there altogether in 3H₂SO₄?
questions.explain: Each H₂SO₄ contains 2 + 1 + 4 = 7 atoms. Three units contain 3 × 7 = 21 atoms.

questions.q: A diagram of a molecule shows two carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms. What is its molecular formula?
questions.explain: The molecular formula gives the actual number of each atom in one molecule: 2 carbon and 6 hydrogen, so C₂H₆. CH₃ is only the simplest ratio.

questions.q: Which row is correct?
questions.explain: NaCl has two elements. In H₂O there are 2 elements (3 atoms), in CH₄ 2 elements (5 atoms) and in NH₃ 2 elements (4 atoms): the other rows count atoms instead of elements.

questions.q: The equation N₂(g) + H₂(g) → NH₃(g) is balanced by adding numbers in front of the formulae. What number goes in front of H₂?
questions.explain: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ has 2 N and 6 H on each side, so H₂ needs the number 3.

questions.q: Which formula represents an element?
questions.explain: Cl₂ contains only chlorine atoms, so it is an element. HCl, CO and H₂O each contain two different elements and are compounds.

questions.q: Calcium carbonate lumps react with dilute hydrochloric acid to give calcium chloride solution, water and carbon dioxide gas. Which equation has the correct state symbols?
questions.explain: Lumps are solid (s), the acid and the salt solution are (aq), water is a liquid (l) and carbon dioxide escapes as a gas (g).

questions.q: Which symbol equation, with state symbols, is correctly balanced?
questions.explain: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO has 2 Mg and 2 O on each side. The others have unequal numbers of atoms on the two sides, or use the wrong formula MgO₂.

questions.q: How many oxygen atoms are there in one formula unit of Al₂(SO₄)₃?
questions.explain: There are 3 sulfate groups and each contains 4 oxygen atoms, so 3 × 4 = 12.

questions.q: The equation Al(s) + O₂(g) → Al₂O₃(s) is balanced using the smallest whole numbers. What number goes in front of O₂?
questions.explain: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ has 4 Al and 6 O on each side.

questions.q: What is the relative formula mass, Mr, of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16, Mg = 24)
Chlorine has two isotopes: 75% is chlorine-35 and 25% is chlorine-37. What is the relative atomic mass of chlorine?
What is the relative formula mass, Mr, of iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃? (Ar: O = 16, Fe = 56)
Which gas has the largest relative molecular mass? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32)
questions.explain: Mr values: SO₂ = 64, N₂ = 28, CO = 28 and NH₃ = 17, so SO₂ is the largest.

questions.q: What is the relative molecular mass, Mr, of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)
What is the relative formula mass, Mr, of ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄? (Ar: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32)
An element has two isotopes: 50.0% is atoms of mass number 79 and 50.0% is atoms of mass number 81. What is its relative atomic mass?
Which statement describes the relative atomic mass, Ar, of an element?
options: The mass of one atom of the element in grams
The mass of the most common isotope compared with 1/12th of the mass of an atom of carbon-12
The average mass of the isotopes of the element compared with 1/12th of the mass of an atom of carbon-12
The number of protons and neutrons in the most common isotope
questions.explain: Ar uses the average mass of all the naturally occurring isotopes of the element, compared with 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

questions.q: Boron has two isotopes: 20% is boron-10 and 80% is boron-11. What is the relative atomic mass of boron?
Which statement about the relative molecular mass, Mr, of a substance is correct?
options: It has no units because it is a comparison with 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
questions.explain: Mr is a ratio of masses, so it has no units. Molar mass (the mass of one mole) has units of g/mol.

questions.q: What is the relative molecular mass, Mr, of ethanol, C₂H₅OH? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
In the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 4 g of hydrogen forms 36 g of water. What mass of water forms from 1 g of hydrogen in excess oxygen?
questions.explain: 1 g is a quarter of 4 g, so the mass of water is a quarter of 36 g, which is 9 g.

questions.q: Carbon burns in oxygen: 12 g of carbon forms 44 g of carbon dioxide. What mass of carbon dioxide forms from 3 g of carbon?
questions.explain: 3 g is a quarter of 12 g, so the carbon dioxide formed is a quarter of 44 g, which is 11 g.

questions.q: Why is the relative atomic mass of an element often not a whole number?
options: Atoms contain a fraction of a proton
The mass of the electrons is added to the mass of the nucleus
The mass of an atom cannot be measured exactly
It is an average over the isotopes present, taking their abundances into account
questions.explain: Different isotopes have different mass numbers, and Ar is the weighted average of these, which is usually not a whole number.

questions.q: What is the relative formula mass, Mr, of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·5H₂O? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16, S = 32, Cu = 64)
Heating 124 g of copper(II) carbonate forms 80 g of copper(II) oxide. What mass of copper(II) oxide forms from 12.4 g of copper(II) carbonate?
questions.explain: 12.4 g is one tenth of 124 g, so the mass of copper(II) oxide is one tenth of 80 g, which is 8.0 g.

questions.q: What is the relative formula mass, Mr, of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16, Ca = 40)
questions.explain: Mr = 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 40 + 34 = 74. The bracket means two OH groups.

questions.q: What is the relative formula mass, Mr, of hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23)
The chloride XCl₂ has a relative formula mass of 95. What is the relative atomic mass of X? (Ar: Cl = 35.5)
questions.explain: 2 Cl = 71, so X = 95 − 71 = 24 (magnesium).

questions.q: What is the relative formula mass, Mr, of magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO₃)₂? (Ar: N = 14, O = 16, Mg = 24)
Neon has two isotopes: 90% is neon-20 and 10% is neon-22. What is the relative atomic mass of neon?
In the reaction 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, 48 g of magnesium reacts with 32 g of oxygen. What mass of oxygen reacts with 12 g of magnesium?
questions.explain: 12 g is a quarter of 48 g, so the oxygen needed is a quarter of 32 g, which is 8 g.

questions.q: The oxide X₂O₃ has a relative formula mass of 102. What is the relative atomic mass of X? (Ar: O = 16)
questions.explain: 3 O = 48, so 2X = 102 − 48 = 54 and X = 27 (aluminium).

questions.q: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 24 g of magnesium forms 40 g of magnesium oxide. What mass of magnesium oxide forms from 6 g of magnesium?
questions.explain: 6 g is a quarter of 24 g, so the mass of magnesium oxide is a quarter of 40 g, which is 10 g.

questions.q: Heating 100 g of calcium carbonate gives 56 g of calcium oxide. What mass of calcium oxide forms from 25 g of calcium carbonate?
questions.explain: 25 g is a quarter of 100 g, so the mass of calcium oxide is a quarter of 56 g, which is 14 g.

questions.q: Which row is correct? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23, Mg = 24, Ca = 40)
questions.explain: Mr of MgO = 24 + 16 = 40. The others should be 100 for CaCO₃, 44 for CO₂ and 40 for NaOH.

questions.q: Copper(II) oxide is reduced by hydrogen to copper: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. What mass of copper forms from 16 g of copper(II) oxide? (Ar: Cu = 64, O = 16)
questions.explain: Mr of CuO = 80, so 16 g = 0.20 mol. The ratio CuO : Cu is 1 : 1, so 0.20 mol of Cu = 0.20 × 64 = 12.8 g.

questions.q: What is the relative molecular mass, Mr, of carbon dioxide, CO₂? (Ar: C = 12, O = 16)
What is the relative formula mass, Mr, of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃? (Ar: O = 16, Al = 27, S = 32)
Why is the term relative formula mass used for sodium chloride instead of relative molecular mass?
options: Sodium chloride has a high melting point
Sodium chloride is an ionic compound made of a lattice of ions, not molecules
Sodium chloride has no relative atomic masses
questions.explain: Ionic compounds have giant lattices of ions with no separate molecules, so the formula unit is used and the mass is called the relative formula mass.

questions.q: A hydrocarbon contains 2.4 g of carbon and 0.6 g of hydrogen. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12)
questions.explain: Moles: C = 2.4 ÷ 12 = 0.20; H = 0.6 ÷ 1 = 0.6. The ratio is 1 : 3, so the empirical formula is CH₃.

questions.q: What is the amount, in moles, of 11 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂? (Ar: C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explain: Mr of CO₂ = 44. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 11 ÷ 44 = 0.25 mol.

questions.q: Which pair of units can be used for the concentration of a solution?
questions.explain: Concentration is the amount of solute (in g or mol) in 1 dm³ of solution, so g/dm³ and mol/dm³.

questions.q: Which sample contains the same number of atoms as 12 g of carbon? (Ar: C = 12, Mg = 24)
questions.explain: 12 g of carbon is 1 mol of atoms. 24 g of magnesium is also 1 mol (24 ÷ 24), so it has the same number of atoms.

questions.q: A sample of 0.20 mol of a metal M has a mass of 13 g. What is the relative atomic mass of M?
questions.explain: Molar mass = mass ÷ moles = 13 ÷ 0.20 = 65 g/mol, so Ar = 65.

questions.q: What is the percentage by mass of water in hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·5H₂O? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16, S = 32, Cu = 64)
questions.explain: Mr = 160 + 90 = 250. Percentage of water = 90 ÷ 250 × 100 = 36%.

questions.q: Four solutions of the same solute are made. Which is the most concentrated?
questions.explain: In g/dm³ the concentrations are 10, 8, 5 and 6 respectively, so 1 g in 100 cm³ (10 g/dm³) is the highest.

questions.q: What does a concentration of 0.5 mol/dm³ mean?
options: There is 0.5 mol of solute in every 1 dm³ of solution
There is 0.5 g of solute in every 1 dm³ of solution
There is 0.5 mol of solute in every 1 cm³ of solution
There is 0.5 mol of solute in 100 cm³ of water
questions.explain: mol/dm³ means moles of solute per dm³ of the whole solution.

questions.q: What is the percentage by mass of magnesium in magnesium oxide, MgO? (Ar: O = 16, Mg = 24)
questions.explain: Mr of MgO = 40. Percentage of Mg = 24 ÷ 40 × 100 = 60%.

questions.q: What is 0.025 dm³ in cm³?
4.0 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in water and made up to 500 cm³ of solution. What is the concentration in mol/dm³? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23)
questions.explain: Moles = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.10 mol. Concentration = 0.10 ÷ 0.500 dm³ = 0.20 mol/dm³.

questions.q: 2.50 g of impure limestone reacts with excess hydrochloric acid and gives 0.0150 mol of carbon dioxide. Assume the impurities do not react. What is the percentage purity of the calcium carbonate? (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40)

In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid (NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O). What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?
questions.explain: Moles of HCl = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol. The ratio is 1 : 1, so NaOH = 0.00200 mol in 0.0250 dm³, giving 0.0800 mol/dm³.

questions.q: A hydrocarbon has the empirical formula C₂H₅ and a relative molecular mass of 58. What is its molecular formula? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12)
questions.explain: The empirical formula mass is 29, and 58 ÷ 29 = 2, so the molecular formula is (C₂H₅)₂ = C₄H₁₀.

questions.q: An iron oxide contains 5.6 g of iron and 2.4 g of oxygen. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: O = 16, Fe = 56)
A solution contains 20 g of solute dissolved in 2 dm³ of solution. What is its concentration in g/dm³?
questions.explain: Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 20 g ÷ 2 dm³ = 10 g/dm³.

questions.q: How many particles are there in one mole of any substance?
questions.explain: One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (atoms, ions or molecules). This is the Avogadro constant.

questions.q: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. What mass of iron forms from 80 g of iron(III) oxide? (Ar: O = 16, Fe = 56)
questions.explain: Mr of Fe₂O₃ = 160, so 80 g = 0.50 mol. The ratio Fe₂O₃ : Fe is 1 : 2, so 1.0 mol of Fe = 56 g.

questions.q: Which row correctly matches a quantity with its unit?
questions.explain: Amount of substance is measured in mol. Molar mass is in g/mol, concentration in g/dm³ or mol/dm³ and molar gas volume in dm³/mol.

questions.q: A solution of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, has a concentration of 0.50 mol/dm³. What is its concentration in g/dm³? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)
questions.explain: Mr of H₂SO₄ = 98. Concentration in g/dm³ = 0.50 × 98 = 49 g/dm³.

questions.q: What is the mass of 0.20 mol of sodium hydroxide, NaOH? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23)
questions.explain: Molar mass of NaOH = 40 g/mol. Mass = moles × molar mass = 0.20 × 40 = 8.0 g.

questions.q: A student needs to convert a volume of 250 cm³ to dm³. What is the volume in dm³?
2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. What mass of aluminium forms from 204 g of aluminium oxide? (Ar: O = 16, Al = 27)
questions.explain: Mr of Al₂O₃ = 102, so 204 g = 2.0 mol. The ratio Al₂O₃ : Al is 1 : 2, so 4.0 mol of Al = 4.0 × 27 = 108 g.

questions.q: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Excess acid is added to 6.5 g of zinc. What volume of hydrogen forms at r.t.p.? (Ar: Zn = 65; molar gas volume = 24 dm³)
questions.explain: 6.5 g ÷ 65 g/mol = 0.10 mol of Zn gives 0.10 mol of H₂. Volume = 0.10 × 24 = 2.4 dm³.

questions.q: What is the volume of 0.50 mol of a gas at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.)?
questions.explain: One mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p., so 0.50 mol occupies 0.50 × 24 = 12 dm³.

questions.q: How many moles of solute are in 25.0 cm³ of a solution of concentration 0.20 mol/dm³?
questions.explain: Moles = concentration × volume in dm³ = 0.20 × 0.0250 = 0.0050 mol.

questions.q: Which row is correct? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16; Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ per mol)
questions.explain: 22 g ÷ 44 g/mol = 0.50 mol, and 0.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³. The other rows have the wrong number of particles for the amount shown.

questions.q: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.125 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide (HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O). What is the concentration of the acid in g/dm³? (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
questions.explain: Moles of NaOH = 0.125 × 0.0200 = 0.00250 mol = moles of HCl. Concentration = 0.00250 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.100 mol/dm³, and 0.100 × 36.5 = 3.65 g/dm³.

questions.q: 1.50 g of impure zinc reacts with excess acid to give 360 cm³ of hydrogen at r.t.p. Assume the impurities do not react. What is the percentage purity of the zinc? (Ar: Zn = 65; molar gas volume = 24 dm³)
A solution of sodium hydroxide has a concentration of 40 g/dm³. What mass of sodium hydroxide is in 0.5 dm³ of this solution?
questions.explain: Mass = concentration × volume = 40 g/dm³ × 0.5 dm³ = 20 g.

questions.q: How many molecules are there in 0.50 mol of water? (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ per mol)
questions.explain: Number of molecules = 0.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³.

questions.q: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Excess acid is added to 5.0 g of calcium carbonate. What volume of carbon dioxide forms at r.t.p.? (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40; molar gas volume = 24 dm³)
questions.explain: Mr of CaCO₃ = 100, so 5.0 g = 0.050 mol. The ratio CaCO₃ : CO₂ is 1 : 1, so volume = 0.050 × 24 = 1.2 dm³.

questions.q: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). What volume of 2.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid reacts exactly with 2.4 g of magnesium? (Ar: Mg = 24)
questions.explain: Moles of Mg = 2.4 ÷ 24 = 0.10 mol, so HCl needed = 0.20 mol. Volume = 0.20 ÷ 2.0 = 0.10 dm³ = 100 cm³.

questions.q: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l). What volume of oxygen reacts completely with 48 dm³ of hydrogen at r.t.p.?
questions.explain: The ratio H₂ : O₂ is 2 : 1, so the oxygen volume is half of 48 dm³ = 24 dm³.

questions.q: 12.8 g of copper reacts with oxygen to form 14.4 g of an oxide. What is the empirical formula of the oxide? (Ar: O = 16, Cu = 64)
questions.explain: Mass of oxygen = 14.4 − 12.8 = 1.6 g. Moles: Cu = 12.8 ÷ 64 = 0.20; O = 1.6 ÷ 16 = 0.10. The ratio is 2 : 1, so Cu₂O.

questions.q: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. What mass of water forms when 8.0 g of methane burns completely? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explain: 8.0 g ÷ 16 g/mol = 0.50 mol of CH₄. The ratio CH₄ : H₂O is 1 : 2, so 1.0 mol of H₂O = 18 g.

questions.q: Which sample contains the largest number of molecules? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16)
questions.explain: 4 g of H₂ is 2 mol. 32 g of O₂, 44 g of CO₂ and 17 g of NH₃ are each 1 mol.

questions.q: 0.10 mol of a solute is dissolved in water to make 250 cm³ of solution. What is the concentration in mol/dm³?
questions.explain: 250 cm³ = 0.250 dm³. Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 0.10 ÷ 0.250 = 0.40 mol/dm³.

questions.q: 10 g of calcium carbonate is heated: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. 4.2 g of calcium oxide is obtained. What is the percentage yield? (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40)
questions.explain: 10 g = 0.10 mol of CaCO₃, so the theoretical yield is 0.10 mol of CaO = 5.6 g. Percentage yield = 4.2 ÷ 5.6 × 100 = 75%.

questions.q: What volume does 8.0 g of oxygen gas, O₂, occupy at r.t.p.? (Ar: O = 16; molar gas volume = 24 dm³)
questions.explain: Moles of O₂ = 8.0 ÷ 32 = 0.25 mol. Volume = 0.25 × 24 = 6.0 dm³.

questions.q: A solution of hydrochloric acid has a concentration of 2 mol/dm³ and another has a concentration of 0.2 mol/dm³. Which statement is correct?
options: The 2 mol/dm³ solution contains twice as many moles of HCl in every 1 dm³
Both solutions contain the same number of moles of HCl in every 1 dm³
The 0.2 mol/dm³ solution contains more moles of HCl in every 1 dm³
The 2 mol/dm³ solution contains ten times as many moles of HCl in every 1 dm³
questions.explain: 2 ÷ 0.2 = 10, so the stronger solution has ten times as many moles per dm³.

questions.q: A reaction should give 12.5 g of a product, but only 10.0 g is obtained. What is the percentage yield?
questions.explain: Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100 = 10.0 ÷ 12.5 × 100 = 80%.

questions.q: 4.8 g of magnesium is heated with 1.6 g of oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Which statement is correct? (Ar: O = 16, Mg = 24)
options: Oxygen is the limiting reactant and 8.0 g of magnesium oxide forms
Magnesium is the limiting reactant and 8.0 g of magnesium oxide forms
Magnesium is the limiting reactant and 4.0 g of magnesium oxide forms
Oxygen is the limiting reactant and 4.0 g of magnesium oxide forms
questions.explain: Mg = 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.20 mol and O₂ = 1.6 ÷ 32 = 0.050 mol. 0.050 mol O₂ needs only 0.10 mol Mg, so oxygen limits and 0.10 mol MgO (40 g/mol) = 4.0 g forms.

questions.q: 2.0 mol of nitrogen reacts with 3.0 mol of hydrogen: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. What is the maximum amount of ammonia that can form?
questions.explain: 3.0 mol of H₂ is the limiting reactant (it needs only 1.0 mol of N₂). The ratio H₂ : NH₃ is 3 : 2, so NH₃ = 3.0 × 2/3 = 2.0 mol.

questions.q: A solution has a concentration of 12 g/dm³. What volume of this solution contains 6 g of the solute?
questions.explain: Volume = mass ÷ concentration = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 dm³ = 500 cm³.

questions.q: Which statement correctly defines electrolysis?
options: The production of an electric current from a chemical reaction between two different metals
The decomposition of any compound by heating it until it melts
The decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by passing an electric current through it
The joining of two elements to form an ionic compound using an electric current
questions.explain: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to break down an ionic compound that is molten or dissolved in water. The ions must be free to move.

questions.q: In a simple electrolytic cell, which description of the anode is correct?
options: The molten or aqueous substance that is decomposed
The wire that joins the cell to the power supply
questions.explain: The anode is the electrode connected to the positive terminal of the power supply. The negative electrode is the cathode.

questions.q: In electrolysis, which electrode is the cathode?
options: The positive electrode, which attracts positive ions
The negative electrode, which attracts negative ions
The negative electrode, which attracts positive ions
The positive electrode, where non-metals form
questions.explain: The cathode is connected to the negative terminal, so it attracts positively charged ions (metal ions or hydrogen ions).

questions.q: What is the electrolyte in an electrolysis experiment?
options: The solid rod that carries current into the cell
The battery or power supply that provides the current
The molten or aqueous substance that undergoes electrolysis
The gas given off at one of the electrodes
questions.explain: The electrolyte is the liquid or solution containing mobile ions that is decomposed by the current.

questions.q: Which sample cannot be electrolysed?
questions.explain: In a solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, so no ions are free to carry charge. Molten or aqueous ionic compounds can be electrolysed.

questions.q: Why does molten lead(II) bromide conduct electricity when solid lead(II) bromide does not?
options: The ions are formed only when the compound melts
Electrons are free to move when the compound melts
The ions are free to move when the compound is molten
The compound changes into a metal when it melts
questions.explain: Solid ionic compounds have ions fixed in a lattice. When molten, the ions are mobile and carry the current.

questions.q: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Bromine at the cathode and lead at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Lead at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
questions.explain: Lead is a metal so it forms at the negative cathode. Bromine is a non-metal so it forms at the positive anode.

questions.q: Which observation is made at the anode during the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide with graphite electrodes?
options: Red-brown fumes of bromine are seen
A silvery bead of molten lead forms
Colourless bubbles of hydrogen are seen
A pale green gas that bleaches litmus is seen
questions.explain: Bromide ions lose electrons at the anode to form bromine, which is a red-brown vapour.

questions.q: Which observation is made at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide with graphite electrodes?
options: A pink-brown solid coats the electrode
A silver-grey bead of molten lead forms
questions.explain: Lead ions gain electrons at the cathode to form lead metal, which is molten at the temperature of the experiment.

questions.q: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form at the cathode and anode?
options: Sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
questions.explain: Hydrogen ions from water are discharged at the cathode in preference to sodium ions. Chloride ions in concentrated solution are discharged at the anode as chlorine.

questions.q: Which test and result show that a gas is chlorine?
options: A lighted splint goes out with a squeaky pop
questions.explain: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper. Relighting a glowing splint tests for oxygen, and a squeaky pop tests for hydrogen.

questions.q: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which test confirms the gas formed at the cathode?
options: A lighted splint burns with a squeaky pop
questions.explain: The gas at the cathode is hydrogen, which gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

questions.q: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which gas forms at the anode and how is it identified?
options: Oxygen, which gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint
Hydrogen, which relights a glowing splint
Oxygen, which relights a glowing splint
Sulfur dioxide, which bleaches damp litmus paper
questions.explain: Oxygen is formed at the anode, and it relights a glowing splint.

questions.q: Which row correctly shows the products of the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid with inert electrodes?
questions.explain: Hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, because water is effectively being decomposed.

questions.q: Which statement about the products of electrolysis is correct?
options: Metals form at the anode, and non-metals form at the cathode
Metals or hydrogen form at the cathode, and non-metals other than hydrogen form at the anode
Hydrogen forms at the anode, and metals form at the cathode
questions.explain: Positive ions (metal ions or H⁺) move to the cathode and gain electrons. Negative ions (non-metal ions) move to the anode.

questions.q: Molten potassium iodide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Iodine at the cathode and potassium at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and iodine at the anode
Potassium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Potassium at the cathode and iodine at the anode
questions.explain: A molten binary ionic compound gives the metal at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.

questions.q: Molten zinc chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Chlorine at the cathode and zinc at the anode
Zinc at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Zinc at the cathode and hydrogen at the anode
questions.explain: Zn²⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode and form zinc. Cl⁻ ions are attracted to the anode and form chlorine.

questions.q: Which compound gives a metal at the cathode and oxygen at the anode when it is electrolysed in the molten state?
questions.explain: Lead(II) oxide contains Pb²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, so it forms lead and oxygen. The others contain chloride or bromide ions, or no metal.

questions.q: Why are metal objects such as car bumpers electroplated?
options: To make them more dense and heavier
To make them conduct electricity better
To make them react more quickly with oxygen
To improve their appearance and resistance to corrosion
questions.explain: Electroplating covers an object with a thin layer of a metal that looks attractive and protects the object underneath from corrosion.

questions.q: A steel object is to be electroplated with nickel. How should the object be connected?
options: As the anode, in a solution containing nickel ions
As the cathode, in molten nickel(II) oxide
As the cathode, in a solution containing nickel ions
As the anode, in distilled water
questions.explain: The object to be plated is the cathode so that positive nickel ions are attracted to it and gain electrons.

questions.q: A steel spoon is to be silver-plated. Which row gives a correct set-up?
options: silver rod | spoon | silver nitrate solution
spoon | silver rod | silver nitrate solution
spoon | silver rod | sodium chloride solution
spoon | carbon rod | copper(II) sulfate solution
questions.explain: The spoon is the cathode, the plating metal (silver) is the anode, and the electrolyte contains silver ions.

questions.q: Why are graphite electrodes often used in electrolysis?
options: They dissolve easily so the electrolyte is replaced
They conduct electricity and do not react with most electrolytes
They are positive ions that move into the solution
They have a lower melting point than metals
questions.explain: Graphite is inert and conducts electricity because of its delocalised electrons, so it carries current without taking part in the reaction.

questions.q: A nickel layer is to be electroplated onto an iron fork. Which material should be used as the anode?
questions.explain: The anode is made of the plating metal, so nickel is used. Nickel dissolves and replaces the nickel ions removed at the cathode.

questions.q: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes. How does the volume of hydrogen collected compare with the volume of oxygen?
options: The volume of hydrogen is half the volume of oxygen
The volume of hydrogen is four times the volume of oxygen
The volume of hydrogen is twice the volume of oxygen
questions.explain: Water is decomposed: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, so two volumes of hydrogen form for each volume of oxygen.

questions.q: Which electrolysis gives a metal at the cathode and a non-metal other than a halogen at the anode?
questions.explain: Molten lead(II) oxide gives lead and oxygen. Molten sodium chloride gives a halogen, and the two aqueous electrolytes give hydrogen at the cathode.

questions.q: Which observations are made when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes?
options: Silvery metal at the cathode and pale green gas at the anode
Red-brown fumes at the anode and silvery metal at the cathode
Colourless gas at the cathode and pale green gas at the anode
questions.explain: Hydrogen (colourless) forms at the cathode and chlorine (pale green) forms at the anode.

questions.q: As dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes for a long time, what happens to the acid solution?
options: It becomes more dilute because sulfate ions are used up
Its concentration stays the same because acid is only a catalyst
It turns into sulfur and hydrogen
It becomes more concentrated because water is used up
questions.explain: Only water is decomposed to hydrogen and oxygen, so the same amount of acid is left in less water.

questions.q: Which of these elements is formed at the anode during electrolysis?
questions.explain: Non-metals other than hydrogen form at the anode. Metals and hydrogen form at the cathode.

questions.q: Two graphite rods dip into molten lead(II) bromide and are joined to a battery and a lamp. The lamp lights. What does this show?
options: Graphite rods dissolve in lead(II) bromide
questions.explain: A lit lamp shows a complete circuit, so the molten ionic compound allows current to flow because its ions are mobile.

questions.q: A key is copper-plated using a copper anode and copper(II) sulfate solution. What is seen at the key?
options: A pink-brown layer of copper forms on it
Bubbles of hydrogen form on it
A blue solid forms on it
questions.explain: The key is the cathode, where Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons to form copper metal, a pink-brown solid.

questions.q: Molten sodium bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Sodium at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Bromine at the cathode and sodium at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
questions.explain: Sodium is a metal, forming at the cathode. Bromine is a non-metal, forming at the anode.

questions.q: Which electrolyte could be used to electroplate a brass object with copper?
questions.explain: The electrolyte must contain ions of the plating metal, so a solution of a copper salt is needed.

questions.q: Molten zinc iodide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which product forms at the anode?
questions.explain: Iodide ions are non-metal ions and are attracted to the anode, where they form iodine.

questions.q: Which pair of materials are both suitable for use as inert electrodes?
questions.explain: Platinum and graphite do not react during electrolysis. Reactive metals such as zinc or magnesium can react or dissolve.

questions.q: An iron object is nickel-plated. What happens to the mass of the object during the plating?
options: It increases because nickel is deposited on it
It stays the same because the nickel replaces iron
It increases because hydrogen forms on it
questions.explain: Nickel ions gain electrons at the object, which is the cathode, so a layer of nickel metal builds up on it.

questions.q: During electrolysis, which statement describes the movement of electrons in the external circuit?
options: Electrons flow through the wires from the anode to the cathode, via the power supply
Electrons flow through the wires from the cathode to the anode, via the power supply
Electrons flow through the electrolyte from the anode to the cathode
Electrons flow through the electrolyte from the cathode to the anode
questions.explain: Electrons are released at the anode, pass through the wires and the power supply, and arrive at the cathode. They do not travel through the electrolyte.

questions.q: Which statement about the transfer of charge in the electrolyte is correct?
options: Positive ions move to the cathode and negative ions move to the anode
Electrons move through the electrolyte to the anode
Positive ions move to the anode and negative ions move to the cathode
Only negative ions are free to move
questions.explain: The electrolyte conducts by movement of ions. Oppositely charged electrodes attract them.

questions.q: Which statement about the electrode reactions in electrolysis is correct?
options: Ions lose electrons at the cathode (oxidation) and gain electrons at the anode (reduction)
Ions gain electrons at both electrodes
Ions gain electrons at the cathode (reduction) and lose electrons at the anode (oxidation)
Ions lose electrons at both electrodes
questions.explain: Positive ions are reduced by gaining electrons at the cathode. Negative ions are oxidised by losing electrons at the anode.

questions.q: Which half-equation represents the reaction at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide?
questions.explain: Each Pb²⁺ ion gains two electrons to become a lead atom. Electrons are on the left because this is reduction.

questions.q: Which half-equation represents the reaction at the anode during the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide?
questions.explain: Bromide ions lose electrons (oxidation). Two ions are needed to form one Br₂ molecule, so two electrons are released.

questions.q: Which half-equation represents the reaction at the cathode during the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid?
questions.explain: Hydrogen ions gain electrons at the cathode to form hydrogen molecules. Two ions and two electrons are needed per H₂.

questions.q: Which half-equation represents the reaction at the anode during the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride?
questions.explain: Chloride ions lose electrons at the anode. The equation must balance for atoms and for charge: 2 × (−1) = 0 + 2 × (−1).

questions.q: Which half-equation represents the formation of oxygen at the anode during the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid?
questions.explain: Hydroxide ions from water lose electrons. Check atoms and charge: 4 O, 4 H and four negative charges on each side balance.

questions.q: Aluminium forms at the cathode according to Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al. How many moles of electrons are needed to form 2 mol of aluminium?
questions.explain: Each Al³⁺ needs 3 electrons, so 2 mol of aluminium needs 2 × 3 = 6 mol of electrons.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid with inert electrodes, 48 cm³ of hydrogen is collected at the cathode. What volume of oxygen forms at the anode under the same conditions?
questions.explain: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ gives a 2 : 1 volume ratio of hydrogen to oxygen, so the oxygen volume is 48 ÷ 2 = 24 cm³.

questions.q: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using carbon electrodes. Which products form?
options: Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Copper at the cathode and sulfur dioxide at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and copper at the anode
Copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
questions.explain: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu²⁺ ions are discharged at the cathode. Sulfate ions are not discharged, so hydroxide ions from water form oxygen at the anode.

questions.q: What colour change is seen in aqueous copper(II) sulfate during electrolysis with carbon electrodes?
options: The blue colour gets darker because copper builds up
The blue colour stays the same because the electrodes are inert
The blue colour fades because Cu²⁺ ions are removed
The solution turns green because chlorine forms
questions.explain: Blue Cu²⁺ ions are discharged at the cathode as copper and are not replaced, so the solution becomes paler.

questions.q: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using copper electrodes. Which row correctly describes the changes?
options: increases in mass | decreases in mass | stays blue
decreases in mass | increases in mass | stays blue
decreases in mass | increases in mass | fades
no change in mass | increases in mass | fades
questions.explain: The copper anode dissolves as Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ and copper is deposited on the cathode. Cu²⁺ ions are removed and replaced at the same rate, so the blue colour stays.

questions.q: Which half-equation represents the reaction at a copper anode during the electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate?
questions.explain: A copper anode takes part in the reaction. Copper atoms lose two electrons and dissolve as Cu²⁺ ions.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate with copper electrodes, why does the blue colour of the solution not fade?
options: No ions are discharged at the cathode
Copper electrodes are inert, so the solution is not changed
Cu²⁺ ions form at the anode as fast as they are removed at the cathode
Sulfate ions are changed into copper(II) ions
questions.explain: The anode reaction Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ replaces the Cu²⁺ ions that the cathode reaction Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu removes.

questions.q: Concentrated aqueous potassium bromide is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Potassium at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Potassium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
questions.explain: Hydrogen is less reactive than potassium, so H⁺ ions are discharged at the cathode. In concentrated solution the halide ion is discharged at the anode.

questions.q: Dilute aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
questions.explain: In a dilute halide solution, hydroxide ions rather than halide ions are discharged at the anode, giving oxygen. Hydrogen forms at the cathode.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the electrolysis of concentrated and dilute aqueous sodium chloride using inert electrodes?
options: Chlorine forms at the anode from both solutions
Oxygen forms at the anode from the concentrated solution but chlorine forms from the dilute solution
Chlorine forms at the anode from the concentrated solution but oxygen forms from the dilute solution
Sodium forms at the cathode from the dilute solution but hydrogen forms from the concentrated solution
questions.explain: A high concentration of Cl⁻ ions means they are discharged at the anode. In dilute solution OH⁻ ions are discharged instead. Hydrogen forms at the cathode in both.

questions.q: Which element forms at the cathode when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes?
questions.explain: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions from the water are discharged at the cathode instead.

questions.q: Which electrolyte should be used to silver-plate a ring?
options: A solution containing silver ions, such as silver nitrate
questions.explain: The electrolyte for plating must contain ions of the plating metal so that they can be discharged at the cathode.

questions.q: Which solution is not an electrolyte?
questions.explain: Glucose is a covalent molecule and gives no ions in water. The other solutions contain mobile ions.

questions.q: In which electrolysis would a gas that relights a glowing splint form at the anode?
options: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride with inert electrodes
Dilute sulfuric acid with inert electrodes
Molten lead(II) bromide with inert electrodes
Molten zinc chloride with inert electrodes
questions.explain: Only dilute sulfuric acid gives oxygen at the anode. The other electrolytes give halogens.

questions.q: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Chlorine at the cathode and sodium at the anode
questions.explain: There is no water in the molten compound, so the only ions are Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

questions.q: How can an iron nail be electroplated with zinc?
options: Use the nail as the anode and zinc as the cathode in a solution of a zinc salt
Use the nail as the cathode and graphite as the anode in distilled water
Heat the nail in molten zinc and pass a current through it
Use the nail as the cathode and zinc as the anode in a solution of a zinc salt
questions.explain: The object to be plated is made the cathode and the anode is the plating metal. The electrolyte contains ions of the plating metal.

questions.q: Which statement about electroplating is correct?
options: A thin layer of metal is deposited on the anode
A thin layer of metal is deposited on the cathode
The object being plated is made the positive electrode
The electrolyte must be a molten non-metal
questions.explain: Positive metal ions are attracted to the negative cathode, which is the object being plated.

questions.q: Why should the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide be done in a fume cupboard?
options: The electrodes give off carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Bromine is a poisonous red-brown vapour, so it must be removed safely.

questions.q: Which metal forms at the cathode when molten magnesium bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes?
questions.explain: Mg²⁺ ions are positive, so they move to the cathode and become magnesium atoms.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide with inert electrodes?
questions.explain: Bromine is a non-metal and forms at the anode as red-brown fumes. Lead forms at the cathode.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid, 20 cm³ of oxygen is collected at the anode. What volume of hydrogen forms at the cathode, measured under the same conditions?
questions.explain: The ratio of hydrogen to oxygen is 2 : 1 (2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂), so hydrogen is 2 × 20 = 40 cm³.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, which ion moves towards the anode?
questions.explain: The anode is positive and attracts negative ions, which are the bromide ions.

questions.q: Which half-equation shows oxidation?
questions.explain: Oxidation is loss of electrons. Only the chloride half-equation has electrons on the product side.

questions.q: Which half-equation shows reduction?
questions.explain: Reduction is gain of electrons, so the electrons appear on the left-hand side, as in Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag.

questions.q: Which half-equation represents the reaction at the cathode in the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride?
questions.explain: Each Na⁺ ion gains one electron. The other equations are not balanced for charge or have electrons on the wrong side.

questions.q: Which half-equation represents the reaction at the anode in the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide?
questions.explain: Two oxide ions form one O₂ molecule and release 4 electrons. Check charge: −4 on the left and −4 on the right.

questions.q: Concentrated aqueous potassium iodide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
questions.explain: Hydrogen ions are discharged at the cathode because hydrogen is less reactive than potassium. In a concentrated halide solution, iodine forms at the anode.

questions.q: Why is hydrogen, not sodium, formed at the cathode when aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed?
options: Hydrogen is less reactive than sodium, so H⁺ ions are discharged more easily
Sodium is less reactive than hydrogen, so Na⁺ ions are discharged more easily
Sodium reacts with chlorine as soon as it forms
Sodium ions are not present in the solution
questions.explain: In aqueous solutions, the less reactive element is discharged at the cathode. Hydrogen is below sodium in the reactivity series.

questions.q: Concentrated aqueous copper(II) chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products form?
options: Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Copper at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
questions.explain: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu²⁺ is discharged at the cathode. Cl⁻ is discharged at the anode in a concentrated solution.

questions.q: What happens to the acidity of aqueous copper(II) sulfate during electrolysis with carbon electrodes?
options: It becomes more acidic because H⁺ ions are left in the solution
It becomes more alkaline because OH⁻ ions are left in the solution
It stays neutral because only copper is removed
It becomes more acidic because SO₄²⁻ ions are removed
questions.explain: OH⁻ ions are removed as oxygen at the anode, leaving H⁺ ions with the sulfate ions, so sulfuric acid forms.

questions.q: Which pair of half-equations shows the reactions in aqueous copper(II) sulfate with carbon electrodes?
options: Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; anode: 2OH⁻ → H₂O + O₂ + 2e⁻
questions.explain: Copper ions are reduced at the cathode and hydroxide ions oxidised at the anode. The final option is not balanced (two OH⁻ cannot give H₂O and O₂).

questions.q: How many moles of electrons are needed to deposit 0.25 mol of copper from aqueous copper(II) sulfate?
questions.explain: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu needs 2 mol of electrons per mole of copper, so 0.25 × 2 = 0.50 mol.

questions.q: 1.28 g of copper is deposited at the cathode. The relative atomic mass of copper is 64. How many moles of electrons were transferred?
questions.explain: Moles of Cu = 1.28 ÷ 64 = 0.020 mol. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu so electrons = 2 × 0.020 = 0.040 mol.

questions.q: In the electrolytic purification of copper, which happens at the impure copper anode?
questions.explain: The copper anode takes part, losing electrons to form Cu²⁺ ions. Pure copper is deposited on the cathode.

questions.q: A steel spoon is silver-plated in silver nitrate solution. What reaction occurs at the spoon?
questions.explain: The spoon is the cathode, where silver ions gain electrons (reduction) and form silver metal.

questions.q: A nickel anode is used to nickel-plate an object. Which pair of half-equations describes the changes?
options: Anode: Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni; cathode: Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻
Anode: Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode: Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni
questions.explain: Nickel metal is oxidised at the anode and nickel ions are reduced at the cathode, so the concentration of nickel ions stays constant.

questions.q: Which equation represents the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide?
questions.explain: Lead(II) bromide decomposes into lead and bromine molecules. The equation PbBr₂ → Pb + Br₂ has one Pb and two Br on each side.

questions.q: Which equation represents the overall reaction in the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride?
questions.explain: Two formula units give two sodium atoms and one chlorine molecule. The atoms balance: 2 Na and 2 Cl on each side.

questions.q: Which row correctly shows the products of electrolysing different sodium chloride electrolytes using inert electrodes?
options: concentrated aqueous sodium chloride | sodium | chlorine
concentrated aqueous sodium chloride | hydrogen | oxygen
questions.explain: The molten compound contains only Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. In the concentrated solution hydrogen forms at the cathode, and chlorine at the anode.

questions.q: Why does electroplating iron with chromium help to prevent rusting?
options: Chromium ions react with the iron to make it dense
Chromium is a gas that fills the iron's pores
The current makes the iron unreactive
The chromium layer keeps oxygen and water away from the iron
questions.explain: Rusting needs both oxygen and water. A coating of unreactive metal on the surface stops them reaching the iron.

questions.q: Which ions are present in molten lead(II) bromide?
questions.explain: Lead(II) bromide has the formula PbBr₂, made of Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions in a 1 : 2 ratio.

questions.q: Which row correctly shows the colour of a gas and the test used for it?
options: hydrogen | colourless | relights a glowing splint
chlorine | pale green | bleaches damp litmus paper
oxygen | pale green | squeaky pop with a lighted splint
questions.explain: Chlorine is a pale green gas that bleaches damp litmus paper. Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop. Oxygen relights a glowing splint.

questions.q: Which element could be formed at the cathode during electrolysis?
questions.explain: Hydrogen and metals form at the cathode. Oxygen, chlorine and bromine are non-metals that form at the anode.

questions.q: Which element is formed at the anode in the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid?
questions.explain: Oxygen is a non-metal and forms at the anode. Hydrogen forms at the cathode.

questions.q: A bracelet is to be plated with nickel. What must the electrolyte contain?
questions.explain: The metal ions in the electrolyte are discharged at the cathode, so they must be ions of the plating metal.

questions.q: Which equation represents the overall reaction during the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid with inert electrodes?
questions.explain: Water is decomposed, so the acid acts only as a source of ions. The equation is balanced with 4 H and 2 O on each side.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate, a copper anode replaces a carbon anode. How does the change at the anode differ?
options: Oxygen is no longer produced, and the anode dissolves
More oxygen is produced at the anode
Hydrogen is produced at the anode
Copper is deposited on the anode
questions.explain: Copper atoms are oxidised more easily than hydroxide ions, so the anode dissolves as Cu²⁺ and no oxygen forms.

questions.q: Which ions are present in aqueous copper(II) sulfate?
questions.explain: The salt gives Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions, and a little water also ionises into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions.

questions.q: In concentrated aqueous sodium chloride, why are chloride ions discharged at the anode rather than hydroxide ions?
options: Chloride ions are less negatively charged than hydroxide ions
Hydroxide ions are not present in water
Chloride ions are present in much higher concentration than hydroxide ions
Chloride ions are smaller than hydroxide ions
questions.explain: In a concentrated halide solution the halide ion is discharged in preference to OH⁻. In dilute solution, hydroxide ions are discharged instead.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the movement of charge during electrolysis?
questions.explain: The metal wires and electrodes conduct by movement of electrons. The electrolyte conducts by movement of ions.

questions.q: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. 3 mol of chlorine gas, Cl₂, are formed at the anode. How many moles of electrons are released at the anode?
questions.explain: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ releases 2 mol of electrons per mole of Cl₂, so 3 × 2 = 6 mol.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, which ion is oxidised and which is reduced?
options: Br⁻ is reduced and Pb²⁺ is oxidised
Br⁻ is oxidised and Pb²⁺ is reduced
questions.explain: Bromide ions lose electrons (oxidation) at the anode. Lead ions gain electrons (reduction) at the cathode.

questions.q: Concentrated aqueous copper(II) chloride is electrolysed using carbon electrodes. Which observations are made?
options: Colourless bubbles form at the cathode and a pale green gas at the anode
A pink-brown solid forms at the cathode and a pale green gas at the anode
A pink-brown solid forms at the cathode and colourless bubbles at the anode
Colourless bubbles form at both electrodes
questions.explain: Copper forms at the cathode as a pink-brown solid. Chlorine, a pale green gas, forms at the anode.

questions.q: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is electrolysed using carbon electrodes. Which products form?
options: Chlorine at the cathode and hydrogen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Oxygen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
questions.explain: Hydrogen ions are discharged at the cathode. In concentrated solution chloride ions are discharged at the anode as chlorine.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, which row correctly describes an ion?
questions.explain: Positive Pb²⁺ ions are attracted to the negative cathode, where they gain electrons.

questions.q: Which substances are used by a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell to produce electricity?
questions.explain: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is supplied with hydrogen as the fuel and oxygen, usually from air.

questions.q: What is the only chemical product of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
questions.explain: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form only water, so there are no carbon-containing products.

questions.q: Which equation represents the overall reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
questions.explain: Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water. The equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O is balanced with two atoms of oxygen on each side.

questions.q: What energy change takes place in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
options: Chemical energy is changed into electrical energy
Electrical energy is changed into chemical energy
Heat energy is changed into chemical energy
Light energy is changed into electrical energy
questions.explain: The reaction between hydrogen and oxygen releases energy, which the cell supplies as electricity.

questions.q: Which substances are fed into a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
options: Hydrogen and oxygen mixed together at both electrodes
Water at one electrode and carbon dioxide at the other
Hydrogen at one electrode and oxygen at the other
questions.explain: Hydrogen is fed to one electrode and oxygen to the other, so the reaction produces a flow of charge.

questions.q: Unlike a petrol engine, a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell does not release which gas when it is in use?
questions.explain: Petrol is a hydrocarbon and releases carbon dioxide when burned. The fuel cell has no carbon in its fuel.

questions.q: Which statement about the electricity produced by a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is correct?
options: It is produced continuously while hydrogen and oxygen are supplied
It is stored in the cell and the cell must be recharged
It requires mains electricity to start the reaction
It stops when the electrodes dissolve
questions.explain: A fuel cell is not recharged. It keeps producing electricity as long as the reactants are fed in.

questions.q: Which substance is the fuel in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
questions.explain: Hydrogen is the substance that is oxidised, so it is the fuel. Oxygen is the other reactant, and water is the product.

questions.q: Where does a hydrogen fuel cell car usually get its oxygen from?
options: The decomposition of water in the engine
questions.explain: Air contains about 21% oxygen, so there is no need for the car to carry oxygen.

questions.q: What is the electricity from a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell used for in a fuel cell car?
options: To burn hydrogen in a cylinder
questions.explain: The cell produces electricity, which drives an electric motor to move the vehicle.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell car compared with a petrol car?
options: Hydrogen is easier to store and transport than petrol
The only waste product is water, so no carbon dioxide is released during use
There are more refuelling stations for hydrogen
The fuel cell never needs oxygen
questions.explain: Petrol burning releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. The fuel cell forms only water.

questions.q: Which statement describes a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
options: A cell that stores electricity and is recharged using hydrogen
A cell that uses a continuous supply of hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity
A cell that burns hydrogen to heat water
A cell that makes hydrogen by electrolysing water
questions.explain: A fuel cell converts the chemical energy of a fuel directly into electricity. It does not store charge like a rechargeable battery.

questions.q: Which row correctly compares the waste released from the exhaust of two vehicles?
options: hydrogen fuel cell car | hydrogen | carbon dioxide
hydrogen fuel cell car | hydrogen | water
questions.explain: A fuel cell car releases only water. A petrol car also releases carbon dioxide, and pollutants such as carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides.

questions.q: What is stored in the tank of a hydrogen fuel cell car?
questions.explain: The fuel is hydrogen. The oxygen is taken from the air.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cell cars compared with petrol cars?
options: They need to be recharged for many hours
Hydrogen is a flammable gas that is difficult to store
questions.explain: Hydrogen has a very low density, so it is stored under high pressure, and it forms explosive mixtures with air.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell compared with a petrol engine?
options: It converts chemical energy to electrical energy more efficiently
It uses a fuel that is very easy to store
It is cheaper because hydrogen filling stations are widespread
questions.explain: A fuel cell changes the energy directly to electricity, wasting less as heat than a petrol engine.

questions.q: Which is a practical disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cell vehicles at present?
options: There are few places to refuel them
They produce large amounts of carbon dioxide
The only waste product is water
Petrol is cheaper to make from water
questions.explain: The refuelling network for hydrogen is much smaller than that for petrol, which limits how far and where drivers can go.

questions.q: Why might a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell car not be fully free of carbon dioxide emissions overall?
options: The fuel cell releases carbon dioxide from the air
Most hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide
Water formed in the cell breaks down to carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Hydrogen is often made from natural gas (methane), and this process releases carbon dioxide. The car itself emits none.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives an advantage and a disadvantage of hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell cars?
options: only water is produced | hydrogen is difficult to store safely
only water is produced | nitrogen oxides are produced
carbon dioxide is not produced | the fuel is not flammable
the fuel is easy to store | water is a harmful product
questions.explain: The only chemical product is water, which is an advantage. Storing hydrogen safely is difficult, which is a disadvantage.

questions.q: What happens to hydrogen in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
options: It is reduced by oxygen to form water
It is decomposed to form oxygen
It is oxidised by oxygen to form water
questions.explain: Hydrogen gains oxygen and loses electrons, so it is oxidised. The electron flow gives the electric current.

questions.q: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell uses the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. What volume of oxygen reacts with 12 dm³ of hydrogen, measured under the same conditions?
questions.explain: The equation shows 2 volumes of hydrogen react with 1 volume of oxygen, so oxygen = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 dm³.

questions.q: A fuel cell reacts 4.0 g of hydrogen completely with oxygen. What mass of water forms? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explain: Moles of H₂ = 4.0 ÷ 2 = 2.0 mol. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O gives 2.0 mol of H₂O, so mass = 2.0 × 18 = 36 g.

questions.q: A reaction pathway diagram shows reactants at 80 kJ/mol and products at 30 kJ/mol. What does the diagram show?
options: an exothermic reaction that releases 50 kJ/mol to the surroundings
an exothermic reaction that releases 110 kJ/mol to the surroundings
an endothermic reaction that takes in 50 kJ/mol from the surroundings
an endothermic reaction that takes in 110 kJ/mol from the surroundings
questions.explain: The products are lower than the reactants by 80 − 30 = 50 kJ/mol, so 50 kJ/mol is given out.

questions.q: What is shown on the vertical axis of a reaction pathway diagram?
questions.explain: A reaction pathway diagram plots the energy of the particles against the progress of the reaction.

questions.q: Which statement about the sign of ΔH is correct?
options: ΔH is positive for exothermic reactions and negative for endothermic reactions.
ΔH is positive for both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
ΔH is negative for both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions and positive for endothermic reactions.
questions.explain: A negative ΔH means the system loses energy to the surroundings; a positive ΔH means it gains energy.

questions.q: Which row is correct for respiration and photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Respiration releases energy, while photosynthesis takes in energy from sunlight.

questions.q: A pathway diagram has reactants at 120 kJ/mol and products at 200 kJ/mol. Which statement is correct?
options: 320 kJ/mol of thermal energy is given out to the surroundings.
80 kJ/mol of thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings.
320 kJ/mol of thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings.
80 kJ/mol of thermal energy is given out to the surroundings.
questions.explain: 200 − 120 = 80 kJ/mol higher for the products, so that much energy is absorbed.

questions.q: What is the definition of activation energy, Ea?
options: the minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react
the energy released when the products of a reaction are formed
the average kinetic energy of all the particles in the reaction mixture
the difference in energy between the reactants and the products
questions.explain: Particles that collide with less than the activation energy do not react.

questions.q: Which process is exothermic?
options: the combustion of methane in a Bunsen burner
the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate
the dissolving of ammonium nitrate in water
the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
questions.explain: Burning fuels releases a large amount of thermal energy; the other three take in energy and cool their surroundings.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes two chemical processes?
options: dissolving ammonium nitrate: exothermic | burning methane: exothermic
dissolving ammonium nitrate: exothermic | burning methane: endothermic
dissolving ammonium nitrate: endothermic | burning methane: endothermic
dissolving ammonium nitrate: endothermic | burning methane: exothermic
questions.explain: Ammonium nitrate dissolves with a fall in temperature, while burning methane releases heat.

questions.q: A catalyst is added to a reaction. Which row describes the effect on the activation energy and on ΔH?
options: Ea is lowered | ΔH becomes more negative
Ea is lowered | ΔH is unchanged
Ea is raised | ΔH is unchanged
Ea is unchanged | ΔH is lowered
questions.explain: A catalyst gives an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, but the energy levels of the reactants and the products do not change.

questions.q: The overall equation for aerobic respiration is C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Which statement is correct?
options: The reaction is exothermic and releases energy for the body.
The reaction is endothermic and releases energy for the body.
The reaction is endothermic and takes in energy from the body.
The reaction is exothermic and takes in energy from the body.
questions.explain: Respiration breaks down glucose and releases energy, so it is exothermic.

questions.q: The reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) has ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the reverse reaction, 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g)?
questions.explain: The reverse reaction takes in the same amount of energy that the forward reaction releases, so ΔH changes sign.

questions.q: Which of these processes takes in thermal energy from the surroundings?
options: the rusting of iron in a hand warmer
the thermal decomposition of limestone to make quicklime
the reaction of an acid with an alkali
the burning of coal in a power station
questions.explain: Quicklime production needs a kiln heated to a high temperature, so it is endothermic.

questions.q: During an investigation, which measurement would show that a reaction is exothermic?
options: The volume of the reaction mixture decreases.
The temperature of the reaction mixture decreases.
The temperature of the reaction mixture increases.
The mass of the reaction mixture increases.
questions.explain: A temperature increase of the mixture is the evidence of energy being released.

questions.q: In a reaction the bonds in the reactants are stronger overall than the bonds in the products. Which statement is correct?
options: The same energy is absorbed and released, so ΔH is positive.
More energy is absorbed breaking bonds than is released making bonds, so ΔH is negative.
More energy is absorbed breaking bonds than is released making bonds, so ΔH is positive.
More energy is released making bonds than is absorbed breaking bonds, so ΔH is positive.
questions.explain: Stronger bonds in reactants need more energy to break than the weaker product bonds return, giving a net absorption.

questions.q: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?
options: It transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
It transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
It takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
It takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
questions.explain: In an exothermic reaction thermal energy is given out to the surroundings, which warm up.

questions.q: Which statement about the chemical energy stored in the substances in an exothermic reaction is correct?
options: The products store more chemical energy than the reactants.
The products store less chemical energy than the reactants.
The reactants store no chemical energy.
The products store the same chemical energy as the reactants.
questions.explain: The energy lost from the chemical store is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy.

questions.q: Which description matches the reaction pathway diagram of an exothermic reaction?
options: The curve rises from the reactants to a peak and then falls to a products line that is lower than the reactants line.
The curve falls from the reactants to a minimum and then rises to a products line that is higher than the reactants line.
The curve rises from the reactants to a peak and then falls to a products line that is higher than the reactants line.
The curve is a straight horizontal line from the reactants to the products.
questions.explain: For exothermic reactions the products end at a lower energy level than the reactants.

questions.q: Hydrogen burns in oxygen: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g). Why can hydrogen be used as a rocket fuel?
options: The reaction is endothermic and releases a large amount of thermal energy.
The reaction is endothermic and takes in a large amount of thermal energy.
The reaction is exothermic and releases a large amount of thermal energy.
The reaction is exothermic and takes in a large amount of thermal energy.
questions.explain: Burning hydrogen is exothermic: energy released heats the exhaust gases and drives the rocket.

questions.q: Which description shows the effect of a catalyst on a reaction pathway diagram?
options: A second curve with a lower peak is drawn ending at a lower products level.
A second curve with a lower peak is drawn between the same reactants and products levels.
A second curve with the same peak is drawn between a lower products level.
A second curve with a higher peak is drawn between the same reactants and products levels.
questions.explain: The catalyst lowers Ea but does not change the starting or finishing energy levels, so ΔH is the same.

questions.q: Experiment 1: the temperature of the mixture goes from 18 °C to 27 °C. Experiment 2: the temperature of the mixture goes from 18 °C to 11 °C. Which row is correct?
questions.explain: A temperature rise (Exp. 1) means exothermic; a fall (Exp. 2) means endothermic.

questions.q: An instant cold pack for a sports injury contains solid ammonium nitrate and a bag of water. When the bag is broken the pack becomes cold. Why?
options: Dissolving ammonium nitrate is exothermic and gives out thermal energy to the surroundings.
Dissolving ammonium nitrate is endothermic and gives out thermal energy to the surroundings.
Dissolving ammonium nitrate is exothermic and takes in thermal energy from the surroundings.
Dissolving ammonium nitrate is endothermic and takes in thermal energy from the surroundings.
questions.explain: The pack cools because the process absorbs energy from the water and from the injured skin.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali?
options: endothermic | thermal energy transferred to surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases
exothermic | thermal energy transferred to surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases
endothermic | thermal energy taken in from surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases
exothermic | thermal energy taken in from surroundings | temperature of surroundings decreases
questions.explain: Neutralisation is exothermic: energy is given out and the temperature of the mixture goes up.

questions.q: In a reaction, the total energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants is 1860 kJ/mol. The total energy released when all the bonds in the products form is 1450 kJ/mol. What is ΔH and what type of reaction is it?
questions.explain: ΔH = 1860 − 1450 = +410 kJ/mol; a positive value means endothermic.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (C≡O 1077, O=O 498, C=O 805, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g).
After an exothermic reaction in a beaker, the temperature of the mixture rises to a maximum and then slowly falls back to room temperature. Why does it fall?
options: The products take in the thermal energy that the reactants gave out.
The reaction becomes endothermic after it has finished.
Thermal energy is gradually transferred from the mixture to the cooler surroundings.
Thermal energy is gradually transferred from the cooler surroundings to the mixture.
questions.explain: Once the reaction has finished the warm solution loses energy to the cooler surroundings until the temperatures equalise.
