questions.q: A student writes: 'Because this reaction is exothermic, the products have more energy than the reactants.' How can the statement be corrected?
options: Because this reaction is endothermic, the products have more energy than the reactants.
Because this reaction is exothermic, the temperature of the surroundings falls.
Because this reaction is exothermic, the products have less energy than the reactants.
Because this reaction is exothermic, thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings.
questions.explain: Exothermic means energy is released, so the products must end with less chemical energy.

questions.q: Which description matches the reaction pathway diagram of an endothermic reaction?
options: The curve rises from the reactants to a peak and then falls to a products line that is higher than the reactants line.
The curve is a straight horizontal line from the reactants to the products.
The curve rises from the reactants to a peak and then falls to a products line that is lower than the reactants line.
The curve falls from the reactants to a minimum and then rises to a products line that is lower than the reactants line.
questions.explain: For endothermic reactions the products end at a higher energy level than the reactants.

questions.q: A reaction pathway diagram shows reactants at 50 kJ/mol, a peak at 210 kJ/mol and products at 130 kJ/mol. What are the values of ΔH and Ea?
questions.explain: ΔH = 130 − 50 = +80 kJ/mol (endothermic); Ea = 210 − 50 = 160 kJ/mol.

questions.q: A student mixes two solutions in a polystyrene cup. The thermometer reading falls from 22 °C to 15 °C. What can be concluded?
options: The reaction is exothermic because thermal energy was taken in from the surroundings.
The reaction is exothermic because thermal energy was released to the surroundings.
The reaction is endothermic because thermal energy was released to the surroundings.
The reaction is endothermic because thermal energy was taken in from the surroundings.
questions.explain: A fall in temperature means energy flowed from the solution into the reaction, so it is endothermic.

questions.q: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated and turns white. When water is added to the white solid it turns blue again and the test tube becomes warm. Which row is correct?
columns: Adding water to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate
options: heating the blue solid: endothermic | adding water to the white solid: exothermic
heating the blue solid: exothermic | adding water to the white solid: endothermic
heating the blue solid: endothermic | adding water to the white solid: endothermic
heating the blue solid: exothermic | adding water to the white solid: exothermic
questions.explain: Heat is taken in to remove water (endothermic); the reverse reaction releases energy and warms the tube.

questions.q: Why are fuels such as natural gas burned in homes and power stations?
options: Combustion is endothermic and takes in thermal energy from the surroundings.
Combustion is exothermic and takes in thermal energy from the surroundings.
Combustion is endothermic and transfers thermal energy to the surroundings.
Combustion is exothermic and transfers thermal energy to the surroundings.
questions.explain: Fuels are useful because burning them releases large amounts of thermal energy.

questions.q: Which statement about reaction pathway diagrams is correct?
options: The horizontal axis shows the energy of the particles.
The products are always drawn lower than the reactants.
The height of the peak shows the temperature of the reaction.
The difference in height between the reactants and the products shows the energy transferred in the reaction.
questions.explain: The vertical gap between the reactants and the products levels gives the energy released or absorbed.

questions.q: Which statement explains why a reaction is exothermic in terms of bonds?
options: More energy is released when bonds form in the products than is needed to break the bonds in the reactants.
The bonds in the reactants are broken without any energy being needed.
The number of bonds broken is always greater than the number of bonds made.
More energy is needed to break the bonds in the reactants than is released when bonds form in the products.
questions.explain: If bond making releases more than bond breaking takes in, there is a net release of energy.

questions.q: A reaction pathway diagram for a reaction shows that the products are at a lower energy than the reactants. Which of these observations would also be seen?
options: The thermometer reading in the reaction mixture increases.
The thermometer reading in the reaction mixture decreases.
The reaction stops when heating is stopped.
The mass of the reaction mixture decreases.
questions.explain: A lower energy for the products means energy is released as heat, so the temperature goes up.

questions.q: For the reaction 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g), ΔH = −486 kJ/mol. How much thermal energy is released when 1 mol of hydrogen gas burns in excess oxygen?
questions.explain: The equation uses 2 mol of H₂ for 486 kJ released, so 1 mol releases 486 ÷ 2 = 243 kJ.

questions.q: In a reaction pathway diagram, the energy of the products is lower than the energy of the reactants. Which statement is correct?
options: The reaction takes in thermal energy from the surroundings.
The temperature of the surroundings decreases.
questions.explain: Products at a lower energy level means that energy was released to the surroundings.

questions.q: A student adds 2.0 g of a solid to water. The temperature of the water falls from 25.0 °C to 19.5 °C. What is the correct conclusion?
options: The dissolving is exothermic, and the temperature rose by 5.5 °C.
The dissolving is endothermic, and the temperature rose by 5.5 °C.
The dissolving is exothermic, and the temperature fell by 5.5 °C.
The dissolving is endothermic, and the temperature fell by 5.5 °C.
questions.explain: 25.0 − 19.5 = 5.5 °C fall in temperature, so thermal energy was taken in from the water.

questions.q: Why is a polystyrene cup with a lid used when measuring the temperature change of a reaction in solution?
options: to stop the reactants from reacting with the air
to reduce the transfer of thermal energy between the mixture and the surroundings
to increase the amount of thermal energy released by the reaction
questions.explain: Polystyrene is a good insulator, so less energy is lost to or gained from the room and the temperature change is measured more accurately.

questions.q: Which bonds are broken in the reaction C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g)?
options: one C–C bond and one H–H bond
one C=C bond and two C–H bonds
four C–H bonds and one H–H bond
one C=C bond (becoming C–C) and one H–H bond
questions.explain: Hydrogenation breaks the H–H bond and one of the two bonds in C=C; the bond left is C–C and two new C–H bonds form.

questions.q: Magnesium is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. The temperature of the mixture rises from 20 °C to 31 °C. What is the correct description of the reaction?
options: Endothermic, because thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings.
Endothermic, because the temperature of the mixture increases.
Exothermic, because thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings.
Exothermic, because thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings.
questions.explain: A temperature rise shows that thermal energy is given out, which is the definition of exothermic.

questions.q: In a reaction pathway diagram, the energy of the products is higher than the energy of the reactants. Which statement is correct?
options: The temperature of the surroundings increases.
The reaction releases thermal energy to the surroundings.
questions.explain: When products are at a higher energy level than reactants, energy has been taken in from the surroundings.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for 2HCl(g) → H₂(g) + Cl₂(g).
questions.explain: Broken: 2 × 432 = 864. Made: 436 + 243 = 679. ΔH = 864 − 679 = +185 kJ/mol, so the reaction is endothermic.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = +92 kJ/mol. Which description is correct?
options: The reaction is exothermic and the surroundings become colder.
The reaction is endothermic and the surroundings become warmer.
The reaction is exothermic and the surroundings become warmer.
The reaction is endothermic and the surroundings become colder.
questions.explain: A positive ΔH shows that thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings, which cool.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (H–H 436, O=O 498, O–H 464, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g).
A student increases the temperature of a reaction. What happens to the activation energy of the reaction?
questions.explain: Activation energy depends on the reaction pathway; a higher temperature just means more particles have energy greater than Ea.

questions.q: For H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(g), what is ΔH given that ΔH for 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g) is −486 kJ/mol?
questions.explain: The equation is halved so ΔH is halved: −486 ÷ 2 = −243 kJ/mol.

questions.q: A student mixes citric acid solution with sodium hydrogencarbonate. Bubbles are seen and the temperature falls by 6 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: Energy is transferred from the reaction to the surroundings.
The reaction is neither endothermic nor exothermic.
questions.explain: A fall in temperature means energy is absorbed from the surroundings.

questions.q: The enthalpy change for H₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2HF(g) is −542 kJ/mol. The bond energies are H–H 436 kJ/mol and F–F 158 kJ/mol. What is the bond energy of H–F?
A reaction pathway diagram shows reactants at 200 kJ/mol, a peak at 350 kJ/mol and products at 120 kJ/mol. What are the values of ΔH and Ea?
A reaction pathway diagram shows reactants at 100 kJ/mol, a peak at 250 kJ/mol and products at 40 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy for the reverse reaction?
questions.explain: The reverse reaction starts at the products level (40) and must climb to the peak (250): 250 − 40 = 210 kJ/mol.

questions.q: Magnesium burns in air with a bright white flame to form magnesium oxide. Which statement about the energy change is correct?
options: Thermal energy (and light) is released, so the reaction is exothermic.
Light is released, so the reaction is endothermic.
Thermal energy is absorbed, so the reaction is endothermic.
No energy is transferred because a solid is formed.
questions.explain: Burning in air gives out heat and light, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate?
options: exothermic | transferred to surroundings | surroundings become cooler
endothermic | transferred to surroundings | surroundings become warmer
endothermic | taken in from surroundings | surroundings become cooler
exothermic | taken in from surroundings | surroundings become cooler
questions.explain: Decomposing calcium carbonate needs heat to be supplied, so energy is taken in and the surroundings cool.

questions.q: In a reaction, the total energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants is 2800 kJ/mol and the total energy released when the bonds in the products form is 3300 kJ/mol. What is ΔH and what type of reaction is it?
questions.explain: ΔH = 2800 − 3300 = −500 kJ/mol; a negative value means exothermic.

questions.q: Which reaction mixture would you expect to get colder as the reaction proceeds?
options: dilute sulfuric acid added to sodium hydroxide solution
solid barium hydroxide and solid ammonium thiocyanate being stirred together
questions.explain: The reaction between barium hydroxide and ammonium thiocyanate is strongly endothermic, so the flask becomes very cold.

questions.q: What is the name given to the transfer of thermal energy during a chemical reaction?
questions.explain: ΔH is the symbol for the enthalpy change, the thermal energy transferred in a reaction.

questions.q: Which expression gives the enthalpy change of a reaction using bond energies?
options: ΔH = energy needed to break bonds + energy released when bonds form
ΔH = energy released when bonds form − energy needed to break bonds
ΔH = energy needed to break bonds − energy released when bonds form
ΔH = energy of the products ÷ energy of the reactants
questions.explain: Breaking bonds is endothermic (+) and making bonds is exothermic (−), so ΔH = broken − made.

questions.q: Nitrogen gas is very unreactive at room temperature, even though many of its reactions are exothermic. What is the best explanation?
options: The strong N≡N triple bond gives a very high activation energy.
The N≡N bond is so weak that it breaks again immediately.
All reactions of nitrogen are endothermic.
Nitrogen reactions have a ΔH of zero.
questions.explain: Large amounts of energy are needed to break the strong triple bond, so few collisions are energetic enough.

questions.q: A student claims, "Burning is endothermic because a match must be used to start it." Why is the student wrong?
options: Overall, burning transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so it is exothermic.
Overall, burning transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so it is endothermic.
Overall, burning takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so it is exothermic.
Overall, burning takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so it is endothermic.
questions.explain: The match only starts the reaction; once going, burning releases far more energy than it needs.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (H–H 436, I–I 151, H–I 299, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g).
Which pair of substances would give an increase in temperature when mixed in a beaker?
options: citric acid solution and sodium hydrogencarbonate
sodium hydroxide solution and dilute hydrochloric acid
questions.explain: Neutralisation is exothermic; the other three mixtures all cool down.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes a catalysed and an uncatalysed reaction pathway for the same reaction?
options: lower ΔH with a catalyst | same Ea
higher ΔH with a catalyst | lower Ea with a catalyst
same ΔH | higher Ea with a catalyst
same ΔH | lower Ea with a catalyst
questions.explain: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy without changing the overall energy change.

questions.q: A student adds a sample of an unknown solid to dilute acid and observes that the temperature of the mixture rises. Which row is correct?
options: endothermic | energy absorbed from the surroundings
exothermic | energy absorbed from the surroundings
endothermic | energy released to the surroundings
exothermic | energy released to the surroundings
questions.explain: A temperature rise means that thermal energy is given out, which defines an exothermic reaction.

questions.q: Many exothermic reactions, such as burning methane, do not start until a flame or spark is applied. What is the reason?
options: ΔH only becomes negative after the reaction is started.
The colliding particles must first be given enough energy to overcome the activation energy.
The reaction is actually endothermic until it has started.
The activation energy is released as soon as the reactants are mixed.
questions.explain: Even exothermic reactions have an energy barrier; the spark supplies the energy for the first collisions to react.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (H–H 436 kJ/mol, Cl–Cl 243 kJ/mol, H–Cl 432 kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g).
questions.explain: Bonds broken: 436 + 243 = 679. Bonds made: 2 × 432 = 864. ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ/mol.

questions.q: Which statement about endothermic reactions is correct?
options: The surroundings gain thermal energy and the products have more chemical energy than the reactants.
The surroundings gain thermal energy and the products have less chemical energy than the reactants.
The surroundings lose thermal energy and the products have more chemical energy than the reactants.
The surroundings lose thermal energy and the products have less chemical energy than the reactants.
questions.explain: Energy taken from the surroundings ends up stored in the products.

questions.q: Which statement about activation energy is correct?
options: Activation energy is equal to the energy released in an exothermic reaction.
Exothermic and endothermic reactions can both have a high or a low activation energy.
A reaction with a negative ΔH has no activation energy.
Exothermic reactions always have a lower activation energy than endothermic reactions.
questions.explain: Ea depends on the height of the peak above the reactants and is independent of the sign of ΔH.

questions.q: Which equation represents an endothermic reaction?
questions.explain: Thermal decomposition reactions are endothermic; combustion and neutralisation are exothermic.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes an exothermic reaction?
columns: Energy of products compared with reactants
options: thermal energy given out to surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases | energy of products higher than reactants
thermal energy given out to surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases | energy of products lower than reactants
thermal energy given out to surroundings | temperature of surroundings decreases | energy of products lower than reactants
thermal energy taken in from surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases | energy of products lower than reactants
questions.explain: In an exothermic reaction energy is released, the surroundings warm and the products end up lower in energy.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g).
On a reaction pathway diagram, which part represents the activation energy?
options: the energy of the reactants measured from the horizontal axis
the energy difference between the products and the highest point of the curve
the energy difference between the reactants and the highest point of the curve
the energy difference between the reactants and the products
questions.explain: Ea is the energy barrier that must be climbed from the reactants level up to the peak.

questions.q: A self-heating food can contains calcium oxide and water kept apart. When the two are mixed the can gets hot. What type of reaction takes place?
options: both exothermic and endothermic at the same time
questions.explain: The mixture gets hotter because thermal energy is released, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g).
On a reaction pathway diagram, a downward arrow drawn from the reactants level to the lower products level represents what?
options: the thermal energy released to the surroundings in the reaction
the thermal energy absorbed from the surroundings in the reaction
the time taken for the reaction
the temperature of the reaction mixture
questions.explain: The size of the drop in energy is the amount of energy transferred to the surroundings.

questions.q: Which is a use of an endothermic process?
options: using a self-heating can to warm soup
using an instant cold pack on a sprained ankle
using a hand warmer in winter
questions.explain: A cold pack works because dissolving the solid takes in thermal energy.

questions.q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium hydroxide solution. The temperature rises from 20.0 °C to 26.5 °C. What is the temperature change and the type of reaction?
questions.explain: 26.5 − 20.0 = 6.5 °C rise, showing that energy is given out, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: The temperature of the surroundings rises during a reaction. Which statement about the energy of the substances must be correct?
options: The products contain more energy than the reactants.
Thermal energy is transferred from the surroundings to the products as chemical energy.
No energy is transferred between the reactants and the surroundings.
Chemical energy is transferred from the reactants to the surroundings as thermal energy.
questions.explain: Surroundings gain energy only if the reacting chemicals have lost it.

questions.q: Zinc powder is added to copper(II) sulfate solution and the temperature rises by 8 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: The reaction takes in thermal energy from the solution.
The solution loses energy to the zinc.
questions.explain: A rise in temperature of the solution means thermal energy has been transferred to it, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes bond breaking and bond making?
options: bond breaking: endothermic | bond making: exothermic
bond breaking: exothermic | bond making: endothermic
bond breaking: exothermic | bond making: exothermic
bond breaking: endothermic | bond making: endothermic
questions.explain: Energy must be put in to break bonds, and energy is released when new bonds form.

questions.q: The equation for the combustion of methane is CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). Which statement is correct?
options: Thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings during the reaction.
The temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings during the reaction.
questions.explain: All combustion reactions are exothermic.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (H–H 436, Br–Br 193, H–Br 366, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for H₂(g) + Br₂(g) → 2HBr(g).
The enthalpy change for the reaction H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g) is −185 kJ/mol. What is the enthalpy change for 2H₂(g) + 2Cl₂(g) → 4HCl(g)?
questions.explain: The equation has been doubled, so twice as much energy is released: 2 × (−185) = −370 kJ/mol.

questions.q: A reaction pathway diagram shows reactants at 150 kJ/mol, a peak at 400 kJ/mol and products at 90 kJ/mol. What are ΔH and Ea?
Use the bond energies (C=C 614, H–H 436, C–C 347, C–H 413, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g).
Which statement about the surroundings is correct?
options: In both endothermic and exothermic reactions the surroundings lose thermal energy.
In an endothermic reaction the surroundings lose thermal energy; in an exothermic reaction they gain it.
In both endothermic and exothermic reactions the surroundings gain thermal energy.
In an endothermic reaction the surroundings gain thermal energy; in an exothermic reaction they lose it.
questions.explain: Energy is transferred from the reaction to the surroundings in exothermic changes, and the other way round in endothermic ones.

questions.q: Which process releases thermal energy to its surroundings?
options: the dissolving of ammonium chloride in water
the thermal decomposition of copper(II) carbonate
questions.explain: Respiration releases energy to the organism and its surroundings; the other processes absorb energy.

questions.q: A student holds a test tube while two solutions react in it. The tube feels cold. What is the explanation?
options: The reaction is endothermic and takes in thermal energy from the student's hand.
The reaction is exothermic and takes in thermal energy from the student's hand.
The reaction is endothermic and gives out thermal energy to the student's hand.
The reaction is exothermic and gives out thermal energy to the student's hand.
questions.explain: Cold means energy is leaving the surroundings and entering the reaction, so it is endothermic.

questions.q: Which statement about reactions is correct?
options: Reactions that produce a gas are always exothermic.
All reactions that need heating to start are endothermic.
Reactions in which the temperature of the surroundings rises are endothermic.
Reactions in which the temperature of the surroundings rises are exothermic.
questions.explain: The sign of the temperature change of the surroundings tells you the type of reaction; needing a start-up does not.

questions.q: Which row correctly links the sign of ΔH to the type of reaction and the effect on the surroundings?
options: ΔH negative | exothermic | surroundings get warmer
ΔH positive | exothermic | surroundings get colder
ΔH positive | endothermic | surroundings get warmer
ΔH negative | endothermic | surroundings get warmer
questions.explain: Negative ΔH = energy released = exothermic = surroundings warm up.

questions.q: Which statement describes an endothermic reaction?
options: It takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
It transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
It takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
It transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
questions.explain: An endothermic reaction absorbs thermal energy from its surroundings, which therefore get colder.

questions.q: Which reaction would make a thermometer in the mixture show the largest fall in temperature?
options: an exothermic reaction giving out a small amount of thermal energy
an endothermic reaction taking in a large amount of thermal energy
a reaction that gives out and takes in no thermal energy
an exothermic reaction giving out a large amount of thermal energy
questions.explain: The more energy an endothermic reaction absorbs, the bigger the temperature drop.

questions.q: Green copper(II) carbonate is heated in a test tube. It turns black as copper(II) oxide forms and carbon dioxide is given off. What type of reaction is this?
options: exothermic, because the solid changes colour
exothermic, because energy is continuously taken in from the burner
endothermic, because energy is continuously taken in from the burner
endothermic, because energy is released to the burner
questions.explain: Thermal decomposition needs a continual supply of heat, so it is endothermic.

questions.q: On a labelled reaction pathway diagram for an endothermic reaction, which two features are always drawn?
options: an arrow for Ea from the reactants level up to the peak, and an arrow for ΔH upward from the reactants level to the higher products level
an arrow for Ea from the reactants level to the products level, and an arrow for ΔH from the reactants level up to the peak
an arrow for Ea from the products level to the peak, and an arrow for ΔH downward from the reactants level to the lower products level
an arrow for Ea from the reactants level up to the peak, and an arrow for ΔH downward from the reactants level to the lower products level
questions.explain: For endothermic reactions the products sit above the reactants, so ΔH points up; Ea is always measured from the reactants to the peak.

questions.q: A reaction pathway diagram shows reactants at 20 kJ/mol and products at 90 kJ/mol. What does the diagram show?
options: an endothermic reaction that takes in 70 kJ/mol from the surroundings
an endothermic reaction that takes in 110 kJ/mol from the surroundings
an exothermic reaction that releases 70 kJ/mol to the surroundings
an exothermic reaction that releases 110 kJ/mol to the surroundings
questions.explain: The products are higher than the reactants by 90 − 20 = 70 kJ/mol, so 70 kJ/mol is absorbed.

questions.q: What is the energy change for the process Cl₂(g) → 2Cl(g), given that the Cl–Cl bond energy is 243 kJ/mol?
questions.explain: Breaking one mole of Cl–Cl bonds is endothermic and requires 243 kJ.

questions.q: Which process is endothermic?
options: the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide
the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
the burning of magnesium in air
questions.explain: Calcium carbonate only decomposes if thermal energy is continually supplied, so it is endothermic.

questions.q: On a labelled reaction pathway diagram for an exothermic reaction, in which direction does the arrow for ΔH point?
options: upwards, from the level of the reactants to the top of the curve
upwards, from the level of the reactants to the level of the products
downwards, from the top of the curve to the horizontal axis
downwards, from the level of the reactants to the level of the products
questions.explain: ΔH is the change in energy from reactants to products; for an exothermic reaction the products are lower, so the arrow points down.

questions.q: Fireworks burn quickly and give out heat, light and sound. Which statement about the chemical reactions is correct?
options: They are endothermic because the temperature rises.
They are exothermic because energy is taken in from the surroundings.
They are endothermic because light energy is produced.
They are exothermic because energy is transferred to the surroundings.
questions.explain: Heat, light and sound are all forms of energy released to the surroundings.

questions.q: Why does a candle flame keep the surrounding air warm?
options: The wax is a reactant that stores thermal energy only.
The combustion of wax is exothermic and absorbs thermal energy.
The combustion of wax is exothermic and releases thermal energy.
The combustion of wax is endothermic and releases thermal energy.
questions.explain: Combustion transfers thermal energy to the surroundings.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes an exothermic reaction in terms of bond energies?
options: negative | energy to break bonds is greater than energy released making bonds
positive | energy to break bonds is equal to energy released making bonds
positive | energy to break bonds is less than energy released making bonds
negative | energy to break bonds is less than energy released making bonds
questions.explain: In an exothermic reaction ΔH = broken − made is negative because making bonds releases more energy.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes an endothermic reaction?
columns: Energy of products compared with reactants
options: thermal energy given out to surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases | energy of products higher than reactants
thermal energy taken in from surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases | energy of products lower than reactants
thermal energy taken in from surroundings | temperature of surroundings decreases | energy of products higher than reactants
thermal energy given out to surroundings | temperature of surroundings decreases | energy of products higher than reactants
questions.explain: In an endothermic reaction energy goes in, the surroundings cool and the products end up higher in energy.

questions.q: Which of these changes would show a temperature decrease if carried out in an insulated cup?
options: magnesium reacting with dilute sulfuric acid
questions.explain: Dissolving ammonium chloride is endothermic; the other three give out heat.

questions.q: Which statement about a reaction pathway diagram of an exothermic reaction is correct?
options: The temperature of the surroundings falls because the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants.
The temperature of the surroundings rises because the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants.
The temperature of the surroundings rises because the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants.
The temperature of the surroundings falls because the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants.
questions.explain: The energy lost by the chemicals is gained by the surroundings, which warm up.

questions.q: How many moles of O–H bonds are formed when 1 mol of methane burns completely in oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O?
questions.explain: Each H₂O has two O–H bonds and 2 mol of water are formed, so 2 × 2 = 4 mol of O–H bonds.

questions.q: Which observation would a student expect when ammonium nitrate dissolves in water in a beaker?
options: The beaker feels warm because thermal energy is given out to the surroundings.
The beaker feels cold because thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings.
The beaker feels warm because thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings.
The beaker feels cold because thermal energy is given out to the surroundings.
questions.explain: Dissolving ammonium nitrate is endothermic, so the water and the beaker cool.

questions.q: Which of these correctly pairs a process with the effect on the temperature of its surroundings?
options: thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate: increases
questions.explain: Burning ethanol is exothermic so the surroundings warm; the other two absorb energy.

questions.q: Solid sodium hydroxide dissolves in water and the beaker becomes warm. What type of change is this?
options: exothermic, because thermal energy is absorbed from the surroundings
exothermic, because thermal energy is released to the surroundings
endothermic, because thermal energy is released to the surroundings
questions.explain: A warming beaker shows thermal energy is released, so dissolving sodium hydroxide is exothermic.

questions.q: Which statement explains why a reaction is endothermic in terms of bonds?
options: More energy is needed to break the bonds in the reactants than is released when bonds form in the products.
Bond making takes in energy and bond breaking releases energy.
Energy is released when the bonds in the reactants break.
More energy is released when bonds form in the products than is needed to break the bonds in the reactants.
questions.explain: A net absorption of energy occurs when bond breaking costs more than bond making returns.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (N≡N 945, O=O 498, N=O 630, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g).
Which equation represents an exothermic reaction?
questions.explain: Burning carbon in oxygen is combustion, which is exothermic; the others take in energy.

questions.q: Which statement about breaking and making bonds when hydrogen burns, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, is correct?
options: H–H and O=O bonds are broken, releasing energy, and O–H bonds are formed, taking in energy.
H–H and O=O bonds are broken, taking in energy, and O–H bonds are formed, releasing energy.
H–H and O=O bonds are formed, releasing energy, and O–H bonds are broken, taking in energy.
Only O–H bonds are involved and no bonds are broken.
questions.explain: In the reactants the H–H and O=O bonds are broken (endothermic); in the product the new O–H bonds form (exothermic).

questions.q: The enthalpy change for burning 1 mol of hydrogen in oxygen is written as ΔH = −286 kJ/mol. What does the negative sign tell you?
options: Thermal energy is released to the surroundings.
Thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings.
questions.explain: A negative ΔH is the sign of an exothermic reaction.

questions.q: Calcium carbonate must be heated strongly the whole time for it to decompose; if heating stops, the decomposition stops. Why?
options: The reaction is exothermic, so the energy released stops the reaction.
The reaction is endothermic, so it continuously gives out thermal energy to the surroundings.
The reaction is exothermic, so it continuously needs thermal energy from the surroundings.
The reaction is endothermic, so it continuously needs thermal energy from the surroundings.
questions.explain: Endothermic reactions take in energy, so they carry on only while energy is supplied.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (C=C 614, Br–Br 193, C–C 347, C–Br 285, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for C₂H₄(g) + Br₂(g) → C₂H₄Br₂(g).
Which row correctly links an observation to the type of reaction?
options: temperature of mixture falls | endothermic | energy taken in from surroundings
temperature of mixture falls | exothermic | energy given out to surroundings
temperature of mixture rises | endothermic | energy given out to surroundings
temperature of mixture rises | endothermic | energy taken in from surroundings
questions.explain: A falling temperature indicates an endothermic reaction that absorbs energy from its surroundings.

questions.q: Reaction X and reaction Y both have ΔH = −100 kJ/mol. Reaction X has Ea = 60 kJ/mol and reaction Y has Ea = 120 kJ/mol. Which statement is correct?
options: They release the same energy overall, but at a given temperature X has more particles able to react.
Y releases more energy overall because its activation energy is greater.
X releases more energy overall because its activation energy is less.
questions.explain: ΔH is the same so the overall energy released is the same; the lower Ea of X means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

questions.q: Which is a use of an exothermic reaction?
options: using ammonium nitrate in an instant cold pack
burning natural gas to heat a home
questions.explain: Burning natural gas gives out thermal energy; the other uses involve reactions that take in energy.

questions.q: Use the bond energies (C–H 413, Cl–Cl 243, C–Cl 339, H–Cl 432, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for CH₄(g) + Cl₂(g) → CH₃Cl(g) + HCl(g).
On a reaction pathway diagram for any reaction, where are the reactants shown?
options: on the vertical axis, at the bottom
at the right-hand end of the curve, after the reaction is finished
at the left-hand end of the curve, on the horizontal line before the reaction starts
at the top of the curve, at the highest point
questions.explain: The pathway reads from left to right: reactants first, then the climb to the peak, then the products.

questions.q: The equation for photosynthesis is 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g). Which statement is correct?
options: The reaction is exothermic because oxygen is produced.
The reaction is endothermic because it takes in energy from sunlight.
The reaction is endothermic because it gives out energy to the plant.
The reaction is exothermic because it takes in energy from sunlight.
questions.explain: Photosynthesis absorbs energy from light, so it is endothermic.

questions.q: A hand warmer contains iron powder that reacts with oxygen from the air and gets warm. What does this show about the reaction?
options: It is exothermic because thermal energy is released to the surroundings.
It is endothermic because oxygen is used up.
It is exothermic because thermal energy is taken in from the air.
It is endothermic because the pack becomes warm.
questions.explain: The pack warms up because the reaction gives out thermal energy, which is exothermic.

questions.q: Which change is a chemical change?
options: Ethanol evaporating from an open dish
Magnesium ribbon burning in air to leave a white powder
questions.explain: Burning magnesium forms a new substance, magnesium oxide. The other changes only alter the state or mix substances, and no new substance forms.

questions.q: Which statement about a chemical change is correct?
options: No energy is transferred to or from the surroundings
The substance changes state but keeps the same formula
The change can always be reversed by cooling
At least one new substance is formed
questions.explain: A chemical change always makes one or more new substances. Energy is normally transferred, and most chemical changes are not simply reversed by cooling.

questions.q: Which row correctly classifies the change?
options: Dissolving copper(II) sulfate crystals in water | physical
questions.explain: Dissolving only mixes the solid with the water and no new substance forms, so it is physical. Cooking an egg and rotting fruit make new substances, and boiling is a change of state.

questions.q: A white solid is heated strongly. It gives off a gas that turns limewater milky and leaves a different white solid behind. Which statement is correct?
options: It is a physical change because heating only changes the state
It is a physical change because a gas has escaped
It is a chemical change because new substances have formed
It is a physical change because the solid stays white
questions.explain: A gas (carbon dioxide) and a different solid are new substances, so this is a chemical change. The colour of the residue does not decide the type of change.

questions.q: Iron filings and sulfur powder are mixed and a magnet removes the iron. The remaining mixture of the two is then heated strongly and a black solid forms that the magnet does not attract. Which is correct?
options: Using the magnet is physical; forming the black solid is chemical
Using the magnet is chemical; forming the black solid is physical
questions.explain: The magnet separates a mixture without making a new substance (physical). Heating iron with sulfur makes iron sulfide, a new compound, so that change is chemical.

questions.q: Which pair contains two physical changes?
options: Freezing water and dissolving sugar in water
Cooking an egg and condensing steam
questions.explain: Freezing and dissolving form no new substances. Burning, rusting and cooking each make new substances.

questions.q: Solid iodine is warmed gently and purple vapour forms. On a cold surface the vapour turns back into solid iodine crystals. Which description is correct?
options: A physical change, because a new substance has formed
A chemical change, because the colour has changed
A physical change, because the same substance is present before and after
A chemical change, because a gas has formed
questions.explain: Iodine changes state (sublimation then deposition) and is iodine throughout, so it is physical. A gas forming or a colour appearing does not prove a new substance.

questions.q: A solid is warmed and becomes a liquid. On cooling it becomes a solid again with the same properties as at the start. Which statement is correct?
options: This is a physical change because bonds between atoms are broken
This is a chemical change because heat was needed
This is a physical change because no new substance forms
This is a chemical change because the state changed
questions.explain: Melting and freezing change only the state of the same substance. A change of state needs heat but does not make a new substance.

questions.q: Marble chips (calcium carbonate) react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which change would make the reaction faster, with everything else the same?
options: Using the same mass of powdered marble instead of chips
questions.explain: Powder has a larger surface area than chips, so the reaction is faster. Larger lumps, lower temperature and dilution all slow it down.

questions.q: Which statement about a catalyst is correct?
options: It speeds up a reaction and is chemically unchanged at the end
It speeds up a reaction by increasing the amount of product formed
It slows down a reaction and is unchanged at the end
It speeds up a reaction and is used up in the process
questions.explain: A catalyst increases the rate but is not used up, so it can be recovered unchanged. It does not change how much product is made.

questions.q: Food keeps fresh for longer in a refrigerator than on a kitchen table. What is the best explanation?
options: The lower temperature slows down the reactions that make the food go bad
The lower temperature speeds up the reactions that make the food go bad
The refrigerator removes all the oxygen from the air
The refrigerator acts as a catalyst for the reactions
questions.explain: Lowering the temperature decreases the rate of reaction, including the reactions that spoil food.

questions.q: Excess zinc is added to 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid in one experiment and to 50 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid in another, at the same temperature. Which statement about the initial rate is correct?
options: It is faster with the 0.5 mol/dm³ acid
It is faster with the 1.0 mol/dm³ acid
It is the same in both experiments
It is zero in both until the mixtures are heated
questions.explain: A higher concentration of acid gives a faster rate of reaction, all other conditions being equal.

questions.q: Which change increases the rate of a reaction between two gases in a sealed container at constant temperature?
options: Removing some of the gas to reduce the pressure
Reducing the volume of the container to increase the pressure
questions.explain: Increasing the pressure squeezes the gas particles closer together, so the reaction speeds up. The other changes decrease the rate.

questions.q: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give hydrogen gas. Which apparatus allows the rate to be found by following the gas produced?
options: A condenser and a separating funnel
A pipette and a pH meter
A gas syringe attached to the flask, and a stopwatch
A filter funnel and filter paper
questions.explain: The volume of hydrogen collected in the gas syringe can be read at regular times, and the rate is found from volume against time.

questions.q: Calcium carbonate reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid in an open flask on a balance. The mass reading falls and then stops falling. Why does it stop falling?
options: All the calcium carbonate has reacted, so no more carbon dioxide is made
The balance cannot detect small changes
The carbon dioxide has all dissolved in the acid
questions.explain: The mass falls because carbon dioxide escapes. When the limiting reactant (calcium carbonate) is used up, the reaction stops and the mass is constant.

questions.q: A graph of volume of gas against time starts steeply, becomes less steep and then goes horizontal. What does the steep start show?
options: The rate of reaction is greatest at the start
A catalyst is made during the reaction
The rate of reaction is lowest at the start
questions.explain: The gradient of the curve is the rate. It is steepest at the start when the reactant concentrations are highest.

questions.q: The table shows gas volumes collected at 10 s intervals: 0 s, 0 cm³; 10 s, 30 cm³; 20 s, 50 cm³; 30 s, 58 cm³; 40 s, 60 cm³; 50 s, 60 cm³. In which interval was the average rate greatest?
questions.explain: The volumes produced in the intervals are 30, 20, 8, 2 and 0 cm³, so the greatest volume in 10 s, and so the fastest rate, is in the first interval.

questions.q: In an experiment with a fixed mass of magnesium and excess acid, a second experiment gives a steeper curve but the same final volume of hydrogen. Which change was made?
options: A larger volume of the same acid was used
The magnesium was used in larger pieces
questions.explain: A higher temperature increases the rate but not the final volume, because the amount of magnesium is unchanged. Larger pieces or dilution would slow the reaction, and extra acid would not change the rate.

questions.q: What is an enzyme?
options: A biological catalyst that speeds up reactions in living things
A metal catalyst used in industrial processes
A reactant that is used up during respiration
A product that slows down fermentation
questions.explain: Enzymes are catalysts made by living organisms, and they speed up biological reactions without being used up.

questions.q: A reaction produces 48 cm³ of gas in 120 s. What is the average rate of reaction?
questions.explain: Average rate = volume ÷ time = 48 ÷ 120 = 0.40 cm³/s.

questions.q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Black manganese(IV) oxide powder is added and oxygen forms quickly. When the fizzing stops the powder is filtered off, washed and dried. What is found?
options: A larger mass, because it reacted with oxygen
The same mass of manganese(IV) oxide as at the start
A smaller mass, because some was used up
questions.explain: Manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst. It speeds up the decomposition but is not used up, so it can be recovered with the same mass.

questions.q: Which change does NOT increase the rate of reaction between zinc and dilute sulfuric acid?
options: Using zinc powder instead of zinc granules
Using a larger volume of acid of the same concentration
questions.explain: The rate depends on concentration, not on the volume of solution. The other three changes all increase the rate.

questions.q: Which row correctly shows the effect on the rate of reaction?
options: Using smaller pieces of a solid | rate increases
Lowering the concentration of a solution | rate increases
Decreasing the pressure of a gas | rate increases
questions.explain: Smaller pieces give a larger surface area and a faster rate. Lower concentration, lower pressure and lower temperature all decrease the rate.

questions.q: Why does the rate of a reaction decrease as the reaction proceeds?
options: The catalyst is gradually used up
The surface area of the reactants increases
The temperature of the mixture rises
The reactants are being used up, so their concentration falls
questions.explain: As reactants are used up their concentration drops, so collisions are less frequent and the rate falls.

questions.q: A flask containing marble chips and excess acid, with a plug of cotton wool in the neck, is placed on a balance. Which describes the graph of mass against time?
options: It falls quickly at first, then more slowly, and then becomes horizontal
It falls at a constant rate for the whole experiment
It stays horizontal and then falls
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide escapes so the mass falls. The rate is fastest at the start and drops to zero when the reaction ends.

questions.q: Flour dust suspended in the air of a mill can explode, but a heap of flour on the floor only burns slowly. Why?
options: The dust has a much larger surface area exposed to oxygen
The dust is at a lower temperature
questions.explain: Fine dust exposes far more surface to oxygen than a heap, so the reaction is very fast.

questions.q: Which unit is suitable for the rate of a reaction measured by the volume of gas produced?
questions.explain: A rate is an amount produced per unit time, so volume divided by time (cm³/s) is suitable.

questions.q: A student compares the rate of reaction of magnesium ribbon with acid at 20 °C and at 40 °C. Which variable must be kept the same?
options: The temperature of the reaction mixture
The time taken for the reaction
The concentration and volume of the acid
questions.explain: To make a fair test only one variable (temperature) is changed. Concentration and volume of acid, and the mass and form of magnesium, must stay the same.

questions.q: The graph of gas volume against time becomes horizontal at 80 cm³ and stays there. What does this show?
options: Gas is still forming at 80 cm³ per second
The catalyst has been used up
The reaction is at its fastest rate
The reaction has finished and 80 cm³ of gas was made in total
questions.explain: A horizontal line means the volume is no longer changing, so a reactant has been used up and the reaction has stopped.

questions.q: In one experiment 1 g of magnesium powder is added to excess acid. In another, 1 g of magnesium ribbon is added to the same excess acid. How do the results compare?
options: The ribbon gives a larger total volume of hydrogen
The total volume of hydrogen is the same, but the powder reacts faster
The ribbon reacts faster but gives the same total volume
The powder gives a larger total volume of hydrogen
questions.explain: The same mass of magnesium gives the same amount of hydrogen. Powder has a larger surface area so it reacts faster.

questions.q: Which explains why increasing the concentration of a solution increases the rate of reaction?
options: The particles become larger, so they collide more often
The particles move faster, so more have enough energy to react
The activation energy of the reaction is lower
There are more particles per unit volume, so collisions are more frequent
questions.explain: A higher concentration puts more particles in each unit volume. The frequency of collisions rises and so does the rate.

questions.q: Which is the best explanation of why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction?
options: The particles have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and more collisions have energy of at least Ea
The extra heat adds more reactant particles
The particles move faster but the number of collisions stays the same
The activation energy of the reaction becomes lower
questions.explain: At a higher temperature particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent, and a greater proportion of them have energy of at least the activation energy.

questions.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
options: It increases the concentration of the reactants
It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
It increases the kinetic energy of the reactant particles
It raises the energy of the reactants above the activation energy
questions.explain: A catalyst offers a different route with a lower Ea, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

questions.q: What is meant by the activation energy, Ea, of a reaction?
options: The average kinetic energy of the particles in the mixture
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products
The total energy released when the reaction is complete
questions.explain: Activation energy is the minimum collision energy needed to break bonds and start the reaction.

questions.q: Why does a solid in powder form react faster than the same mass in large lumps?
options: The activation energy of the solid is lower
The particles of the solid have more kinetic energy
The solid has a higher concentration
More particles of the solid are exposed, so collisions with the other reactant happen more frequently
questions.explain: Powdering increases the surface area. More solid particles are available to collide, so the collision frequency and the rate increase.

questions.q: Which is the correct explanation of why increasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction increases its rate?
options: The activation energy of the reaction decreases
The gas particles are closer together, so there are more particles per unit volume and collisions are more frequent
The gas particles gain kinetic energy and move faster
questions.explain: Raising the pressure compresses the gas, which increases the number of particles in a given volume and so the collision frequency.

questions.q: Which statement about adding a catalyst to a reaction is correct?
options: The activation energy decreases but the energy of the reactants and products is unchanged
The mass of product formed is increased
The activation energy increases and the energy of the products decreases
The activation energy is unchanged and the energy of the products decreases
questions.explain: A catalyst lowers Ea by giving an alternative pathway. It does not change the energies of reactants and products or the amount of product.

questions.q: Which row is correct?
columns: Effect on proportion with energy ≥ Ea
options: Increasing surface area | collision frequency increases | proportion of particles with energy ≥ Ea increases
Increasing pressure of a gas | collision frequency decreases | proportion of particles with energy ≥ Ea stays the same
Increasing concentration | collision frequency increases | proportion of particles with energy ≥ Ea stays the same
Increasing temperature | collision frequency stays the same | proportion of particles with energy ≥ Ea increases
questions.explain: Higher concentration only raises the collision frequency. Higher temperature raises both, and surface area and pressure changes do not affect the proportion of particles with enough energy.

questions.q: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Why is the loss-in-mass method less suitable than collecting the gas in a syringe?
options: Hydrogen is very soluble in the acid
Hydrogen is so light that the loss in mass is too small to measure accurately
Hydrogen is heavier than the other products
Magnesium chloride gives off a gas as well
questions.explain: Hydrogen has a very low relative formula mass so only a tiny mass is lost. Calcium carbonate with acid loses more mass as heavier carbon dioxide escapes.

questions.q: Calcium carbonate reacts with dilute acid and the carbon dioxide is collected in an inverted measuring cylinder over water. Why is a gas syringe better?
options: Water would react with the calcium carbonate
A syringe makes the reaction faster
Carbon dioxide dissolves in water, so some gas would not be measured over water
Carbon dioxide reacts with the glass of the cylinder
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide is soluble in water, which would make the measured volume too low. A gas syringe avoids this problem.

questions.q: In a loss-in-mass experiment a loose plug of cotton wool is put in the neck of the flask. What is its purpose?
options: It stops the gas leaving the flask
It acts as a catalyst for the reaction
It stops acid spray leaving the flask but lets the gas escape
questions.explain: Spray carried out with the gas would give a false loss in mass. The loose plug keeps liquid in while gas can still escape.

questions.q: In a gas collection experiment, 36 cm³ is collected at 20 s and 60 cm³ at 60 s. What is the average rate between 20 s and 60 s?
questions.explain: Volume formed = 60 − 36 = 24 cm³ in 60 − 20 = 40 s. Rate = 24 ÷ 40 = 0.60 cm³/s.

questions.q: Excess magnesium reacts with 25.0 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What is the maximum volume of hydrogen at room temperature and pressure? (1 mol of gas occupies 24 000 cm³)
questions.explain: Moles of HCl = 0.0250 × 2.0 = 0.050 mol. Moles of H₂ = 0.050 ÷ 2 = 0.025 mol. Volume = 0.025 × 24 000 = 600 cm³.

questions.q: A catalysed and an uncatalysed reaction use the same amounts of reactants. How do their gas-volume curves compare?
options: The catalysed curve levels off at a higher final volume
The catalysed curve is less steep but levels off at the same final volume
The catalysed curve is steeper but levels off at the same final volume
questions.explain: The catalyst increases the rate, so the curve is steeper, but the amount of reactant limits the final volume, which stays the same.

questions.q: At room temperature most collisions between reactant particles do not lead to a reaction. What is the best reason?
options: The colliding particles do not have energy of at least the activation energy
The particles are too small to react
The particles are moving too fast to react
questions.explain: A reaction occurs only if colliding particles have at least the activation energy. At low temperature few collisions meet this requirement.

questions.q: A reaction takes 20 s at 40 °C and 80 s at 20 °C, with all other conditions the same. What does this show?
options: The reaction is faster at the higher temperature
Temperature has no effect on the rate
The reaction is faster at the lower temperature
questions.explain: A shorter time for the same change means a faster rate, so raising the temperature increased the rate.

questions.q: Which symbol shows that a chemical reaction is reversible?
questions.explain: The two-way arrow ⇌ shows that the reaction can go in both directions.

questions.q: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals are heated gently in a test tube. What is observed?
options: The crystals turn white and water droplets form on the cooler part of the tube
The crystals turn black and a gas that relights a glowing splint forms
The crystals turn from white to blue
questions.explain: Heating drives off the water of crystallisation, leaving white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. The water condenses on the cooler glass.

questions.q: A few drops of water are added to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. Which observation is correct?
options: It turns blue and becomes cooler
It turns blue and becomes warm
It turns pink and becomes warm
It stays white and dissolves to give a colourless solution
questions.explain: The anhydrous solid combines with water to form blue hydrated crystals, and the reaction is exothermic so the solid warms up.

questions.q: A piece of blue cobalt(II) chloride paper is dipped in water. What is observed?
questions.explain: Water changes anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride from blue to pink, so the paper is used to test for water.

questions.q: Which row gives the correct colours?
questions.explain: Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride is pink and the anhydrous form is blue. Hydrated copper(II) sulfate is blue and the anhydrous form is white.

questions.q: Which equation represents a reversible reaction?
questions.explain: Only the hydration of copper(II) sulfate is shown with ⇌, because it can go in either direction depending on the conditions.

questions.q: What is the result of a positive test for water using anhydrous copper(II) sulfate?
questions.explain: Water turns white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue.

questions.q: What does the word hydrated mean in hydrated copper(II) sulfate?
options: The solid has been dissolved in water
The crystals contain water as part of their structure
The solid has water only on its surface
The solid has reacted with hydrogen
questions.explain: A hydrated compound has water of crystallisation locked in its crystal structure.

questions.q: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate has been heated until it is white. How can the blue colour be restored?
options: Place the white solid in a desiccator
Heat the white solid more strongly
Add sodium chloride to the white solid
Add water to the white solid
questions.explain: The reaction is reversible. Adding water to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate forms the blue hydrated crystals again.

questions.q: Which statement describes a reversible reaction?
options: All the reactants are used up and cannot be recovered
The reaction can only take place if a catalyst is present
The products can react to form the reactants again
The reaction takes place in only one direction
questions.explain: In a reversible reaction the reaction can go forwards and backwards, so products can turn back into reactants.

questions.q: A piece of cobalt(II) chloride paper has turned pink after testing a liquid. It is gently heated. What happens?
questions.explain: Heating removes the water, so the pink hydrated cobalt(II) chloride changes back to blue anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride.

questions.q: A student heats 5.0 g of blue crystals of copper(II) sulfate and the mass falls. What is the best explanation?
options: The crystals dissolve in their own water
Copper is lost as a vapour
Water is driven off, leaving anhydrous copper(II) sulfate
questions.explain: The crystals lose their water of crystallisation as steam, so the solid becomes lighter and turns white.

questions.q: What is the white solid left when blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated strongly?
questions.explain: Gentle heating only removes the water. The white solid is copper(II) sulfate without water, which is called anhydrous.

questions.q: What is the effect of heating hydrated cobalt(II) chloride crystals?
options: Blue crystals turn pink as water is lost
Pink crystals turn blue as water is lost
questions.explain: Heating drives off the water of crystallisation, changing pink hydrated cobalt(II) chloride into blue anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride.

questions.q: Which statement describes a reversible reaction at equilibrium in a closed system?
options: The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
The forward reaction has stopped and the reverse reaction continues
All of the reactants have been converted into products
The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate and the concentrations stay constant
questions.explain: At equilibrium both reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations do not change. They are constant but not necessarily equal.

questions.q: Why must a reversible reaction be carried out in a closed system for equilibrium to be reached?
options: So that no reactants or products can escape
So that a catalyst can be added
So that the forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction
questions.explain: If a gas could escape, the reaction mixture could not be returned to the reactants and equilibrium would not be reached.

questions.q: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) at equilibrium, which statement is correct?
options: Both the forward and reverse reactions are still taking place
Only the forward reaction is taking place
Only the reverse reaction is taking place
questions.explain: Equilibrium is dynamic. Both reactions continue but at equal rates, so there is no overall change.

questions.q: Which symbol equation represents the reaction in the Haber process?
questions.explain: Only N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ has equal numbers of N atoms (2) and H atoms (6) on each side.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives a raw material and its source for the Haber process?
questions.explain: Nitrogen comes from the air. Hydrogen comes from methane (natural gas).

questions.q: Which are the typical conditions used in the Haber process?
questions.explain: The Haber process uses about 450 °C, 20 000 kPa (200 atm) and an iron catalyst.

questions.q: Which are the typical conditions used for the conversion of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide in the Contact process?
questions.explain: The Contact process uses about 450 °C, 200 kPa (2 atm) and a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.

questions.q: Which equation shows the conversion of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide in the Contact process?
questions.explain: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ has 2 S atoms and 6 O atoms on each side. The others are unbalanced or show a different reaction.

questions.q: What are the sources of sulfur dioxide for the Contact process?
options: Burning sulfur or roasting sulfide ores in air
questions.explain: Sulfur dioxide is made by burning sulfur in air or by roasting metal sulfide ores. Oxygen comes from the air.

questions.q: The forward reaction in the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), is exothermic. What happens to the equilibrium yield of ammonia if the temperature is increased at constant pressure?
options: It increases, because the equilibrium shifts to the right
It increases, because the rate of reaction increases
It decreases, because the equilibrium shifts to the left
questions.explain: Increasing the temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction, so the equilibrium shifts to the left and less ammonia is present.

questions.q: Why does increasing the pressure increase the equilibrium yield of ammonia in N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
options: The reaction is exothermic, so high pressure favours it
There are fewer gas molecules on the right, so the equilibrium shifts to the right
High pressure acts as a catalyst
There are more gas molecules on the right, so the equilibrium shifts to the right
questions.explain: There are 4 gas molecules on the left and 2 on the right. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.

questions.q: The reaction H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) is at equilibrium. What is the effect of increasing the pressure at constant temperature?
options: The position of equilibrium does not change, as there are equal numbers of gas molecules on both sides
The equilibrium shifts to the left
The equilibrium shifts to the right
questions.explain: There are 2 gas molecules on each side, so pressure does not favour either direction.

questions.q: The equilibrium 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) has NO₂ as a brown gas and N₂O₄ as a colourless gas. The forward reaction is exothermic. A sealed tube of the equilibrium mixture is cooled. What is observed?
options: The mixture becomes paler as the equilibrium shifts to the right
The mixture becomes paler as the equilibrium shifts to the left
The mixture becomes darker brown as the equilibrium shifts to the left
questions.explain: Cooling favours the exothermic forward reaction, so more colourless N₂O₄ forms and the brown colour fades.

questions.q: In the Haber process, ammonia is removed as it forms. What is the effect on the position of equilibrium?
options: It shifts to the right, so more ammonia is formed
The reaction can no longer take place
It shifts to the left, so less ammonia is formed
questions.explain: Removing a product lowers its concentration, so the system makes more of it to restore equilibrium.

questions.q: What is the effect of the iron catalyst on the Haber process?
options: It shifts the equilibrium to the left
It shifts the equilibrium to the right
It does not change the position of equilibrium but equilibrium is reached faster
questions.explain: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but the position is unchanged.

questions.q: Why is a temperature of 450 °C used in the Haber process rather than a much lower temperature?
options: A lower temperature would decrease the rate and also decrease the yield
A lower temperature would give too slow a rate, so 450 °C is a compromise between rate and yield
450 °C gives the highest possible yield of ammonia
A lower temperature would increase the rate but decrease the yield
questions.explain: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature gives a higher yield but too slow a rate. 450 °C gives an acceptable rate and yield.

questions.q: Why is a pressure much higher than 200 atm not used in the Haber process?
options: Higher pressure would decrease the equilibrium yield of ammonia
Higher pressure would decrease the rate of reaction
The equipment would be very expensive to build and run, and more dangerous
The iron catalyst stops working above 200 atm
questions.explain: Higher pressure increases the yield but needs stronger, more costly equipment and creates a greater safety risk, so 200 atm is a compromise.

questions.q: Why is the Contact process carried out at only about 2 atm?
options: Vanadium(V) oxide does not work above 2 atm
Higher pressure would shift the equilibrium to the left
Sulfur dioxide would become a solid at higher pressure
The yield of sulfur trioxide is already high, so higher pressure would add cost for little gain
questions.explain: The conversion of SO₂ to SO₃ is high at about 2 atm and 450 °C. High-pressure equipment would add cost and safety risk with little extra yield.

questions.q: The forward reaction in the Contact process is exothermic. Why is a temperature of 450 °C used instead of 100 °C?
options: At 100 °C the vanadium(V) oxide catalyst would be used up
At 100 °C the yield of sulfur trioxide would be lower
At 100 °C the rate would be too slow, even though the equilibrium yield would be higher
At 450 °C the equilibrium yield is the highest possible
questions.explain: Lower temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction but the rate becomes too slow. 450 °C is a compromise.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the vanadium(V) oxide catalyst in the Contact process?
options: To increase the rate at which equilibrium is reached
To increase the equilibrium yield of sulfur trioxide
questions.explain: The catalyst makes the reaction faster but does not change the position of equilibrium.

questions.q: In the Haber process the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled to the reactor. What is the reason?
options: The gases must be cooled before they are used
The reaction cannot start without recycled gases
The recycled gases act as a catalyst
Only part of the mixture reacts on each pass, and recycling avoids wasting the reactants
questions.explain: At equilibrium the mixture still contains much unreacted gas, so recycling it makes use of all the reactants and saves money.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the Haber process?
options: Contact | nitrogen from air, hydrogen from methane | vanadium(V) oxide
Haber | nitrogen from air, hydrogen from methane | iron
Contact | sulfur dioxide from burning sulfur, oxygen from air | iron
Haber | nitrogen from air, hydrogen from methane | vanadium(V) oxide
questions.explain: The Haber process uses nitrogen from air and hydrogen from methane with an iron catalyst. The Contact process uses vanadium(V) oxide and different raw materials.

questions.q: For a reversible reaction the forward reaction is endothermic. Which change increases the yield of products at equilibrium?
options: Adding a catalyst and decreasing the temperature
questions.explain: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, so the equilibrium shifts towards the products. A catalyst does not change the position.

questions.q: A reversible reaction starts with only reactants and reaches equilibrium in a closed system. Which statement about the rates is correct?
options: The reverse rate is always greater than the forward rate
The forward rate increases until it is zero
The forward rate decreases and the reverse rate increases until they are equal
The rates stay different but the concentrations stop changing
questions.explain: The forward rate falls as reactants are used, and the reverse rate rises as products build up. At equilibrium they are equal.

questions.q: In the Haber process N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what is the maximum amount of ammonia that could be made from 3.0 mol of hydrogen with excess nitrogen if the reaction went to completion?
questions.explain: The mole ratio H₂ : NH₃ is 3 : 2, so 3.0 mol of H₂ gives 3.0 × 2/3 = 2.0 mol of NH₃.

questions.q: Which two colours are shown by cobalt(II) chloride when it is anhydrous and when it is hydrated?
options: Blue when anhydrous and white when hydrated
Blue when anhydrous and pink when hydrated
Pink when anhydrous and blue when hydrated
White when anhydrous and blue when hydrated
questions.explain: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue and it turns pink when it takes in water to become hydrated.

questions.q: What is the name of the compound with formula Fe₂O₃?
questions.explain: Two Fe ions balance three O²⁻ ions (total 6−), so each iron ion is 3+. The Roman numeral III shows the oxidation number of iron.

questions.q: What is the formula of copper(I) oxide?
questions.explain: Copper(I) has an oxidation number of +1, so two Cu⁺ ions are needed to balance one O²⁻ ion.

questions.q: Which compound contains iron in the +2 oxidation state?
questions.explain: In FeCl₂ two Cl⁻ ions balance one Fe²⁺. The other compounds contain iron(III).

questions.q: What does the (IV) mean in the name manganese(IV) oxide?
options: There are four manganese atoms in the formula
There are four oxygen atoms in the formula
Manganese is in Group IV of the Periodic Table
The oxidation number of manganese is +4
questions.explain: The Roman numeral gives the oxidation number of the metal. Manganese(IV) oxide is MnO₂.

questions.q: Which statement describes a redox reaction?
options: A solution changes from acidic to neutral
Oxidation and reduction take place at the same time
questions.explain: Redox means reduction and oxidation together. One substance is oxidised while another is reduced.

questions.q: Which is the definition of oxidation in terms of oxygen?
questions.explain: A substance is oxidised when it gains oxygen, and reduced when it loses oxygen.

questions.q: Copper(II) oxide is heated with hydrogen: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Which statement is correct?
options: Hydrogen is reduced because it gains oxygen
Copper(II) oxide is reduced because it gains oxygen
Copper(II) oxide is oxidised because it loses oxygen
Copper(II) oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen
questions.explain: CuO loses oxygen to form Cu so it is reduced. Hydrogen gains oxygen to form water so it is oxidised.

questions.q: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Which statement is correct?
options: Oxygen is oxidised because it gains magnesium
Magnesium is reduced because it loses oxygen
Magnesium is reduced because it gains oxygen
Magnesium is oxidised because it gains oxygen
questions.explain: Magnesium gains oxygen and is oxidised. A gain of oxygen is oxidation.

questions.q: Which equation represents a redox reaction?
questions.explain: In 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂, CuO loses oxygen (reduced) and carbon gains oxygen (oxidised). The other equations involve no gain or loss of oxygen.

questions.q: In the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, which statement is correct?
options: Iron(III) oxide is reduced and carbon monoxide is oxidised
Iron(III) oxide is oxidised and carbon monoxide is reduced
questions.explain: Fe₂O₃ loses oxygen so it is reduced, while CO gains oxygen to become CO₂ so it is oxidised.

questions.q: In the reaction 2Mg + CO₂ → 2MgO + C, which row is correct?
questions.explain: Magnesium gains oxygen so it is oxidised, and carbon dioxide loses oxygen so it is reduced.

questions.q: Iron rusts when it reacts with oxygen and water. In terms of oxygen, what happens to the iron?
options: It is oxidised because it loses oxygen
It is reduced because it loses oxygen
It is oxidised because it gains oxygen
It is reduced because it gains oxygen
questions.explain: Rust is a compound of iron with oxygen, so the iron has gained oxygen and been oxidised.

questions.q: Black copper(II) oxide is heated with carbon and a pink-brown solid forms. What does this show?
options: The change is a physical change
Copper has been oxidised to copper(II) oxide
Copper(II) oxide has been reduced to copper
questions.explain: Loss of oxygen from copper(II) oxide to give copper is reduction.

questions.q: Which reaction involves the reduction of a metal oxide?
options: Heating copper in air to make copper(II) oxide
Heating iron(III) oxide with carbon monoxide to make iron
Rusting of iron in damp air
questions.explain: Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen to carbon monoxide, so it is reduced. Copper and magnesium gain oxygen, and rusting is oxidation.

questions.q: Which row correctly links the change with its name?
questions.explain: Gain of oxygen is oxidation and loss of oxygen is reduction.

questions.q: In the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe, which statement is correct?
options: Aluminium is reduced and iron(III) oxide is oxidised
Aluminium is oxidised and iron(III) oxide is reduced
questions.explain: Aluminium gains oxygen to form Al₂O₃ (oxidation). Fe₂O₃ loses oxygen to form iron (reduction).

questions.q: Which row correctly defines oxidation and reduction?
options: decrease in oxidation number | increase in oxidation number
loss of electrons | gain of electrons
decrease in oxidation number | gain of electrons
gain of electrons | loss of electrons
questions.explain: Oxidation is loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is gain of electrons or a decrease in oxidation number.

questions.q: The change Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ takes place. Which statement is correct?
options: It is oxidation because electrons are lost
It is reduction because electrons are lost
It is oxidation because electrons are gained
It is reduction because electrons are gained
questions.explain: The iron ion loses an electron and its oxidation number rises from +2 to +3, which is oxidation.

questions.q: The change Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ takes place. Which statement is correct?
options: It is oxidation because electrons are gained
It is reduction because electrons are gained
It is oxidation because chlorine gains oxygen
It is reduction because electrons are lost
questions.explain: Chlorine gains electrons and its oxidation number falls from 0 to −1, which is reduction.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
questions.explain: Each oxygen is −2, so S + 4(−2) = −2. Therefore S = +6.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of manganese in the manganate(VII) ion, MnO₄⁻?
Which species contains nitrogen with an oxidation number of +5?
questions.explain: In NO₃⁻, N + 3(−2) = −1, so N = +5. NO₂ is +4, NH₃ is −3 and N₂O is +1.

questions.q: Zinc is added to copper(II) sulfate solution: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Which change in oxidation number happens?
options: Zinc goes from 0 to +2, so zinc is oxidised
Copper goes from 0 to +2, so copper is oxidised
Zinc goes from +2 to 0, so zinc is oxidised
Zinc goes from 0 to +2, so zinc is reduced
questions.explain: Zinc atoms (0) become Zn²⁺ (+2), so the oxidation number increases and zinc is oxidised. Copper goes from +2 to 0 and is reduced.

questions.q: Which reaction is NOT a redox reaction?
questions.explain: In the CuO and acid reaction every oxidation number stays the same (Cu +2, O −2, H +1, S +6). The other reactions all include an element changing its oxidation number.
