questions.q: Which change is a reduction?
options: Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ changing to Cr³⁺
Sulfur in SO₂ changing to sulfur in SO₄²⁻
questions.explain: Chromium goes from +6 to +3, a decrease in oxidation number. The other changes all show an increase in oxidation number.

questions.q: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) solution is added to a solution of a reducing agent. What colour change is seen?
questions.explain: Purple manganate(VII) is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺ by a reducing agent.

questions.q: Aqueous potassium iodide is added to a solution of an oxidising agent. What colour change shows that a redox reaction has taken place?
questions.explain: Iodide ions are oxidised to iodine, which makes the solution brown.

questions.q: Which is the correct definition of an oxidising agent?
options: A substance that oxidises another substance and is itself reduced
A substance that reduces another substance and is itself reduced
A substance that oxidises another substance and is itself oxidised
A substance that reduces another substance and is itself oxidised
questions.explain: An oxidising agent takes electrons from another substance, which is oxidised, and is itself reduced.

questions.q: In the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, which is the reducing agent?
questions.explain: CO takes oxygen from the iron(III) oxide and is itself oxidised to CO₂, so it is the reducing agent.

questions.q: In the reaction Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂, which is the oxidising agent?
questions.explain: Chlorine gains electrons (0 to −1) and is reduced, so it oxidises the bromide ions and is the oxidising agent.

questions.q: Magnesium reacts with dilute acid: Mg + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂. Which statement is correct?
options: H⁺ is the oxidising agent because it gains electrons
H⁺ is the reducing agent because it gains electrons
Mg²⁺ is reduced because it gains electrons
Mg is the oxidising agent because it loses electrons
questions.explain: Mg loses electrons (oxidised, reducing agent). H⁺ gains electrons (reduced) so it is the oxidising agent.

questions.q: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) is decolourised by a solution of iron(II) sulfate. Which statement is correct?
options: Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺, so iron(II) sulfate is acting as a reducing agent
Manganate(VII) is oxidised, so it is the reducing agent
Fe²⁺ is reduced to Fe³⁺, so iron(II) sulfate is acting as a reducing agent
Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺, so iron(II) sulfate is acting as an oxidising agent
questions.explain: Loss of purple colour shows the manganate(VII) has been reduced. Fe²⁺ loses electrons, so it is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent.

questions.q: In the reaction 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O, which statement about sulfur is correct?
options: Sulfur is neither oxidised nor reduced
Sulfur is both oxidised and reduced
questions.explain: Sulfur in H₂S goes from −2 to 0 (oxidised) and sulfur in SO₂ goes from +4 to 0 (reduced).

questions.q: Which row gives the correct oxidation number?
questions.explain: In Cr₂O₇²⁻, 2Cr + 7(−2) = −2, so Cr = +6. S in SO₂ is +4, Cl in ClO₃⁻ is +5 and N in NH₄⁺ is −3.

questions.q: Calcium carbonate is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation is correct?
questions.explain: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Calcium forms Ca²⁺, so two Cl⁻ are needed and 2HCl balances the equation.

questions.q: A solution turns red litmus paper blue and turns thymolphthalein blue. What can be concluded?
options: The solution is a salt solution only.
questions.explain: Both red litmus turning blue and thymolphthalein turning blue are positive tests for an alkali.

questions.q: Solutions of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid have the same concentration of 0.1 mol/dm³. Which statement is correct?
options: Hydrochloric acid has the lower pH.
Ethanoic acid has the lower pH.
Ethanoic acid has the higher concentration of H⁺ ions.
questions.explain: Hydrochloric acid is fully dissociated so it has more H⁺ ions per dm³ and a lower pH than the partly dissociated ethanoic acid.

questions.q: A solution has a pH of 10. What is the colour of litmus in this solution?
questions.explain: pH 10 is alkaline and litmus is blue in alkaline solutions.

questions.q: Which substance acts as a proton acceptor in the equation NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺?
options: The H⁺ ion and NH₄⁺ ion together
questions.explain: NH₃ gains an H⁺ ion, so it accepts a proton and is acting as a base.

questions.q: Ammonia reacts with water: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Which species acts as the proton donor in the forward reaction?
questions.explain: Water donates an H⁺ ion to ammonia, which accepts it. The proton donor is the acid.

questions.q: Which equation shows that hydrochloric acid is a strong acid?
questions.explain: The single forward arrow shows complete dissociation into H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

questions.q: A student adds magnesium ribbon to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which observation is correct?
options: The ribbon turns blue and no bubbles are seen.
The ribbon gets smaller and bubbles are seen.
A white precipitate forms at once.
The solution turns red and the ribbon grows.
questions.explain: Magnesium reacts with the acid, dissolving and releasing bubbles of hydrogen gas.

questions.q: What is meant by a strong acid?
options: an acid with a high concentration
an acid that reacts only with metals
an acid that is partially dissociated in aqueous solution
an acid that is completely dissociated in aqueous solution
questions.explain: Strength describes the extent of dissociation, not concentration. A strong acid dissociates fully into ions.

questions.q: A 25.0 cm³ sample of aqueous sodium hydroxide of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³ is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. What is the concentration of the acid?
questions.explain: Moles NaOH = 0.0250 × 0.100 = 0.00250 mol. NaOH and HCl react 1:1, so the concentration of HCl = 0.00250 ÷ 0.0200 = 0.125 mol/dm³.

questions.q: Which solution would turn universal indicator paper purple?
questions.explain: Strongly alkaline solutions of about pH 13 turn universal indicator purple.

questions.q: Which ions are always present in aqueous solutions of alkalis?
questions.explain: Alkalis produce hydroxide ions, OH⁻(aq), in water. Not all alkalis contain Na⁺.

questions.q: What is the colour of litmus in dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explain: Litmus is red in acidic solutions and blue in alkaline solutions.

questions.q: Ammonium nitrate is warmed with calcium hydroxide. The gas produced turns damp red litmus paper blue. Which gas is it?
questions.explain: Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas, so it turns damp red litmus blue. It is displaced from ammonium salts by bases.

questions.q: What happens when hydrochloric acid dissolves in water?
options: The molecules are partially dissociated into H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
The molecules stay intact as HCl molecules.
The molecules react to make H₂ and Cl₂.
The molecules are completely dissociated into H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
questions.explain: HCl is a strong acid, so every molecule dissociates in aqueous solution.

questions.q: Aqueous potassium hydroxide and dilute nitric acid are mixed in the correct proportions. Which ionic equation represents the reaction?
questions.explain: K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions. Only H⁺ and OH⁻ combine to form water.

questions.q: Which pair of solutions contains the same concentration of acid but a different concentration of hydrogen ions?
questions.explain: A strong acid releases all its H⁺, whereas the weak acid releases only a small fraction, even at the same concentration.

questions.q: In the reaction HCl(g) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), which species acts as a base?
questions.explain: Water accepts a proton from HCl to form H₃O⁺, so water is the proton acceptor.

questions.q: Which equation for the reaction of zinc with dilute sulfuric acid is correct?
questions.explain: A metal and an acid form a salt and hydrogen. Zinc forms Zn²⁺, so the salt is ZnSO₄ and the equation is already balanced.

questions.q: Which of these is the best description of an alkali in terms of ions?
options: a substance that produces OH⁻ ions in aqueous solution
a substance that produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution
a substance that releases electrons in water
a substance that is insoluble in water
questions.explain: Alkalis form hydroxide ions in water. They are soluble bases.

questions.q: Which substance is a base but is not an alkali?
questions.explain: Copper(II) oxide is a metal oxide so it is a base, but it is insoluble in water so it does not form an alkaline solution.

questions.q: Which statement about strong and weak acids is correct?
options: A strong acid must be concentrated.
A weak acid does not react with carbonates.
A weak acid can have a high concentration.
A strong acid is partially dissociated.
questions.explain: Strength and concentration are different. Concentration is how much acid is dissolved; strength is how much dissociates.

questions.q: Which equation shows that ethanoic acid is a weak acid?
questions.explain: The reversible arrow shows that only some molecules dissociate, so ethanoic acid is weak.

questions.q: Copper(II) oxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid. Which are the products?
questions.explain: An acid and a base form a salt and water: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. No gas is made.

questions.q: Which row shows the colours of the indicators correctly?
questions.explain: Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali. Litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali. Thymolphthalein is colourless in acid and blue in alkali.

questions.q: Which statement about a solution of a weak acid is correct?
options: It contains both undissociated molecules and ions.
It always has a pH above 7.
questions.explain: Only some molecules of a weak acid dissociate, so molecules and ions are both present.

questions.q: An acid is added to a solid and the mixture fizzes. The gas turns limewater milky. Which type of substance was the solid?
questions.explain: Fizzing with CO₂ produced shows the solid is a carbonate. A metal would give hydrogen instead.

questions.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid and to 0.1 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid at the same temperature. What is seen?
options: Bubbles form faster in the ethanoic acid.
Bubbles form only in the hydrochloric acid.
Bubbles form at the same rate in both.
Bubbles form faster in the hydrochloric acid.
questions.explain: Hydrochloric acid has the higher concentration of H⁺ ions, so the reaction is faster. Ethanoic acid still reacts, but more slowly.

questions.q: Universal indicator turns green in solution X. What does this show?
options: Solution X is a strong acid.
Solution X is neutral, with a pH of about 7.
Solution X is a weak alkali.
Solution X has a pH of about 12.
questions.explain: Universal indicator is green at pH 7, which is neutral. Acids give red, orange or yellow and alkalis give blue or purple.

questions.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which products form?
questions.explain: An acid reacts with a reactive metal to form a salt and hydrogen gas: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid?
questions.explain: Hydrochloric acid is strong and dissociates fully (→). Ethanoic acid is weak and partially dissociates (⇌).

questions.q: Which statement defines a base?
options: a substance that releases H⁺ ions in water
questions.explain: In the Brønsted–Lowry definition, an acid donates protons (H⁺) and a base accepts them.

questions.q: Which statement about methyl orange is correct?
options: It is blue in alkaline solutions.
It is yellow in alkaline solutions.
It is colourless in acidic solutions.
It is yellow in acidic solutions.
questions.explain: Methyl orange is red in acids and yellow in alkalis.

questions.q: Which statement about ethanoic acid is correct?
options: It does not react with carbonates because it is weak.
It is completely dissociated in water.
It reacts with metals to produce oxygen.
It reacts with sodium carbonate to produce carbon dioxide.
questions.explain: Weak acids still show the typical acid reactions. Ethanoic acid reacts with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which substance, when warmed with ammonium chloride, releases ammonia gas?
questions.explain: A base displaces ammonia from ammonium salts; calcium hydroxide is a base. Salts and acids do not do this.

questions.q: What is the colour of methyl orange in aqueous sodium hydroxide?
questions.explain: Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali.

questions.q: Which statement defines an acid?
options: a substance with a pH above 7
questions.explain: An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor.

questions.q: What is the colour of thymolphthalein in dilute nitric acid?
questions.explain: Thymolphthalein is colourless in acids and blue in alkalis.

questions.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is warmed with ammonium chloride. Which gas is given off?
questions.explain: A base displaces ammonia from an ammonium salt: NaOH + NH₄Cl → NaCl + H₂O + NH₃. Ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue.

questions.q: Which ions are present in all aqueous solutions of acids?
questions.explain: Acids produce hydrogen ions, H⁺(aq), in water. This is what makes them acidic.

questions.q: Dilute sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium carbonate and the gas given off is bubbled through limewater. What is seen in the limewater?
questions.explain: Acids react with carbonates to give carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky because insoluble calcium carbonate forms.

questions.q: Which pair of solutions would neutralise each other?
options: dilute sulfuric acid and aqueous potassium hydroxide
dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute nitric acid
aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous potassium hydroxide
questions.explain: Neutralisation needs an acid and a base or alkali. The other pairs contain two acids, two alkalis, or no acid or alkali.

questions.q: Which statement about bases and alkalis is correct?
options: All bases dissolve in water to form alkalis.
An alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
An alkali is any oxide of a non-metal.
A base is an acid that has been diluted.
questions.explain: Bases are metal oxides or hydroxides; only the soluble ones are called alkalis, so every alkali is a base but not every base is an alkali.

questions.q: Four solutions have the pH values shown. Which has the highest concentration of hydrogen ions?
questions.explain: The lower the pH, the higher the hydrogen ion concentration, so pH 1 is the most acidic.

questions.q: Which metal does not produce hydrogen when added to dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explain: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute acids.

questions.q: In the reaction HCl + NH₃ → NH₄Cl, what is the role of HCl?
options: It accepts a proton from NH₃.
It donates a proton to NH₃.
It accepts an electron from NH₃.
questions.explain: HCl transfers H⁺ to the lone pair on NH₃, so HCl is the proton donor (acid).

questions.q: Which indicator is colourless in dilute acid and blue in aqueous alkali?
questions.explain: Thymolphthalein is colourless in acids and blue in alkalis. Litmus is red/blue and methyl orange red/yellow.

questions.q: Which equation represents the neutralisation reaction between an acid and an alkali?
questions.explain: Neutralisation is the combination of hydrogen ions from the acid with hydroxide ions from the alkali to form water.

questions.q: What colour does universal indicator paper turn in a strongly acidic solution such as pH 1?
questions.explain: Universal indicator is red in strongly acidic solutions, green when neutral and purple in strongly alkaline solutions.

questions.q: Which of these is a base?
questions.explain: Bases are oxides or hydroxides of metals. Magnesium oxide is a metal oxide; the other three are non-metal compounds.

questions.q: Which statement about the oxide of an element X is correct if the solution made by dissolving it in water turns litmus red?
options: X is probably a noble gas.
X must be a transition element.
questions.explain: A non-metal oxide dissolving in water gives an acidic solution, which turns litmus red.

questions.q: Which observation is expected when excess dilute sodium hydroxide is added to solid aluminium oxide with stirring?
questions.explain: Because it is amphoteric, aluminium oxide reacts with the alkali and dissolves.

questions.q: Which equation for the reaction of zinc oxide with sulfuric acid is correct?
questions.explain: Zinc forms Zn²⁺, so the salt is ZnSO₄. The metal oxide acts as a base, giving a salt and water.

questions.q: Which oxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form a salt and water?
questions.explain: A basic oxide neutralises an acid. CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O.

questions.q: Which statement about the oxides of period 3 elements and their character is correct?
options: Aluminium oxide shows both acidic and basic properties.
questions.explain: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric, sodium oxide is basic and sulfur dioxide is acidic.

questions.q: Calcium oxide is added to water and the solution is tested with red litmus paper. What is observed?
questions.explain: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ forms an alkaline solution, which turns red litmus blue.

questions.q: Which two oxides are amphoteric?
questions.explain: Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are the amphoteric oxides in the syllabus. CuO and CaO are basic and CO₂ and SO₂ are acidic.

questions.q: Solid zinc oxide dissolves in both dilute hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide. What does this show?
questions.explain: Reacting with both acid and alkali shows amphoteric behaviour.

questions.q: Aluminium oxide reacts with both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. Which is the correct reason?
options: It is a strong oxidising agent.
questions.explain: Amphoteric oxides react as bases with acids and as acids with alkalis.

questions.q: Which oxide is basic?
questions.explain: Oxides of metals are basic. CaO is a metal oxide, but the other three are non-metal oxides, which are acidic.

questions.q: Which row classifies the oxides correctly?
questions.explain: CuO and CaO are metal oxides so they are basic, while CO₂ and SO₂ are acidic.

questions.q: Sulfur dioxide, SO₂, is a non-metal oxide. How is it classified?
questions.explain: Non-metal oxides such as SO₂ and CO₂ are acidic oxides because they react with bases and form acidic solutions.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide is bubbled through aqueous sodium hydroxide. What does this show about carbon dioxide?
options: It is a basic oxide because it reacts with a base.
It is a basic oxide because it forms a salt.
It is an acidic oxide because it reacts with acids.
It is an acidic oxide because it reacts with a base.
questions.explain: Acidic oxides react with bases to form a salt (here sodium carbonate) and water.

questions.q: Which compound is formed when sulfur trioxide reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
questions.explain: An acidic oxide with an alkali gives salt and water: SO₃ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O.

questions.q: Which equation for the reaction of aluminium oxide with hydrochloric acid is correct?
questions.explain: Al³⁺ needs three Cl⁻, and each O²⁻ from the oxide combines with 2H⁺ to give water. The balanced equation shows 6HCl, 2AlCl₃ and 3H₂O.

questions.q: Which row about aluminium oxide is correct?
options: reacts with acids: yes | reacts with alkalis: no
reacts with acids: no | reacts with alkalis: yes
reacts with acids: no | reacts with alkalis: no
reacts with acids: yes | reacts with alkalis: yes
questions.explain: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric, so it reacts with both.

questions.q: Which two oxides are both acidic?
questions.explain: SO₂ and CO₂ are both non-metal oxides, so both are acidic.

questions.q: A white oxide Y dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid and also in aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which could be Y?
questions.explain: Dissolving in both acid and alkali shows amphoteric behaviour. Al₂O₃ is amphoteric.

questions.q: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water. What is the pH of the solution formed?
questions.explain: SO₂ is an acidic oxide so its solution is acidic, with pH below 7.

questions.q: Which type of element usually forms an acidic oxide?
questions.explain: Non-metals form acidic oxides while metals form basic oxides.

questions.q: Which compound is classified differently from the other three?
questions.explain: ZnO is amphoteric, whereas CaO, CuO and MgO are basic oxides.

questions.q: Which statement describes an amphoteric oxide?
options: It reacts only with acids to form a salt and water.
It reacts with both acids and bases to form a salt and water.
It reacts only with bases to form a salt and water.
It does not react with acids or bases.
questions.explain: An amphoteric oxide has both acidic and basic behaviour, reacting with acids and with bases.

questions.q: Copper(II) oxide does not dissolve in aqueous sodium hydroxide but dissolves in dilute nitric acid. How is copper(II) oxide classified?
questions.explain: It reacts only with acids, not with alkalis, so it is purely basic.

questions.q: Which statement about metal oxides and non-metal oxides is correct?
options: Metal oxides are generally acidic and non-metal oxides generally basic.
Metal oxides are generally basic and non-metal oxides generally acidic.
questions.explain: The character of an oxide is linked to whether the element is metallic or non-metallic.

questions.q: What is the product (other than water) when zinc oxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explain: ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂O. This is typical of a base reacting with an acid.

questions.q: Iron(III) oxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. What does this indicate about iron(III) oxide?
questions.explain: Reaction with an acid to give a salt and water is characteristic of a basic oxide, which is a metal oxide.

questions.q: What is meant by an anhydrous substance?
options: a substance that absorbs water from air
a substance chemically combined with water
questions.explain: Anhydrous means 'without water'.

questions.q: A student wants to prepare pure crystals of potassium nitrate. Which reagents should be used?
options: potassium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid
potassium hydroxide and dilute sulfuric acid
potassium hydroxide solution and dilute nitric acid
questions.explain: Potassium is too reactive to add directly. The alkali and acid are mixed in exact amounts found by titration.

questions.q: What is meant by water of crystallisation?
options: water used to dissolve a solid before crystallising
water left on the crystals after filtering
water molecules that are part of the structure of hydrated crystals
water formed when an acid reacts with a base
questions.explain: Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules chemically combined within the crystals.

questions.q: Which acid and base are used to prepare copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide?
options: dilute sulfuric acid and excess copper(II) oxide
dilute hydrochloric acid and excess copper(II) oxide
dilute sulfuric acid and excess copper
dilute nitric acid and excess copper(II) oxide
questions.explain: The salt contains sulfate, so sulfuric acid is needed. Copper(II) oxide is an insoluble base that can be added in excess.

questions.q: Pink cobalt(II) chloride crystals, CoCl₂•6H₂O, are heated. Which colour change occurs?
questions.explain: Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride is pink. When heated it loses water and turns blue.

questions.q: Which pair of aqueous solutions could be used to make lead(II) sulfate?
questions.explain: Pb²⁺ with SO₄²⁻ gives insoluble lead(II) sulfate; the sodium nitrate formed is soluble and stays in the filtrate.

questions.q: Why can lead(II) nitrate not be made by adding excess lead to dilute nitric acid?
options: Lead is too unreactive to react well with dilute acid.
questions.explain: Lead reacts only very slowly with dilute acids. Lead(II) oxide or carbonate is usually used instead.

questions.q: Which compound is formed when excess zinc carbonate is added to dilute sulfuric acid?
questions.explain: ZnCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.

questions.q: What is the formula of hydrated copper(II) sulfate?
questions.explain: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals contain five molecules of water per formula unit.

questions.q: A salt solution is cooled and crystals form. What should be done to dry the crystals?
options: Pat them dry between filter paper.
Heat them strongly in a crucible.
questions.explain: Gentle drying keeps the water of crystallisation; strong heating would drive it off.

questions.q: Which pair of solutions, when mixed, forms a white precipitate?
options: aqueous sodium nitrate and aqueous potassium chloride
aqueous potassium sulfate and aqueous sodium nitrate
aqueous ammonium chloride and aqueous sodium sulfate
aqueous silver nitrate and aqueous sodium chloride
questions.explain: Silver chloride is an insoluble chloride. The other mixtures contain only soluble products.

questions.q: Why can sodium chloride not be prepared by adding excess sodium to dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Sodium does not react with acids.
questions.explain: Sodium is too reactive and would react explosively with the acid. Titration with sodium hydroxide is used instead.

questions.q: Which pair of aqueous solutions does NOT form a precipitate when mixed?
questions.explain: Sodium chloride and potassium nitrate can only form soluble compounds (NaNO₃ and KCl), so no precipitate forms.

questions.q: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals are heated strongly. What is the colour change?
questions.explain: Heating removes the water of crystallisation to form white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.

questions.q: Which row correctly shows the solubility of the salts in water?
questions.explain: Lead(II) sulfate is one of the insoluble sulfates. Nitrates, most chlorides and sulfates of potassium are soluble.

questions.q: Which compound is soluble in water?
questions.explain: All nitrates are soluble. Lead chloride, sulfate and carbonate are insoluble.

questions.q: Which statement about nitrates is correct?
options: All nitrates are insoluble in water.
All nitrates are soluble in water.
questions.explain: Every nitrate dissolves in water, so no precipitate forms from a nitrate by itself.

questions.q: Which hydroxide is soluble in water?
questions.explain: Hydroxides are insoluble except sodium, potassium, ammonium and calcium (partially).

questions.q: Excess calcium carbonate is added to dilute nitric acid. Which observation shows the reaction is complete?
options: Bubbles stop and some solid remains.
The solution becomes hot and boils.
questions.explain: CO₂ bubbles stop when all the acid is used, and the leftover solid shows the carbonate is in excess.

questions.q: Which salts are always soluble?
questions.explain: All salts of sodium, potassium and ammonium are soluble.

questions.q: Excess zinc is added to dilute hydrochloric acid until no more reacts. Which step is carried out next?
questions.explain: Excess zinc is removed by filtration, leaving zinc chloride solution.

questions.q: Which acid is used to prepare a nitrate salt?
questions.explain: The name of the salt comes from the acid: nitric acid gives nitrates, hydrochloric acid gives chlorides and sulfuric acid gives sulfates.

questions.q: Which compound is soluble in water?
questions.explain: Carbonates are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium.

questions.q: Water is added to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. What is seen?
options: The solid turns blue and gets hot.
questions.explain: Water recombines with copper(II) sulfate to give blue hydrated crystals in an exothermic change; this is a test for water.

questions.q: Aqueous barium nitrate is added to aqueous potassium sulfate. Which ionic equation is correct?
questions.explain: Barium sulfate is the insoluble product. The K⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions are spectators and stay in solution.

questions.q: During a titration to make a soluble salt, why is the experiment repeated without the indicator?
options: to make the solution more acidic
because the indicator reacts with the salt
so the crystals are not contaminated by the indicator
questions.explain: The volumes found with indicator are used again with no indicator, so the salt solution is pure.

questions.q: Which pair could be used to prepare magnesium sulfate?
options: dilute hydrochloric acid and magnesium carbonate
dilute sulfuric acid and excess copper
dilute sulfuric acid and excess magnesium carbonate
dilute nitric acid and magnesium hydroxide
questions.explain: The sulfate comes from sulfuric acid and the magnesium from magnesium carbonate, an insoluble carbonate that can be used in excess.

questions.q: After a precipitation reaction, the solid is filtered. What should be done to remove soluble impurities?
options: dissolve it in aqueous sodium hydroxide
wash the solid with distilled water
questions.explain: The insoluble salt will not dissolve in water, but soluble impurities will wash away.

questions.q: Which salt is insoluble in water?
questions.explain: Chlorides are soluble except those of silver and lead.

questions.q: A student adds copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid until no more dissolves. What is the next step?
options: filter the mixture to remove the excess solid
questions.explain: Excess copper(II) oxide is removed by filtration, leaving copper(II) sulfate solution as the filtrate.

questions.q: Which salt is insoluble in water?
questions.explain: Sulfates are soluble except those of barium, calcium and lead.

questions.q: What is meant by a hydrated substance?
options: a substance chemically combined with water
a substance with water on its surface
questions.explain: A hydrated substance has water molecules as part of its crystal structure.

questions.q: What is the percentage by mass of water in CuSO₄•5H₂O? (Ar: Cu = 64, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)
Which method is suitable for preparing insoluble barium sulfate?
options: adding excess barium to dilute sulfuric acid
titrating barium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid
precipitation by mixing aqueous barium chloride and aqueous sodium sulfate
adding excess barium oxide to dilute nitric acid
questions.explain: An insoluble salt is made by mixing two soluble salts that contain its ions, followed by filtering, washing and drying.

questions.q: Which method is used to prepare sodium chloride crystals from hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide?
options: adding excess sodium metal and filtering
titration followed by evaporation and crystallisation
adding excess sodium carbonate and filtering
questions.explain: Both reactants are soluble, so exact amounts are found by titration, then the solution is evaporated and crystallised.

questions.q: A salt solution is warmed until about half the water has evaporated, then left to cool. Why is the solution not heated to dryness?
options: Crystals form on cooling and heating to dryness could decompose the salt.
The salt would evaporate with the water.
Heating to dryness would make the salt insoluble.
Crystals only form when the solution is hot.
questions.explain: Heating until a saturated solution forms, then cooling lets crystals grow. Complete evaporation can spoil or decompose hydrated salts.

questions.q: A white solid forms when aqueous lead(II) nitrate is added to aqueous potassium chloride. Which equation, with state symbols, represents the reaction?
questions.explain: Lead chloride is insoluble. Two Cl⁻ ions balance one Pb²⁺, so the equation is Pb²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ → PbCl₂.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents the formation of silver chloride when aqueous silver nitrate is added to aqueous sodium chloride?
questions.explain: Only silver and chloride ions combine to form the insoluble solid. Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions.

questions.q: In the preparation of a soluble salt from an insoluble base, why is the base added in excess?
options: to make the reaction go faster
to make sure all the acid is used up
to make the salt purer after crystallising
questions.explain: Adding excess solid ensures all the acid is neutralised; the unreacted solid is then filtered off.

questions.q: Which sequence of steps gives crystals of zinc nitrate from excess zinc carbonate and dilute nitric acid?
options: evaporate the acid, add carbonate, then filter
add carbonate, cool, filter, then add more acid
add carbonate until no more dissolves, filter, evaporate part of the water, cool
filter the acid, add indicator, boil to dryness
questions.explain: Excess carbonate ensures neutralisation. The unreacted solid is filtered off, the filtrate is partly evaporated and then cooled to crystallise.

questions.q: What is the mass of 0.0100 mol of CuSO₄•5H₂O? (Ar: Cu = 64, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)
Which statement about the preparation of a soluble salt by titration is correct?
options: The salt is formed by precipitation.
An excess of insoluble base is added.
An indicator is used to find the volumes needed for neutralisation.
questions.explain: Titration uses an indicator to find the end-point, giving exactly the volumes needed for a pure solution of the salt.

questions.q: 2.50 g of CuSO₄•5H₂O is heated until all the water is removed. What is the mass of anhydrous CuSO₄ left? (Ar: Cu = 64, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.explain: Mr of CuSO₄•5H₂O = 250 and Mr of CuSO₄ = 160. 2.50 × 160 ÷ 250 = 1.60 g.

questions.q: Which statement about precipitation is correct?
options: It always requires an acid and an alkali.
It forms an insoluble salt when two solutions are mixed.
questions.explain: A precipitate forms when ions of an insoluble compound meet in solution.

questions.q: Element X reacts with cold water more violently than potassium does. Where is X most likely to be in the Periodic Table?
questions.explain: Reactivity of Group I metals increases down the group, so X is a Group I metal below potassium.

questions.q: Which pair of elements is in the same period of the Periodic Table?
questions.explain: Sodium and chlorine both have three occupied shells (Period 3); the other pairs are in the same group.

questions.q: The boiling points of three halogens are: chlorine −35 °C, bromine 59 °C, iodine 184 °C. Which is the most likely boiling point of astatine?
questions.explain: Boiling points rise down Group VII, so astatine, below iodine, should be above 184 °C.

questions.q: Which statement about the positions of metals and non-metals in the Periodic Table is correct?
options: Metals are mainly on the right; non-metals are mainly on the left.
Metals are found only in the centre; non-metals are found only at the edges.
Metals are mainly on the left and in the centre; non-metals are mainly on the right.
Metals and non-metals are mixed evenly across every period.
questions.explain: Metallic character is strongest on the left and in the centre, and non-metals are grouped towards the right.

questions.q: Which row correctly names the horizontal rows and the vertical columns of the Periodic Table?
questions.explain: Horizontal rows are called periods and vertical columns are called groups.

questions.q: In the Periodic Table the elements are arranged in order of increasing
questions.explain: The modern Periodic Table is ordered by proton (atomic) number, the number of protons in the nucleus.

questions.q: An atom has the electronic configuration 2,8,8,1. Which statement about its position is correct?
options: It is in Group IV and Period 1.
It is in Group I and Period 3.
It is in Group VIII and Period 4.
It is in Group I and Period 4.
questions.explain: One outer electron gives Group I; four occupied shells give Period 4.

questions.q: Sodium is in Group I and oxygen is in Group VI. What is the formula of sodium oxide?
questions.explain: Na⁺ and O²⁻ combine in the ratio 2 : 1, giving Na₂O.

questions.q: Which statement describes the elements from lithium to neon across Period 2?
options: The number of occupied electron shells increases by one each time.
The number of outer-shell electrons decreases by one each time.
The number of outer-shell electrons increases by one from each element to the next.
The number of protons stays the same.
questions.explain: All Period 2 atoms have two shells, while the outer electron count rises from 1 to 8.

questions.q: What happens to the character of the elements across Period 3, from sodium to chlorine?
options: non-metallic character changes to metallic character
metallic character changes to non-metallic character
questions.explain: Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals on the left; sulfur and chlorine are non-metals on the right.

questions.q: Fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas and bromine is a red-brown liquid. What is the most likely appearance of iodine at r.t.p.?
questions.explain: Halogens get darker and denser down the group, and the physical state changes from gas to liquid to solid.

questions.q: The melting points of three Group I metals are: lithium 181 °C, sodium 98 °C, potassium 63 °C. Which value is most likely for rubidium?
questions.explain: Melting points fall steadily down Group I, so rubidium must be lower than potassium (63 °C).

questions.q: Magnesium forms MgO and calcium forms CaO. Which is the formula of barium oxide?
questions.explain: Barium is in Group II and forms Ba²⁺, which combines 1 : 1 with O²⁻.

questions.q: Calcium is in Group II. What is the charge on a calcium ion?
questions.explain: Group II atoms have two outer electrons, which they lose to form 2+ ions.

questions.q: Strontium, Sr, is in Group II. Which formula is most likely for strontium chloride?
questions.explain: Group II elements form 2+ ions and chloride is Cl⁻, so two chloride ions balance one Sr²⁺ ion.

questions.q: Which element in Period 3 is a non-metal?
questions.explain: Sulfur is on the right-hand side of Period 3 and is a non-metal; the other three are metals.

questions.q: An atom of an element in Group III has how many outer-shell electrons?
questions.explain: The group number equals the number of outer-shell electrons for these groups, so Group III has 3.

questions.q: Which two elements are most likely to have similar chemical properties?
questions.explain: Calcium and strontium are both in Group II, so their atoms have the same number of outer electrons.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the element sulfur?
questions.explain: Sulfur has six outer electrons (Group VI) and gains two electrons to form S²⁻.

questions.q: Aluminium is in Group III and Period 3. What is the electronic configuration of an aluminium atom?
questions.explain: Three shells are occupied (Period 3) and there are three outer electrons (Group III): 2,8,3.

questions.q: An atom has the electronic configuration 2,8,6. Which row gives its position in the Periodic Table?
questions.explain: Six outer electrons place it in Group VI, and three occupied shells place it in Period 3.

questions.q: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical properties?
options: Their atoms have the same number of electron shells.
Their atoms have the same number of protons.
Their atoms have the same number of outer-shell electrons.
Their atoms have the same relative atomic mass.
questions.explain: Chemical reactions involve outer electrons, so the same number of outer electrons gives similar reactions.

questions.q: Elements in Group V (such as nitrogen) form ions with a charge of
questions.explain: Group V atoms have 5 outer electrons and gain 3 electrons to complete the shell, forming 3− ions.

questions.q: Which statement compares atoms of lithium, sodium and potassium?
options: They have a different number of outer electrons but the same number of shells.
They have the same number of shells and the same number of protons.
They have the same number of protons but a different number of outer electrons.
They have the same number of outer electrons but a different number of shells.
questions.explain: Group I atoms each have one outer electron; each lower element has one more occupied shell.

questions.q: Which block of elements lies between Group II and Group III in the Periodic Table?
questions.explain: The transition elements form a central block between Groups II and III in the long periods.

questions.q: An element has proton number 12. Where is it in the Periodic Table?
questions.explain: Proton number 12 gives the configuration 2,8,2: two outer electrons (Group II) in three shells (Period 3).

questions.q: Which element forms an ion with a charge of 1−?
questions.explain: Fluorine is in Group VII and gains one electron to form F⁻. Oxygen forms 2− ions, sodium forms 1+ ions and neon forms no ions.

questions.q: Element P does not displace chlorine from aqueous sodium chloride but does displace iodine from aqueous sodium iodide. Which could P be?
questions.explain: P is less reactive than chlorine but more reactive than iodine, so it lies between them in Group VII: bromine.

questions.q: A newly discovered element has atoms with 7 outer electrons and 5 occupied electron shells. Where is it in the Periodic Table?
questions.explain: Outer electrons give the group number (VII) and the number of occupied shells gives the period (5).

questions.q: Which prediction about astatine, At, below iodine in Group VII, is most likely to be correct?
options: It is more reactive than chlorine.
It would displace iodine from potassium iodide.
It is a pale-coloured gas at r.t.p.
It is less reactive than iodine.
questions.explain: Reactivity decreases down Group VII, and the elements become darker solids, so At is less reactive than I.

questions.q: Potassium has a relative atomic mass of 39. What volume of hydrogen at r.t.p. is made when 0.39 g of potassium reacts completely with water? (1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.)
Caesium is in Group I below rubidium. Which property is it most likely to have compared with potassium?
questions.explain: Melting points decrease down Group I, so caesium melts at a lower temperature than potassium.

questions.q: Which equation correctly shows lithium reacting with water?
questions.explain: The balanced equation has two Li, four H and two O on each side, with LiOH as the alkali.

questions.q: A Group I metal M is predicted to react with chlorine. Which equation is correct?
questions.explain: M forms M⁺ ions, so the product is MCl; two atoms of M are needed for one Cl₂ molecule.

questions.q: Potassium is added to water. Which observation is correct?
options: It sinks to the bottom and fizzes slowly.
It stays still and slowly dissolves.
It floats and burns with a red flame.
It moves quickly on the surface and burns with a lilac flame.
questions.explain: Potassium reacts vigorously, melts and the hydrogen produced burns with a lilac flame.

questions.q: Sodium reacts with water to give sodium hydroxide. When all of 2.3 g of sodium (Aᵣ = 23) is used to make 1.0 dm³ of solution, what is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?
questions.explain: 2.3 g is 0.10 mol Na, which gives 0.10 mol NaOH in 1.0 dm³, so the concentration is 0.10 mol/dm³.

questions.q: What is the test for the gas produced when potassium reacts with water?
options: A lit splint goes out with a squeaky pop.
questions.explain: Hydrogen is tested with a burning splint, which gives a squeaky pop.

questions.q: A freshly cut piece of sodium quickly becomes dull. What is the reason?
options: The surface melts in the air.
The surface reacts with nitrogen to form a gas.
The surface dissolves in the air.
The surface reacts with oxygen in the air.
questions.explain: Sodium is reactive and its shiny surface is quickly covered with a layer of oxide.

questions.q: Which row shows the general trends down Group I?
questions.explain: Down Group I the melting point decreases while the density and the reactivity generally increase.

questions.q: Rubidium is in Group I below potassium. How does it react with water?
options: At the same rate as potassium
questions.explain: Reactivity increases down the group, so rubidium reacts more vigorously than potassium.

questions.q: What is the charge on the ion formed by every Group I metal?
questions.explain: Each Group I atom has one outer electron which it loses to form a 1+ ion.

questions.q: Why are sodium and potassium stored under oil?
options: They react with oxygen and water in the air.
They are too dense to be kept in air.
They would melt at room temperature.
questions.explain: Group I metals are very reactive and would react with oxygen and moisture if they were left exposed.

questions.q: Which equation correctly shows potassium reacting with water?
questions.explain: Potassium forms K⁺, so the hydroxide is KOH; two K and two H₂O balance the equation.

questions.q: Which gas is made when sodium reacts with water?
questions.explain: Group I metals displace hydrogen from water, forming hydrogen gas and a metal hydroxide.

questions.q: After sodium reacts completely with water, Universal Indicator is added to the solution. What colour does it turn?
questions.explain: Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali, so the indicator turns purple (high pH).

questions.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react with water to form an alkaline solution. Which ion in the solution makes it alkaline?
questions.explain: The metal hydroxide dissolves to release hydroxide ions, OH⁻, which make the solution alkaline.

questions.q: Which statement about lithium, sodium and potassium is correct?
options: They are hard metals with very high melting points.
They are soft metals that can be cut with a knife.
They are dense metals that sink in oil.
questions.explain: Group I metals are soft enough to cut, and they have low melting points and low densities.

questions.q: What is the formula of rubidium chloride, given that rubidium is in Group I?
questions.explain: Group I metals form 1+ ions, so Rb⁺ combines 1 : 1 with Cl⁻.

questions.q: Which Group I metal is the most reactive?
questions.explain: Reactivity increases down Group I, so of these three potassium is the most reactive.

questions.q: Why is potassium more reactive than lithium?
options: Its outer electron is closer to the nucleus, so it is lost more easily.
Its outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily.
It has more outer electrons to lose than lithium.
Its atoms have fewer protons than lithium atoms.
questions.explain: A potassium atom has more shells, so the single outer electron is held less strongly and is lost more readily.

questions.q: Lithium is added to a trough of water. Which observation is correct?
options: It floats and fizzes steadily as a gas is produced.
It sinks and dissolves without bubbles.
It melts into a ball and burns with a lilac flame.
It stays unchanged on the surface.
questions.explain: Lithium floats on water and fizzes steadily as hydrogen gas is made. It does not melt or ignite.

questions.q: Sodium has a relative atomic mass of 23. What volume of hydrogen at r.t.p. is made when 2.3 g of sodium reacts completely with water? (1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.)
questions.explain: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂: 2.3 g = 0.10 mol Na gives 0.050 mol H₂, which is 0.050 × 24 = 1.2 dm³.

questions.q: 4.6 g of sodium (Aᵣ = 23) reacts completely with water. What mass of sodium hydroxide (Mᵣ = 40) is formed?
questions.explain: 4.6 g is 0.20 mol Na; 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ gives 0.20 mol NaOH; 0.20 × 40 = 8.0 g.

questions.q: How does the melting point change down Group I from lithium to potassium?
questions.explain: The melting points are lithium 181 °C, sodium 98 °C and potassium 63 °C, so they decrease down the group.

questions.q: Which statement describes how sodium differs from a typical transition element such as iron?
options: Sodium is harder and has a higher melting point.
Sodium is softer and has a lower melting point.
Sodium is denser and has a higher melting point.
Sodium is softer and has a higher melting point.
questions.explain: Group I metals are soft with low melting points; iron is hard with a high melting point.

questions.q: Which statement about the density of Group I metals is correct?
options: All Group I metals are denser than iron.
Lithium is much less dense than water.
Lithium sinks in water because it is dense.
Densities decrease strongly from lithium to caesium.
questions.explain: Lithium has a very low density (0.53 g/cm³) and floats on water; the general trend is an increase down the group.

questions.q: Reactivity of the halogens decreases down Group VII. Which halogen is the most reactive?
questions.explain: Reactivity decreases down Group VII, so chlorine, at the top of this list, is the most reactive.

questions.q: 0.10 mol of chlorine reacts with excess aqueous potassium bromide. What mass of bromine (relative molecular mass 160) is formed?
questions.explain: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ gives 0.10 mol Br₂, and 0.10 × 160 = 16 g.

questions.q: What is the appearance of bromine at r.t.p.?
questions.explain: Bromine is a red-brown liquid at r.t.p.; chlorine is a gas and iodine is a solid.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes chlorine, bromine and iodine at r.t.p.?
questions.explain: Chlorine is a gas, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid, so the state changes down the group.

questions.q: Astatine is below iodine in Group VII. Which property is it most likely to have?
questions.explain: Halogens get darker and denser down the group, so astatine is a dark solid.

questions.q: How many electrons does a chlorine atom gain to form a chloride ion?
questions.explain: A chlorine atom has 7 outer electrons and gains one electron to complete its outer shell.

questions.q: Which equation shows chlorine displacing bromine from aqueous potassium bromide?
questions.explain: Two bromide ions must be displaced to form one Br₂ molecule, so the equation needs 2KBr and 2KCl.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents the reaction of chlorine with aqueous potassium iodide?
questions.explain: Potassium ions are spectators. The halide ions are exchanged and the charges balance on both sides.

questions.q: How does the density of the halogens change down Group VII?
questions.explain: The density increases down the group, as shown by the change from gas to liquid to solid.

questions.q: How does the colour of the halogens change down the group?
options: It changes from dark to pale and back.
questions.explain: The colours go from pale yellow-green to red-brown to grey-black, getting darker.

questions.q: Bromine water is added to aqueous potassium iodide. Which observation and explanation are correct?
options: The solution turns brown because iodine displaces bromine.
The solution turns brown because bromine displaces iodine.
The solution stays orange because bromine is less reactive than iodine.
The solution turns colourless because bromine reacts with water.
questions.explain: Bromine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodine, which colours the solution brown.

questions.q: Chlorine, bromine and iodine each have how many electrons in their outer shell?
questions.explain: They are all in Group VII, so each has 7 outer-shell electrons.

questions.q: Which formula is correct for sodium fluoride?
questions.explain: Na⁺ and F⁻ have equal and opposite charges, so they combine 1 : 1.

questions.q: In the reaction Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, which statement is correct?
options: Chlorine is oxidised and bromide ions are reduced.
Both chlorine and bromide ions are reduced.
Chlorine is reduced and bromide ions are oxidised.
Both chlorine and bromide ions are oxidised.
questions.explain: Chlorine gains electrons (reduction); bromide ions lose electrons (oxidation).

questions.q: Which row gives a halogen and its correct appearance at r.t.p.?
questions.explain: Bromine is a red-brown liquid; chlorine is a gas and iodine is a solid.

questions.q: What is the appearance of chlorine at r.t.p.?
questions.explain: Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas at room temperature and pressure.

questions.q: Fluorine is at the top of Group VII. Which prediction is most likely to be correct?
options: It is a very reactive pale yellow gas.
It is an unreactive dark solid.
questions.explain: Halogens are most reactive at the top of the group, and the elements get paler and less dense up the group.

questions.q: Which pair of solutions would react together?
options: aqueous iodine and aqueous potassium bromide
aqueous iodine and aqueous sodium chloride
aqueous bromine and aqueous sodium chloride
aqueous bromine and aqueous potassium iodide
questions.explain: Only a more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halide ion: Br₂ is more reactive than I₂.

questions.q: Why is chlorine more reactive than iodine?
options: A chlorine atom has more outer electrons than an iodine atom.
A chlorine atom has more electron shells than an iodine atom.
A chlorine atom attracts an extra electron more strongly than an iodine atom.
A chlorine atom loses electrons more easily than an iodine atom.
questions.explain: Chlorine's outer shell is nearer the nucleus, so the incoming electron is attracted more strongly.

questions.q: Which formula represents a molecule of chlorine?
questions.explain: Halogens are diatomic: two atoms are joined by a covalent bond in each molecule.

questions.q: Which mixture shows no reaction?
questions.explain: A halogen only displaces a less reactive halogen; iodine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace it.

questions.q: Which halide ion is displaced from solution by both chlorine and bromine?
questions.explain: Iodide is the least reactive halogen of these, so both chlorine and bromine, being more reactive, displace it as iodine.

questions.q: Which statement about halogens is correct?
questions.explain: Halogens consist of non-metal atoms joined in pairs by covalent bonds.

questions.q: Which halogen is the most reactive of chlorine, bromine and iodine?
questions.explain: Reactivity decreases down the group, so chlorine, at the top, is the most reactive of the three.

questions.q: How does the reactivity of the halogens change down Group VII?
questions.explain: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, which is more reactive than iodine.

questions.q: What is the appearance of iodine at r.t.p.?
questions.explain: Iodine is a grey-black solid at r.t.p.

questions.q: A halogen X₂ does not react with aqueous sodium chloride or aqueous sodium bromide, but it does react with aqueous sodium iodide. What is X₂?
questions.explain: Bromine does not displace chloride or bromide ions, but it displaces iodide. Only bromine fits all three results.

questions.q: Chlorine gas is bubbled through aqueous potassium bromide. What is seen?
questions.explain: Chlorine displaces bromine, because it is more reactive. Aqueous bromine is orange-brown.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of iron in Fe₂O₃?
questions.explain: Three O²⁻ give a total of 6−, so each of the two iron atoms must be +3.

questions.q: Compared with Group I metals, transition elements are generally
questions.explain: Transition metals are hard and strong with high densities, unlike soft, low-density Group I metals.

questions.q: Manganese(IV) oxide is added to hydrogen peroxide solution. Oxygen is released rapidly. Which statement is correct?
options: The manganese(IV) oxide acts as a catalyst.
The manganese(IV) oxide is the reactant that makes oxygen.
The manganese(IV) oxide is permanently used up.
The manganese(IV) oxide acts as an oxidising agent only.
questions.explain: Manganese(IV) oxide speeds up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide and is unchanged at the end.

questions.q: Iron is used in the Haber process to speed up the reaction without being used up. What is iron acting as?
questions.explain: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction and is not used up, and transition elements often act as catalysts.

questions.q: Which property shows that iron is a transition element?
options: It forms ions with different oxidation numbers.
It forms only one type of ion.
It has a lower density than Group I metals.
questions.explain: Transition elements have variable oxidation numbers: iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.

questions.q: Which element is a transition element?
questions.explain: Nickel lies in the central block of the Periodic Table; the others are in Groups I, II and VII.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the physical properties of transition elements such as iron and copper?
questions.explain: Transition elements are dense metals with high melting points.

questions.q: Which compound is blue in colour?
questions.explain: Copper(II) compounds are coloured (blue), while compounds of Group I and II metals are usually white.

questions.q: Which statement about copper(II) and iron(II) compounds is correct?
options: Both can be coloured because they are compounds of transition elements.
Both are white because they contain metal ions.
Both are unreactive because the metals are unreactive.
questions.explain: Compounds of transition elements are generally coloured, such as blue copper(II) and green iron(II) compounds.

questions.q: Which change is the oxidation of an iron(II) ion?
questions.explain: Oxidation is loss of electrons: Fe²⁺ loses one electron to form Fe³⁺.

questions.q: In which part of the Periodic Table are the transition elements found?
options: on the far right, next to the noble gases
in the central block between Groups II and III
on the far left, in Group I
at the top of Group VII
questions.explain: Transition elements form a block of metals between Group II and Group III.

questions.q: Which description fits a transition element?
options: a non-metal with a low melting point and colourless compounds
a metal with a low melting point and white compounds
a metal with a high melting point and coloured compounds
questions.explain: Transition elements are metals with high melting points and coloured compounds.

questions.q: What is the name of the compound with the formula Fe₂(SO₄)₃?
questions.explain: The two Fe ions balance three SO₄²⁻ ions (total 6−), so each Fe is 3+.

questions.q: The compound FeCl₂ is named iron(II) chloride. What is the formula of iron(III) chloride?
questions.explain: Iron(III) forms Fe³⁺, which needs three Cl⁻ ions to balance the charge.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares iron with sodium?
options: Iron has a higher melting point and a higher density.
Iron has a lower melting point and a higher density.
Iron has a higher melting point and a lower density.
Iron has a lower melting point and a lower density.
questions.explain: Iron is a typical transition metal with a high melting point and high density; sodium is soft with a low melting point and a low density.

questions.q: Which row correctly shows the oxidation numbers of iron in the two compounds?
questions.explain: FeSO₄ contains Fe²⁺ with SO₄²⁻, and Fe₂(SO₄)₃ contains Fe³⁺ ions.

questions.q: Which statement is a property of transition elements and their compounds?
options: They have very low melting points.
questions.explain: Transition element compounds are typically coloured, for example blue copper(II) sulfate.

questions.q: Which statement about transition elements as catalysts is correct?
options: They are never used as catalysts.
They are often used as catalysts as elements and in compounds.
Only their compounds, not the elements, can act as catalysts.
They are used up when they act as catalysts.
questions.explain: Both transition elements and their compounds are often catalysts, for example iron and manganese(IV) oxide.

questions.q: Why can iron form two different chlorides, FeCl₂ and FeCl₃?
options: It has different numbers of protons in each compound.
It is a Group II element.
It can form ions with different charges.
It forms molecules rather than ions.
questions.explain: Transition elements like iron can lose different numbers of electrons, forming Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.

questions.q: Iron reacts with chlorine to form iron(III) chloride. Which equation is correct?
questions.explain: Two Fe and six Cl are required on each side for balance, so 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃.

questions.q: Which compound is likely to be coloured?
questions.explain: Compounds of transition elements are coloured; compounds of Group I and II elements are generally white.

questions.q: A balloon is filled with helium. Which property of helium makes it suitable?
options: It is reactive and denser than air.
It is unreactive and denser than air.
It is unreactive and less dense than air.
It is flammable and less dense than air.
questions.explain: Helium is unreactive, so it is safe, and it has a lower density than air so the balloon rises.

questions.q: The densities of three noble gases at r.t.p. are: helium 0.17 g/dm³, neon 0.84 g/dm³, argon 1.66 g/dm³. Which is the most likely density of krypton?
questions.explain: Density rises down the group, so krypton, below argon, must be greater than 1.66 g/dm³.

questions.q: Why are the noble gases unreactive?
options: Their atoms have a single outer electron.
Their atoms are very large and heavy.
Their atoms have full outer shells of electrons.
questions.explain: A full outer shell is stable, so noble gas atoms do not need to gain, lose or share electrons.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes chlorine and argon at r.t.p.?
questions.explain: Chlorine exists as Cl₂ molecules, whereas argon is monatomic and exists as single atoms.

questions.q: Which statement describes the noble gases?
questions.explain: Noble gases exist as separate single atoms because they do not form bonds.

questions.q: Which group of the Periodic Table contains the noble gases?
questions.explain: The noble gases are in Group VIII (also called Group 0).

questions.q: Which statement is true for noble gases?
options: Their atoms do not form ions in ordinary reactions.
Their atoms form diatomic molecules by covalent bonds.
questions.explain: Because their outer shells are full, they do not form ions or covalent bonds under ordinary conditions.

questions.q: Why do the noble gases not form compounds easily?
options: They have only one outer electron.
They do not need to gain, lose or share electrons.
questions.explain: The outer shells are full, so atoms have no tendency to react.

questions.q: Why is argon used to fill filament lamps?
options: It reacts with the filament to make light.
It does not react with the hot filament.
It is denser than the filament.
It reacts with oxygen to protect the filament.
questions.explain: Argon is unreactive, so it prevents the filament from burning without reacting with it.

questions.q: Which atom has a full outer shell of electrons?
questions.explain: Neon has the configuration 2,8, which is a full outer shell; the other atoms have incomplete outer shells.

questions.q: What is the electronic configuration of an argon atom?
questions.explain: Argon has 18 electrons; its outer shell holds 8 electrons and is full.

questions.q: Which explanation of the unreactivity of neon is correct?
options: Its outer shell has 7 electrons and needs one more.
Its outer shell is full, so it neither gains nor loses electrons nor shares them easily.
Its outer shell has 1 electron which is lost easily.
Its atoms are joined in pairs by covalent bonds.
questions.explain: The configuration of 2,8 is stable, so neon does not form ions or covalent bonds.

questions.q: Which formula represents helium gas?
questions.explain: Helium is monatomic, so its formula is simply He.

questions.q: The noble gases are in Group VIII. Which statement about the elements in this group is correct?
options: They are all liquids at r.t.p.
They are all solids at r.t.p.
They are all gases at r.t.p.
questions.explain: The elements of Group VIII, from helium to radon, are gases at room temperature.

questions.q: How many electrons are in the outer shell of a neon atom?
questions.explain: Neon is 2,8, so its outer shell holds 8 electrons.

questions.q: Which row describes a typical metal?
questions.explain: Metals conduct heat well, usually have high melting points and are malleable, unlike most non-metals.

questions.q: What does it mean when a metal is described as ductile?
options: It can be hammered into thin sheets
It can be drawn out into wires
It makes a ringing sound when struck
questions.explain: Ductile means a material can be stretched into wire; being hammered into sheets is malleability.

questions.q: A solid conducts electricity and can be bent without breaking. What is it most likely to be?
questions.explain: Metals conduct as solids and are malleable, whereas sulfur, ionic solids and simple covalent solids do not conduct and are brittle or crumbly.

questions.q: Which products form when a metal such as zinc reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?
questions.explain: Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series displace hydrogen from acids, giving a salt and hydrogen gas.

questions.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which gas is given off and how is it identified?
options: Hydrogen, which relights a glowing splint
Hydrogen, which burns with a squeaky pop
Oxygen, which burns with a squeaky pop
Chlorine, which bleaches damp litmus paper
questions.explain: The gas is hydrogen, and a lighted splint held at the mouth of the tube makes a squeaky pop.

questions.q: Which type of oxide do most metals form when they react with oxygen?
questions.explain: Metal oxides are basic (they react with acids to form salts), while many non-metal oxides are acidic.

questions.q: Calcium reacts with cold water. Which pair of products forms?
questions.explain: A reactive metal and cold water give the metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

questions.q: Magnesium ribbon is heated in air until it ignites. Which observation is correct?
options: An orange flame and a black solid
A blue flame and a colourless gas
A bright white flame and a white solid
A red flame and a green solid
questions.explain: Magnesium burns with a bright white flame to form white magnesium oxide, MgO.

questions.q: Which statement about metals is correct?
options: Most are liquids at room temperature
Most have lower melting points than non-metals
Most are solids at room temperature with high melting points
questions.explain: Only mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature, and most metals have high melting and boiling points.

questions.q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
options: Positive ions move through the structure
Electrons are held in fixed positions between atoms
Delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice
Mobile negative ions carry the charge
questions.explain: In a metal the outer electrons are delocalised and move, carrying charge; the positive ions stay in fixed positions.

questions.q: A student tests four solids. Which result is the best evidence that solid X is a metal?
options: It conducts electricity when solid and is malleable
It has a low melting point and does not conduct
It conducts electricity only when molten
questions.explain: Conduction as a solid together with malleability is typical of metals; ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved.

questions.q: Which statement about non-metals is correct?
options: Most solid non-metals are brittle and poor conductors of heat
Most solid non-metals are malleable and ductile
Most solid non-metals conduct electricity well
questions.explain: Non-metals are generally brittle as solids and poor thermal and electrical conductors; graphite is an exception.

questions.q: 0.24 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess dilute sulfuric acid. What volume of hydrogen forms at room temperature and pressure? (Ar: Mg = 24; 1 mol of gas = 24 000 cm³)
questions.explain: Moles of Mg = 0.24 ÷ 24 = 0.010 mol; Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂ gives 0.010 mol H₂, which is 0.010 × 24 000 = 240 cm³.

questions.q: Which is a chemical property of metals rather than a physical property?
questions.explain: Reacting with acids changes the metal into a new substance, so it is chemical; the others describe physical behaviour.

questions.q: Which property of aluminium makes it suitable for the body of an aircraft?
questions.explain: A low density keeps the aircraft light so less fuel is needed.

questions.q: Which pair of properties makes aluminium suitable for overhead electrical cables?
options: Low density and good electrical conductivity
High density and good electrical conductivity
Low density and poor electrical conductivity
High density and poor electrical conductivity
questions.explain: The cables must carry current and also be light enough to be supported between pylons.

questions.q: Why is aluminium used to make food containers?
options: It has a very high melting point
questions.explain: Aluminium does not corrode easily, so the container and the food stay in good condition.

questions.q: Which row correctly matches a metal, a use and the property that makes it suitable?
options: Copper | electrical wiring | ductile and a good conductor
questions.explain: Copper can be drawn into wires and conducts electricity well, so it is used in wiring.

questions.q: Copper wires in a household cable are covered with plastic. Why?
options: Plastic conducts electricity better than copper
Plastic reacts with the copper to make it stronger
questions.explain: The plastic insulates the wire so people are not shocked and current stays in the copper.

questions.q: Which property of copper makes it suitable for the base of a cooking pan?
options: It is a good electrical insulator
It is a good conductor of heat
questions.explain: Heat must pass quickly from the cooker through the base into the food.

questions.q: Aluminium is a reactive metal, yet aluminium food containers hardly corrode. Why?
options: Aluminium is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
A thin layer of aluminium oxide on the surface protects the metal
Aluminium does not react with oxygen
Manufacturers always coat it with zinc
questions.explain: Aluminium reacts quickly with oxygen to form an unreactive oxide layer that stops further reaction.

questions.q: Why are aluminium cables preferred to copper cables on long overhead power lines?
options: Aluminium is a better electrical conductor than copper
Aluminium has a higher density so the cables are stronger
Aluminium has a lower density so the cables are lighter
Aluminium is magnetic and stays on the pylon
questions.explain: Aluminium conducts well enough and is much less dense than copper, so the cables put less load on the pylons.

questions.q: Which property of metals allows steel to be pressed into car body panels?
questions.explain: Malleable metals can be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking.

questions.q: The density of aluminium is 2.7 g/cm³ and of copper is 9.0 g/cm³. How much less mass does 1000 cm³ of aluminium have than 1000 cm³ of copper?
questions.explain: Mass = density × volume: copper 9.0 × 1000 = 9000 g, aluminium 2.7 × 1000 = 2700 g, so the difference is 6300 g.

questions.q: Which property of copper allows it to be pulled into long thin wires?
questions.explain: Ductile metals can be drawn out into wire.

questions.q: Which statement about aluminium is correct?
options: It has a high density and is a poor conductor
It has a low density and conducts electricity well
questions.explain: These properties explain its use in aircraft and overhead cables.

questions.q: What is an alloy?
options: A mixture of a metal with other elements
A pure metal with a coating
questions.explain: An alloy is a mixture, not a compound, and contains at least one metal.

questions.q: Which two metals are mixed to make brass?
questions.explain: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc; copper and tin make bronze.

questions.q: Which elements are mixed with iron in stainless steel?
questions.explain: Stainless steel is iron with other elements such as chromium, nickel and carbon.

questions.q: Stainless steel is used for cutlery. Which properties make it suitable?
options: It is hard and resists rusting
It is soft and easily shaped
It is a good conductor of electricity
It has a very low density
questions.explain: Cutlery must stay hard and must not rust when washed and used with food.

questions.q: How do alloys generally compare with the pure metals they are made from?
options: They are always softer and weaker
They are often harder and stronger
They always have lower melting points
questions.explain: Mixing in other atoms usually makes the metal harder and stronger, so alloys are often more useful.

questions.q: Which description of a structure represents an alloy?
options: A lattice of identical atoms in regular layers
A lattice with atoms of two different sizes mixed together
A lattice of alternating positive and negative ions
Separate small molecules held by weak forces
questions.explain: An alloy contains atoms of different sizes, which disturbs the regular layers of a pure metal.

questions.q: Which description of a structure represents a pure metal?
options: Atoms of two different sizes mixed together
Identical atoms arranged in regular layers
Positive and negative ions alternating in a lattice
Small molecules arranged in a lattice
questions.explain: A pure metal has only one type of atom, so the layers are regular.

questions.q: Why are alloys often harder than the pure metals in them?
options: Atoms of different sizes stop the layers sliding over each other easily
Alloys have stronger metallic bonds because they contain more electrons
All the atoms are the same size so the layers lock together
Alloys contain covalent bonds between the metals
questions.explain: The different-sized atoms distort the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over one another as easily.

questions.q: Why is a pure metal usually soft and malleable?
options: The atoms are held by weak covalent bonds
The positive ions are free to move out of the lattice
The layers of identical atoms can slide over each other
The metal contains many different sizes of atom
questions.explain: In a pure metal the regular layers slide when a force is applied, so the metal changes shape without breaking.

questions.q: Which of these is an alloy?
questions.explain: Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc; zinc is an element and the other two are compounds.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes an alloy?
options: Brass | copper and tin | harder than copper
Stainless steel | iron and chromium | resists rusting
Stainless steel | iron and copper | resists rusting
Brass | iron and zinc | harder than copper
questions.explain: Stainless steel contains iron with chromium and other elements and does not rust easily, while brass is copper and zinc.

questions.q: Pure iron is soft, but steel is hard. Why does adding a little carbon make the iron harder?
options: Carbon atoms make the iron atoms smaller so they fit together better
Carbon forms ionic bonds with iron
Carbon atoms add delocalised electrons that stop the layers moving
Carbon atoms are a different size so the layers of iron atoms cannot slide easily
questions.explain: The carbon atoms differ in size from iron atoms, distorting the layers and making sliding more difficult.

questions.q: Steel is stronger than pure iron. What is steel?
options: Iron mixed with a small amount of carbon
A compound of iron and carbon only
Pure iron with a layer of rust
Iron mixed with a large amount of zinc
questions.explain: Steel is an alloy, a mixture of iron with a small percentage of carbon.

questions.q: Why is mild steel not suitable for making cutlery?
options: It is too hard to shape
It rusts in contact with water and air
It has too low a density
questions.explain: Mild steel is mostly iron and rusts, whereas stainless steel resists rusting.

questions.q: Which change would make a pure metal harder?
options: Adding atoms of a different size
questions.explain: Different-sized atoms stop the layers sliding, which is how alloys are made harder.

questions.q: A 200 g sample of brass contains 130 g of copper, and the rest is zinc. What is the percentage of zinc by mass?
questions.explain: Zinc = 200 − 130 = 70 g, so the percentage is 70 ÷ 200 × 100 = 35%.

questions.q: Which list shows metals in order of decreasing reactivity, most reactive first?
questions.explain: The reactivity series runs … calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper …

questions.q: Which pair of non-metals is included in the reactivity series?
questions.explain: Carbon and hydrogen are placed in the series as reference points, for extraction and for reaction with acids.

questions.q: Which statement describes sodium added to cold water?
options: It melts, moves on the surface and fizzes
It floats and does not react
It burns with a bright white flame
questions.explain: Sodium reacts vigorously with water, producing hydrogen; the heat melts the metal, which floats and moves around.

questions.q: Which equation correctly represents calcium reacting with cold water?
questions.explain: Calcium and cold water give calcium hydroxide and hydrogen, and the equation is balanced with 2H₂O.

questions.q: Which equation correctly represents magnesium reacting with steam?
questions.explain: Magnesium reacts with steam to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen; magnesium oxide is MgO.

questions.q: Which metal does not produce bubbles of hydrogen when added to dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explain: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from acids.

questions.q: Equal pieces of magnesium, zinc and iron are added to separate samples of the same dilute hydrochloric acid. In which order do they bubble, fastest to slowest?
questions.explain: The more reactive the metal, the faster the reaction, and the order of reactivity is magnesium, zinc, iron.

questions.q: Metal W reacts with cold water. Metal X does not react with cold water but reacts with steam. Metal Y does not react with steam but reacts with dilute acid. Metal Z does not react with dilute acid. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?
questions.explain: A metal that reacts with cold water is more reactive than one needing steam, then one reacting only with acid, then one with no reaction.

questions.q: Four metals are added to dilute acid. P gives many bubbles very quickly, Q gives a few bubbles slowly, R gives no bubbles and S gives a moderate stream of bubbles. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?
questions.explain: More vigorous bubbling means a more reactive metal and no reaction means the least reactive.

questions.q: Which of these metals is above hydrogen in the reactivity series?
questions.explain: Iron is above hydrogen and displaces it from acids, while copper, silver and gold are below it.

questions.q: Where is carbon placed in the reactivity series?
questions.explain: Carbon sits between aluminium and zinc, so it can reduce oxides of zinc and iron but not aluminium oxide.

questions.q: Magnesium is added to blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Which observation is correct?
options: The solution turns darker blue and the magnesium dissolves
The solution stays blue and bubbles of hydrogen form
The blue solution turns green and a grey solid forms
The blue colour fades and a brown solid forms
questions.explain: Magnesium displaces copper, which forms as a brown solid, and the blue Cu²⁺ ions are used up.

questions.q: Which mixture will produce no reaction?
options: Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution
Copper added to zinc sulfate solution
Magnesium added to iron(II) sulfate solution
Iron added to silver nitrate solution
questions.explain: Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace zinc from solution.

questions.q: Which ionic equation shows zinc displacing copper from copper(II) sulfate solution?
