questions.explain: Zinc atoms lose two electrons to form Zn²⁺ and Cu²⁺ ions gain them to form copper, and the charges balance.

questions.q: Zinc displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution. What explains this?
options: Zinc atoms gain electrons more easily than copper atoms
Zinc is a better conductor of electricity
Zinc atoms lose electrons more easily than copper atoms
Copper ions are less dense than zinc ions
questions.explain: The more reactive metal has a greater tendency to form positive ions by losing electrons.

questions.q: Iron is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Which statement about the redox change is correct?
options: Iron atoms lose electrons and are oxidised
Iron atoms gain electrons and are reduced
Copper ions lose electrons and are oxidised
Sulfate ions gain electrons and are reduced
questions.explain: Iron forms Fe²⁺ by losing electrons, which is oxidation, and the Cu²⁺ ions gain them and are reduced.

questions.q: Aluminium is above zinc in the reactivity series but reacts very little with dilute acid at first. Why?
options: Aluminium is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
A thin layer of aluminium oxide protects the metal
Aluminium forms an insoluble hydroxide with the acid
questions.explain: The unreactive oxide layer covers the surface and stops the acid reaching the aluminium underneath.

questions.q: A piece of aluminium foil is placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. There is no fizzing at first, but after some time it fizzes vigorously. Why?
options: The acid slowly makes the foil more reactive
The foil warms and changes into a non-metal
Hydrogen first has to be added to the acid
The acid slowly removes the oxide layer
questions.explain: Once the aluminium oxide layer has been dissolved by the acid, the reactive aluminium beneath reacts and gives hydrogen.

questions.q: Metal P displaces metal Q from a solution of Q ions. Metal Q displaces metal R from a solution of R ions. R does not displace P or Q. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?
questions.explain: A metal displaces only the ions of less reactive metals, so P is more reactive than Q, and Q more reactive than R.

questions.q: Which pair of metals react with cold water?
questions.explain: Potassium and calcium react with cold water; zinc, iron and the metals below them do not react with it.

questions.q: Why is potassium stored under oil?
options: It is a liquid that would evaporate
It is a gas at room temperature
It is toxic to the air
It reacts rapidly with oxygen and water vapour in air
questions.explain: Potassium is so reactive that it quickly tarnishes and reacts with moisture, so the oil keeps air and water away.

questions.q: Which equation correctly represents sodium reacting with water?
questions.explain: Sodium and water give sodium hydroxide solution and hydrogen, and the equation balances with 2 Na, 4 H and 2 O on each side.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the reactions of calcium?
questions.explain: Calcium is high in the series so it reacts with both cold water and dilute hydrochloric acid, whereas copper and silver react with neither.

questions.q: Metal X displaces metal Y from a solution of Y ions. Which statement is correct?
options: Y forms positive ions more readily than X
X is lower in the reactivity series than Y
X has a smaller tendency to lose electrons than Y
X forms positive ions more readily than Y
questions.explain: A displacing metal is higher in the series, so it loses electrons and forms positive ions more readily.

questions.q: Which metal reacts most vigorously with cold water?
questions.explain: Calcium is the highest in the series of the four, and zinc and iron do not react with cold water.

questions.q: Which equation represents iron reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explain: Iron forms iron(II) chloride with hydrogen, and the equation needs 2HCl to balance.

questions.q: 1.30 g of zinc reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. What volume of hydrogen forms at room temperature and pressure? (Ar: Zn = 65; 1 mol of gas = 24 000 cm³)
questions.explain: Moles of Zn = 1.30 ÷ 65 = 0.020 mol, which gives 0.020 mol H₂, so the volume is 0.020 × 24 000 = 480 cm³.

questions.q: A piece of zinc is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which observation is correct?
options: A steady stream of bubbles forms and the zinc gets smaller
questions.explain: Zinc reacts at a moderate rate, giving hydrogen bubbles as the metal dissolves.

questions.q: An iron nail is placed in blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Which observation is correct?
options: The nail dissolves and the solution becomes darker blue
The nail and the solution do not change
The nail gets a brown coating and the solution becomes pale green
The nail gets a silvery coating and the solution stays blue
questions.explain: Iron displaces copper, which coats the nail, and Fe²⁺ ions give a pale green solution.

questions.q: Silver does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid. What does this show?
options: Silver is less reactive than hydrogen
Silver is more reactive than hydrogen
Silver is more reactive than zinc
questions.explain: A metal that cannot displace hydrogen from an acid is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

questions.q: Which conditions are needed for iron to rust?
questions.explain: Rusting needs both water and oxygen to be present.

questions.q: What is rust?
questions.explain: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water.

questions.q: Three iron nails are left for a week. Tube A has dry air (anhydrous calcium chloride), tube B has boiled water covered with a layer of oil, and tube C has air and water. In which tubes do the nails rust?
questions.explain: Only tube C has both water and oxygen, since A has no water and B has no dissolved oxygen.

questions.q: Which method of rust prevention does not work by excluding oxygen and water?
questions.explain: A magnesium block is a sacrificial metal that corrodes in place of iron, whereas the other methods form a barrier.

questions.q: How does painting an iron gate prevent rusting?
options: It makes the iron less reactive chemically
It stops oxygen and water from reaching the iron
It removes oxygen from the iron
It reacts with water to make an acid
questions.explain: Paint forms a barrier, and with no contact with oxygen and water the iron cannot rust.

questions.q: Which barrier method is most suitable for the moving chain of a bicycle?
questions.explain: Grease stays on moving parts and excludes water and air, while paint or plastic would crack or wear away.

questions.q: Why must a barrier coating on iron remain unbroken?
options: A gap lets hydrogen escape from the iron
A gap makes the coating react with the iron
A gap makes the iron more reactive
A gap lets oxygen and water reach the iron
questions.explain: The barrier works only by keeping oxygen and water away, so any crack allows rusting to start.

questions.q: Which statement about rusting is correct?
options: Aluminium and copper also rust to form iron(III) oxide
Rust forms from iron and nitrogen
All metals rust in the same way
questions.explain: Rusting is the corrosion of iron and steel, as rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, which needs iron.

questions.q: A galvanised bucket is scratched through the zinc layer. Why does the exposed iron still not rust quickly?
options: Zinc is less reactive than iron, so the iron is protected
The scratch fills with rust that seals the surface
Zinc forms a barrier that cannot be broken
Zinc is more reactive than iron, so the zinc corrodes in preference
questions.explain: Zinc loses electrons more readily than iron, so it is sacrificed and protects the iron even when the coating is broken.

questions.q: Which statement explains sacrificial protection of iron by zinc?
options: Iron atoms lose electrons more readily and give them to zinc
Zinc atoms lose electrons in preference to iron atoms, so zinc corrodes instead
Zinc forms covalent bonds with iron
Zinc atoms gain electrons from iron atoms
questions.explain: Zinc is higher in the reactivity series, so it loses electrons more easily and corrodes in place of iron.

questions.q: Which metal could be attached to the iron pipe as a sacrificial block?
questions.explain: A sacrificial metal must be more reactive than iron, and magnesium is above iron while the others are below it.

questions.q: Iron is coated with a thin layer of copper, and then the coating is scratched to expose the iron. What is likely to happen?
options: The iron may rust because copper is less reactive and gives no sacrificial protection
The copper corrodes first and protects the iron
The scratch is sealed by the copper
The iron cannot rust as copper is a barrier
questions.explain: Copper is below iron in the series, so once the barrier is broken the iron is not protected sacrificially.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes a method of protecting iron?
questions.explain: A zinc coating is a barrier and, because zinc is more reactive than iron, also gives sacrificial protection; paint, grease and plastic are only barriers.

questions.q: Why does rusting continue until an iron object is destroyed?
options: Rust flakes off, exposing fresh iron to oxygen and water
Rust forms a layer that is more reactive than iron
Rust increases the amount of oxygen in the metal
Rust cannot form a flaky layer
questions.explain: Rust is porous and flakes away, so new iron is exposed and the rusting carries on.

questions.q: Which change would slow down the rusting of an iron nail?
options: Putting it in a sealed bottle with water and air
questions.explain: Grease excludes oxygen and water, while the other conditions keep both present.

questions.q: An iron nail does not rust in boiled water covered with a layer of oil. Why?
options: There is no water in the tube
There is no oxygen reaching the nail
The oil reacts with the iron
questions.explain: Boiling removes dissolved oxygen and the oil layer stops air redissolving, so oxygen is missing.

questions.q: An iron nail does not rust in a stoppered tube containing anhydrous calcium chloride. Which condition is missing?
questions.explain: Anhydrous calcium chloride absorbs water vapour from the air in the tube, so water is missing.

questions.q: A block of zinc is attached to the steel hull of a ship as sacrificial protection. What eventually happens to the block?
options: It corrodes away and needs replacing
It becomes a thicker coating of rust
questions.explain: The zinc loses electrons in preference to the iron, so it is gradually used up and must be replaced.

questions.q: How is the position of a metal in the reactivity series related to the ease of obtaining it from its ore?
options: The lower the metal in the series, the easier it is to obtain
The higher the metal in the series, the easier it is to obtain
All metals are equally easy to obtain
Only metals above carbon can be obtained
questions.explain: Unreactive metals lose their compounds easily, while reactive metals hold on to oxygen strongly and need more energy-intensive methods.

questions.q: Which metal is found uncombined in the Earth's crust?
questions.explain: Gold is very unreactive, so it exists as the element, while the others occur as compounds.

questions.q: Which ore is used to extract iron in the blast furnace?
questions.explain: Hematite contains iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃, and bauxite is the aluminium ore.

questions.q: Which set of materials is added to the blast furnace?
options: Bauxite, coke, limestone and hot air
Hematite, cryolite, limestone and hot air
Hematite, coke, limestone and hot air
questions.explain: The furnace uses iron ore, coke as fuel and reducing agent, limestone to remove impurities and hot air for oxygen.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives the role of a substance in the blast furnace?
options: Coke | burns to give heat and carbon dioxide
Limestone | reduces iron(III) oxide to iron
Hot air | forms slag with impurities
questions.explain: Coke burns in the hot air to release heat and form carbon dioxide, which is then reduced to carbon monoxide.

questions.q: What is the role of limestone in the blast furnace?
options: It burns to provide heat for the furnace
It decomposes to form calcium oxide, which removes acidic impurities as slag
It reduces iron(III) oxide to iron
It provides the oxygen needed to burn coke
questions.explain: Limestone breaks down into calcium oxide, which reacts with silicon dioxide impurity to form slag.

questions.q: Which compound forms the slag in the blast furnace?
questions.explain: Calcium oxide from the limestone reacts with silicon dioxide to form calcium silicate.

questions.q: Which substance acts as the reducing agent for iron(III) oxide in the blast furnace?
questions.explain: Carbon monoxide removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide and is oxidised to carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What happens to iron(III) oxide in the blast furnace?
options: It gains oxygen and is oxidised
It loses oxygen and is reduced to iron
It is neutralised by carbon monoxide
questions.explain: Reduction here means the removal of oxygen from the oxide to leave the metal.

questions.q: Which equation shows iron(III) oxide being reduced by carbon monoxide?
questions.explain: Two iron atoms and three oxygen atoms need three CO to take the oxygen, giving 2Fe and 3CO₂ in a balanced equation.

questions.q: Which equation shows carbon dioxide being reduced to carbon monoxide in the blast furnace?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide reacts with hot carbon to form carbon monoxide, with carbon dioxide losing an oxygen atom.

questions.q: Which equation shows the formation of slag in the blast furnace?
questions.explain: Basic calcium oxide reacts with acidic silicon dioxide to make calcium silicate.

questions.q: Molten slag floats on molten iron in the blast furnace. Why?
options: Slag has a higher density than iron
Slag is solid at the furnace temperature
Slag has a lower melting point than the hot air
Slag has a lower density than iron
questions.explain: The less dense slag forms a layer on top, so the two liquids can be run off separately.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the hot air blown into the base of the blast furnace?
options: It provides oxygen for the coke to burn
questions.explain: Oxygen in the air burns the coke, releasing the heat needed and producing carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives an ore and extraction method?
options: Aluminium | hematite | reduction with carbon monoxide
questions.explain: Aluminium is extracted from bauxite by electrolysis, and iron from hematite by reduction in the blast furnace.

questions.q: Why can aluminium not be extracted from its oxide by heating with carbon?
options: Aluminium is less reactive than carbon
Aluminium is more reactive than carbon
Aluminium oxide has a low melting point
Aluminium oxide does not contain oxygen
questions.explain: Carbon cannot remove oxygen from the oxide of a metal more reactive than itself.

questions.q: What is the role of cryolite in the extraction of aluminium?
options: It raises the melting point of the mixture
It is the ore from which aluminium is obtained
It lowers the melting point of aluminium oxide
It reduces aluminium oxide to aluminium
questions.explain: Aluminium oxide melts at a very high temperature, and dissolving it in molten cryolite reduces the temperature and energy needed.

questions.q: Why do the carbon anodes in aluminium extraction need to be replaced regularly?
options: They react with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and burn away
They dissolve in the molten cryolite
They are reduced by the aluminium
They are coated with aluminium and stop working
questions.explain: Oxygen formed at the hot anode reacts with the carbon, which is gradually used up.

questions.q: Which half-equation shows the reaction at the cathode in the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide?
questions.explain: Positive aluminium ions go to the negative cathode and gain electrons (reduction) to form aluminium.

questions.q: Which half-equation shows the reaction at the anode in the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide?
questions.explain: Oxide ions lose electrons at the positive anode (oxidation) to form oxygen gas.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the cell used to extract aluminium?
options: Carbon | aluminium oxide in molten cryolite | cathode
Carbon | aluminium oxide in molten cryolite | anode
Copper | aluminium oxide in molten cryolite | cathode
questions.explain: Carbon electrodes are used with aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite, and aluminium forms at the negative cathode.

questions.q: What mass of iron can be obtained from 320 g of iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃, in the blast furnace? (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)
questions.explain: Mr of Fe₂O₃ = 160, so 320 g is 2.0 mol, which gives 4.0 mol of Fe and so 4.0 × 56 = 224 g.

questions.q: What mass of aluminium can be obtained from 204 g of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃? (Ar: Al = 27, O = 16)
questions.explain: Mr of Al₂O₃ = 102, so 204 g is 2.0 mol, which gives 4.0 mol of Al and so 4.0 × 27 = 108 g.

questions.q: Which metal can be extracted from its oxide by heating with carbon?
questions.explain: Carbon can reduce only oxides of metals below it in the series, which includes zinc.

questions.q: A metal is more reactive than carbon. How is it usually extracted from its ore?
options: By heating the ore with carbon
By heating the ore on its own
By filtering the ore with water
By electrolysis of the molten compound
questions.explain: Carbon cannot reduce the oxides of metals above it in the series, so electrolysis is used.

questions.q: Which equation represents copper(II) oxide being reduced by carbon?
questions.explain: Two CuO supply two oxygen atoms, which react with one carbon to form CO₂, giving a balanced equation.

questions.q: Which substance is not added to the blast furnace?
questions.explain: Cryolite is used in the extraction of aluminium, not iron.

questions.q: Which equation shows carbon (coke) burning completely in air to provide heat in the blast furnace?
questions.explain: The first step is the combustion of carbon in oxygen from the air, an exothermic reaction.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes how the reducing agent forms and acts in the blast furnace?
options: Coke burns to CO₂, CO₂ reacts with more coke to give CO, and CO reduces Fe₂O₃
Coke burns to CO, CO reacts with Fe₂O₃ to give CO₂, and CO₂ reduces coke
CaCO₃ gives CO, CO reacts with coke, and coke reduces Fe₂O₃
Fe₂O₃ gives CO₂, CO₂ reacts with coke, and CO reduces Fe₂O₃
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide from burning coke is reduced by more coke to CO, and the CO then reduces the iron(III) oxide.

questions.q: Which gas is formed when iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide?
questions.explain: Carbon monoxide takes oxygen from the oxide and is oxidised to carbon dioxide.

questions.q: A colourless liquid is added to anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper and the paper changes colour. Which change shows that the liquid contains water?
questions.explain: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue and turns pink when water is added.

questions.q: What happens to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate when water is added to it?
options: It turns from blue to white.
It turns from blue to pink.
It turns from white to blue.
It turns from pink to blue.
questions.explain: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is white; hydrated copper(II) sulfate is blue.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives the colour change when water is detected?
questions.explain: Cobalt(II) chloride goes blue to pink; copper(II) sulfate goes white to blue.

questions.q: What is the boiling point of pure water at normal atmospheric pressure?
questions.explain: Pure water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure.

questions.q: A student wants to show that a sample of water is pure. Which result would be the best evidence?
options: It turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue.
It is colourless and has no smell.
It melts at exactly 0 °C and boils at exactly 100 °C.
It boils at 100 °C but melts over a range of temperatures.
questions.explain: Pure substances have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points. The copper(II) sulfate test only shows that water is present.

questions.q: A colourless liquid turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The liquid contains water but may not be pure water.
The liquid contains no dissolved substances.
questions.explain: The test only detects water. Salt solution or other mixtures containing water give the same result.

questions.q: A sample of water freezes at −2 °C and boils at 102 °C. What does this show?
options: The water contains dissolved oxygen only.
questions.explain: Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point, so the sample is not pure water.

questions.q: Why is distilled water used in practical chemistry rather than tap water?
options: It is always at a lower temperature.
It is a better solvent for ionic compounds.
questions.explain: Tap water contains dissolved substances that could react with the chemicals used or change results.

questions.q: Which substance in natural water is beneficial to aquatic life?
questions.explain: Fish and other aquatic animals need dissolved oxygen to respire.

questions.q: Which statement about metal compounds in natural water is correct?
options: Some provide essential minerals but some are toxic.
All of them are harmful to living things.
All of them are needed for life.
None of them is found in natural water.
questions.explain: Some metal compounds supply minerals needed by living things, while others, such as lead compounds, are toxic.

questions.q: Which statement about sewage in water is correct?
options: It increases the dissolved oxygen needed by fish.
It contains harmful microbes that cause disease.
It is removed from water by adding anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
It is the main source of phosphates from fertilisers.
questions.explain: Sewage contains microbes that can cause diseases such as cholera.

questions.q: What is a harmful effect of plastics in water?
options: They remove nitrates from the water.
They increase the dissolved oxygen concentration.
They kill all microbes in the water.
questions.explain: Animals can swallow plastics or become trapped in them, which damages aquatic life.

questions.q: Nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers run into a river. What is the main harmful effect on the river?
options: The river becomes more acidic and all metals dissolve.
The concentration of dissolved oxygen increases.
The water becomes deoxygenated and aquatic life is damaged.
questions.explain: Excess nitrates and phosphates lead to deoxygenation of the water, which damages aquatic life.

questions.q: Which substances in natural water come from fertilisers?
questions.explain: Fertilisers supply nitrogen as nitrates and phosphorus as phosphates, which wash into water.

questions.q: Which source gives phosphates in natural water?
questions.explain: Phosphates enter water from fertilisers and from detergents.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the sedimentation and filtration stages in treating the domestic water supply?
questions.explain: Sedimentation lets large solids settle and filtration removes smaller solids.

questions.q: Why is carbon used in the treatment of domestic water?
options: to add chlorine to the water
questions.explain: Carbon adsorbs the substances that cause unpleasant tastes and smells.

questions.q: Why is chlorine added to the domestic water supply?
questions.explain: Chlorination kills microbes that could cause disease.

questions.q: Which row correctly matches each water treatment stage with its purpose?
questions.explain: Filtration removes solids; carbon removes tastes and smells; chlorine kills microbes.

questions.q: Which list gives the stages of domestic water treatment in the correct order?
questions.explain: Solids are removed first, then carbon removes tastes and odours, and chlorine is added to kill microbes.

questions.q: A student tests a liquid for water. Which test is suitable?
options: Add damp litmus paper and see if it turns blue.
Add silver nitrate solution and look for a white solid.
Heat the liquid and see if it burns with a pop.
Add anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride and see if it turns pink.
questions.explain: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue and turns pink in the presence of water.

questions.q: What does a sharp melting point of a solid show?
questions.explain: Pure substances melt at one fixed temperature; impure substances melt over a range of temperatures.

questions.q: Which statement about distillation of natural water is correct?
options: It removes dissolved solids because they stay behind when the water evaporates.
It adds dissolved oxygen to the water.
It leaves the dissolved solids in the distillate.
It increases the number of microbes in the water.
questions.explain: Water evaporates and condenses; dissolved solids are left behind, giving distilled water.

questions.q: Why must the domestic water supply be treated before drinking?
options: to remove all the dissolved oxygen
to make it contain only hydrogen and oxygen
to remove solids and kill harmful microbes
questions.explain: Raw water contains solids and microbes that can cause disease.

questions.q: Which description of anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is correct?
options: It is blue and used to test for water.
It is pink and used to test for water.
It is white and used to test for water.
It is blue and used to test for oxygen.
questions.explain: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue; it turns pink when water is present.

questions.q: A student boils a liquid and the thermometer reading rises steadily from 98 °C to 104 °C. What is the best conclusion?
options: The liquid is a pure element.
The liquid contains only dissolved oxygen.
The liquid is a mixture, not a pure substance.
questions.explain: A pure liquid boils at one fixed temperature, so a steady rise through a range means a mixture.

questions.q: A dissolved impurity is added to pure water. How do the melting and boiling points change?
options: The melting point is raised and the boiling point is lowered.
The melting point is lowered and the boiling point is raised.
questions.explain: Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point compared with the pure substance.

questions.q: Which row correctly shows an effect of each substance in natural water?
options: sewage | provides oxygen for aquatic life
questions.explain: Fish use dissolved oxygen; sewage and plastics are pollutants and phosphates cause deoxygenation.

questions.q: Which statement about the effect of nitrates and phosphates on a lake is correct?
options: They lead to deoxygenation of the water, which damages aquatic life.
They increase the oxygen concentration so fish grow faster.
They kill microbes in the lake.
They convert sewage into harmless solids.
questions.explain: Extra nutrients lead to deoxygenation of the water, damaging aquatic life.

questions.q: Why is chlorination carried out after the filtration stage rather than before it?
options: Chlorine would turn into carbon if added earlier.
Filtration produces the microbes that must be killed.
Solids are removed first so the chlorine can kill microbes more effectively.
questions.explain: Removing solids first leaves cleaner water so that chlorine can reach and kill microbes more effectively.

questions.q: A chemist wants to know whether a colourless liquid is pure ethanol or ethanol mixed with water. Which result best shows it is a mixture?
options: The anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns blue.
questions.explain: Pure ethanol would not turn anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue; a colour change shows water is present.

questions.q: Which pair of substances in water both harm aquatic life?
options: minerals from metal compounds and dissolved oxygen
questions.explain: Plastics harm aquatic life and sewage brings harmful microbes; dissolved oxygen and essential minerals are beneficial.

questions.q: Which statement about adding anhydrous copper(II) sulfate to a liquid is correct?
options: It turns pink if the liquid is pure water.
It turns blue only if the liquid is pure water.
It shows the boiling point of the liquid.
It only shows that water is present, not that the water is pure.
questions.explain: The test is for the presence of water; it cannot tell pure water from solutions.

questions.q: In a purity check a student finds that a liquid melts at −5 °C. Which statement is correct if the liquid is supposed to be pure water?
options: The water is impure because its melting point is below 0 °C.
The water is pure because water melts below 0 °C.
The water is impure because its melting point is above 0 °C.
The water is pure because it is liquid.
questions.explain: Pure water melts at exactly 0 °C; a lower melting point shows dissolved impurities.

questions.q: A water company uses carbon in a filter bed. What property of the carbon makes it suitable?
options: It kills microbes by releasing chlorine.
It removes substances that cause bad taste and smell.
It settles out large solid particles.
It adds minerals to the water.
questions.explain: Carbon removes the substances responsible for unpleasant tastes and odours; microbes are killed by chlorine.

questions.q: Which statement about tap water and distilled water is correct?
options: Distilled water contains more dissolved substances than tap water.
Tap water and distilled water contain the same chemicals.
Tap water contains more dissolved substances than distilled water.
Distilled water contains dissolved oxygen but tap water does not.
questions.explain: Tap water contains dissolved substances; distillation removes them.

questions.q: Which of these is a source of harmful microbes in natural water?
questions.explain: Sewage contains microbes that cause disease.

questions.q: Which compound is used as a fertiliser?
questions.explain: Ammonium salts and nitrates supply nitrogen to plants.

questions.q: Which three elements are provided by an NPK fertiliser?
questions.explain: N, P and K are the symbols for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

questions.q: Why do farmers add fertilisers to soil?
options: to kill harmful microbes in the soil
to replace elements that crops have removed so plants grow better
to add carbon dioxide to the air
questions.explain: Crops take up nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium from soil; fertilisers replace them for improved growth.

questions.q: Which of these is an ammonium salt that is used as a fertiliser?
questions.explain: (NH₄)₂SO₄ is ammonium sulfate and contains the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, which provides nitrogen.

questions.q: Which formula is ammonium nitrate?
questions.explain: Ammonium nitrate contains the NH₄⁺ ion and the NO₃⁻ ion in a 1 : 1 ratio.

questions.q: Which row correctly matches the symbol with the element in NPK fertilisers?
questions.explain: N is nitrogen, P is phosphorus and K is potassium.

questions.q: What is meant by an NPK fertiliser?
options: a fertiliser containing compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
a fertiliser made from sodium, phosphorus and krypton
a fertiliser that adds only potassium
questions.explain: NPK fertilisers supply all three of the elements needed for improved plant growth.

questions.q: Potassium nitrate is used as a fertiliser. Which elements does it provide?
questions.explain: KNO₃ contains potassium and nitrogen (in the nitrate ion).

questions.q: Which statement about fertilisers is correct?
options: Fertilisers must dissolve in water so that plant roots can absorb them.
Fertilisers are made only from metals.
Fertilisers remove nitrogen from the soil.
questions.explain: Plants absorb nutrients dissolved in water through their roots.

questions.q: Excess fertiliser is washed from fields into a river. Which problem may this cause?
options: Nitrates and phosphates reduce the oxygen in the water.
Chlorine is formed in the water.
questions.explain: Nitrates and phosphates lead to deoxygenation of water.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT used as a fertiliser?
questions.explain: Sodium chloride does not supply N, P or K in a form useful to plants.

questions.q: Ammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₃PO₄, is used as a fertiliser. Which elements does it supply?
questions.explain: (NH₄)₃PO₄ contains nitrogen (in NH₄⁺) and phosphorus (in PO₄³⁻).

questions.q: What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃? (Ar: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16)
questions.explain: Mr = 14 + 4 + 14 + 48 = 80. The two N atoms have mass 28, so 28 ÷ 80 × 100 = 35%.

questions.q: Which fertiliser has the highest percentage by mass of nitrogen? (Ar: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32)
questions.explain: NH₄NO₃: 28/80 = 35%; (NH₄)₂SO₄: 28/132 = 21%; NH₄Cl: 14/53.5 = 26%; (NH₄)₃PO₄: 42/149 = 28%, so NH₄NO₃ is highest.

questions.q: Ammonia reacts with sulfuric acid to make the fertiliser ammonium sulfate. Which equation is correct?
questions.explain: Two NH₃ each gain one H⁺ to form 2NH₄⁺, which pair with one SO₄²⁻.

questions.q: Which equation represents the formation of the fertiliser ammonium nitrate from ammonia?
questions.explain: One NH₃ accepts one H⁺ from HNO₃ to give NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻.

questions.q: A bag contains 40 kg of ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃. What mass of nitrogen does it contain? (Ar: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16)
questions.explain: Mr = 80 and N is 28/80 = 35% of the mass, so 0.35 × 40 = 14 kg.

questions.q: A student warms a fertiliser with sodium hydroxide solution and a gas is released that turns damp red litmus paper blue. Which ion is present in the fertiliser?
questions.explain: Ammonium ions react with warm sodium hydroxide to release ammonia, an alkaline gas that turns damp red litmus blue.

questions.q: Which statement explains why a farmer might use ammonium nitrate rather than potassium chloride on a field lacking nitrogen?
options: Potassium chloride contains nitrogen but ammonium nitrate does not.
Ammonium nitrate contains nitrogen but potassium chloride does not.
Ammonium nitrate is insoluble but potassium chloride is soluble.
Potassium chloride has a higher percentage of nitrogen.
questions.explain: Plants need nitrogen compounds; KCl contains no nitrogen.

questions.q: Which row correctly lists a fertiliser and the elements from NPK that it provides?
questions.explain: (NH₄)₂HPO₄ has ammonium nitrogen and phosphate phosphorus; KNO₃ gives N and K, NH₄NO₃ gives only N, KCl gives only K.

questions.q: What is the approximate percentage of nitrogen in clean, dry air?
questions.explain: Clean, dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen, N₂.

questions.q: Which gas makes up approximately 21% of clean, dry air?
questions.explain: Oxygen, O₂, is about 21% of clean, dry air.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives the approximate composition of clean, dry air?
questions.explain: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with the remainder noble gases and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What makes up the remainder of clean, dry air after nitrogen and oxygen?
options: a mixture of noble gases and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: The remaining 1% is noble gases (mainly argon) and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What volume of oxygen is in 500 cm³ of clean, dry air? (Take oxygen as 21% of air.)
What volume of nitrogen is in 250 dm³ of clean, dry air? (Take nitrogen as 78% of air.)
Which air pollutant is formed by the complete combustion of carbon-containing fuels?
questions.explain: Complete combustion of carbon-containing fuels forms carbon dioxide and water.

questions.q: Which pollutants are produced by the incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels?
questions.explain: Limited oxygen gives carbon monoxide and particles of carbon (soot).

questions.q: What is a source of methane in the atmosphere?
options: decomposition of vegetation and waste gases from animals
questions.explain: Methane comes from decaying vegetation and waste gases from digestion in animals, e.g. cattle.

questions.q: Which air pollutant is formed in car engines?
questions.explain: At the high temperature in engines nitrogen and oxygen from the air react to form oxides of nitrogen.

questions.q: Where does sulfur dioxide in the air mainly come from?
options: the digestion of food by animals
burning fossil fuels that contain sulfur compounds
questions.explain: Fossil fuels such as coal contain sulfur compounds; burning them produces sulfur dioxide.

questions.q: Which row correctly matches each pollutant with its source?
options: methane | decomposition of waste and vegetation
oxides of nitrogen | digestion in animals
questions.explain: Methane forms when vegetation decays; carbon monoxide forms in incomplete combustion; sulfur dioxide comes from sulfur in fuels; oxides of nitrogen form in car engines.

questions.q: A gas heater is faulty and burns natural gas with too little air. Which poisonous gas may be produced?
questions.explain: Incomplete combustion produces toxic carbon monoxide.

questions.q: What are particulates in air pollution?
options: a harmful gas formed in car engines
an acidic gas formed from sulfur
tiny solid particles, e.g. carbon from incomplete combustion
questions.explain: Particulates are fine solid particles such as soot produced by incomplete combustion.

questions.q: Which pollutant is a toxic gas?
questions.explain: Carbon monoxide is toxic: it stops blood from carrying oxygen.

questions.q: What is a harmful effect of particulates in the air?
options: increased risk of respiratory problems and cancer
questions.explain: Breathing in particulates can cause respiratory problems and cancer.

questions.q: Which pollutant contributes to acid rain?
questions.explain: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain water to form acid rain.

questions.q: Which of these causes acid rain, photochemical smog and respiratory problems?
questions.explain: Oxides of nitrogen from car engines cause acid rain, smog and breathing problems.

questions.q: Which two gases cause increased global warming that leads to climate change?
questions.explain: Higher levels of carbon dioxide and methane lead to increased global warming.

questions.q: Which row correctly links an air pollutant with its adverse effect?
options: particulates | toxic gas that stops blood carrying oxygen
questions.explain: Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain; carbon monoxide is toxic; methane causes warming; particulates cause respiratory problems.

questions.q: Which of these is a problem caused by acid rain?
questions.explain: Acid rain damages buildings made of limestone, kills trees and harms aquatic life.

questions.q: Which action would help reduce climate change?
questions.explain: Trees take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, so planting trees reduces carbon dioxide levels.

questions.q: Which strategy reduces the amount of methane released?
questions.explain: Fewer farm animals mean less methane from digestion.

questions.q: Which strategy helps reduce acid rain?
questions.explain: Low-sulfur fuels release less sulfur dioxide when they burn.

questions.q: Which fuel produces only water when it burns?
questions.explain: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form only water, so burning it does not produce carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What is the purpose of flue gas desulfurisation at a power station?
options: to remove carbon dioxide from the air
to remove nitrogen from the fuel
to remove sulfur dioxide from waste gases
questions.explain: Calcium oxide reacts with the sulfur dioxide in waste gases before they leave the chimney.

questions.q: Which substance is used in flue gas desulfurisation?
questions.explain: Calcium oxide is a base that reacts with acidic sulfur dioxide.

questions.q: Which row gives a correct way of reducing the effects of each environmental issue?
options: climate change | burning more fossil fuels
climate change | use of low-sulfur fuels
questions.explain: Low-sulfur fuels reduce sulfur dioxide; climate change is reduced by fewer fossil fuels, planting trees and renewable energy.

questions.q: Which energy source does NOT release carbon dioxide when generating electricity?
questions.explain: Wind turbines do not burn a fuel, so they release no carbon dioxide while operating.

questions.q: Which statement describes photosynthesis?
options: Glucose and oxygen react to form carbon dioxide and water.
Carbon dioxide and glucose react to form water and oxygen.
Oxygen and water react to form glucose and carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide and water react to form glucose and oxygen.
questions.explain: In photosynthesis plants make glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water.

questions.q: Which two things are needed for photosynthesis to occur, in addition to carbon dioxide and water?
questions.explain: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which drives the reaction.

questions.q: What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide and water form glucose and oxygen.

questions.q: Which gas do plants take in from the air for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen.

questions.q: What is the function of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
options: It is the product of the reaction.
It is a reactant that provides oxygen.
It speeds up the reaction by being a fertiliser.
questions.explain: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs energy from light.

questions.q: Why does planting trees help to reduce the level of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
options: Trees convert carbon dioxide into methane.
Trees react carbon dioxide with nitrogen.
Trees take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
Trees produce carbon dioxide in the light.
questions.explain: Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air.

questions.q: Which substance is made by plants during photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Plants make glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, and oxygen.

questions.q: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide; the other processes release it or other gases.

questions.q: What happens to thermal energy that is radiated from the Earth's surface towards space?
options: All of it passes through the atmosphere into space.
It is absorbed by nitrogen and oxygen only.
It is converted into light energy by methane.
Some is absorbed by greenhouse gases and re-emitted, including back towards the Earth.
questions.explain: Greenhouse gases absorb, reflect and emit thermal energy, reducing loss to space.

questions.q: How do greenhouse gases cause global warming?
options: They reduce the loss of thermal energy to space.
They increase the amount of sunlight reaching Earth.
They react with oxygen to make heat.
questions.explain: By absorbing and re-emitting thermal energy they trap heat near the Earth.

questions.q: Which pair of gases are the greenhouse gases named in the syllabus?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide and methane absorb and emit thermal energy.

questions.q: Why is increased carbon dioxide in the atmosphere linked to climate change?
options: More ultraviolet light enters the atmosphere, making rain acidic.
Carbon dioxide reacts with oxygen to form ozone.
Carbon dioxide increases the number of microbes.
More thermal energy is trapped, so global temperatures rise.
questions.explain: Higher levels of greenhouse gases cause increased global warming, leading to climate change.

questions.q: Which statement about the greenhouse effect is correct?
options: Greenhouse gases absorb, reflect and emit thermal energy.
Greenhouse gases produce thermal energy in the atmosphere from nothing.
Greenhouse gases remove thermal energy and cool the Earth.
questions.explain: The warming effect depends on absorption, reflection and emission of thermal energy.

questions.q: Methane is a more effective greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide per molecule. Which is the main natural source of methane?
options: decomposition of vegetation and waste gases from digestion in animals
reaction of nitrogen and oxygen in car engines
questions.explain: Methane is made by decomposition of vegetation and in the digestive systems of animals.

questions.q: How do oxides of nitrogen form in a car engine?
options: Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at high temperature.
Carbon in the petrol reacts with nitrogen in the air at low temperature.
questions.explain: The very high temperature in the engine, plus spark, makes nitrogen and oxygen from air react.

questions.q: Which equation represents the formation of nitrogen monoxide in a car engine?
questions.explain: One molecule of N₂ and one of O₂ give two molecules of NO; the equation balances as N₂ + O₂ → 2NO.

questions.q: Which equation shows a reaction in a catalytic converter?
questions.explain: Only 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂ has equal numbers of C, O and N on both sides.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a catalytic converter in a car exhaust?
options: to filter out solids using a carbon filter
to make the engine produce more power
to remove carbon dioxide from the exhaust
to convert harmful gases into less harmful gases
questions.explain: It changes carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and unburned hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water.

questions.q: In the catalytic converter reaction 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂, which statement is correct?
options: Carbon monoxide is oxidised and nitrogen monoxide is reduced.
Carbon monoxide is reduced and nitrogen monoxide is oxidised.
questions.explain: CO gains oxygen to become CO₂ (oxidation); NO loses oxygen to become N₂ (reduction).

questions.q: Which substances are the products when carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide react in a catalytic converter?
questions.explain: The equation is 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂.

questions.q: Which equation represents the removal of sulfur dioxide with calcium oxide in flue gas desulfurisation?
questions.explain: The basic oxide CaO reacts with acidic SO₂ to give calcium sulfite, CaSO₃.

questions.q: Why does a catalytic converter reduce the effect of acid rain?
options: It converts sulfur dioxide into carbon dioxide.
It converts oxides of nitrogen into nitrogen.
It converts carbon dioxide into methane.
It filters out solid particulates only.
questions.explain: Removing oxides of nitrogen reduces the acid formed when they dissolve in rain water.

questions.q: Which is the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Both sides have 6 C, 12 H and 18 O.

questions.q: How many moles of oxygen are produced when 1 mole of glucose is made by photosynthesis?
questions.explain: From 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, 6 mol of O₂ form for every 1 mol of glucose.

questions.q: What mass of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, forms when 88 g of carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explain: 6CO₂ (6 × 44 = 264 g) gives 180 g glucose. 88 g is 1/3 of 264 g, so the mass is 180 ÷ 3 = 60 g.

questions.q: What volume of oxygen, measured at room temperature and pressure, is made when 0.50 mol of glucose forms by photosynthesis? (1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³)
questions.explain: 0.50 mol of glucose produces 6 × 0.50 = 3.0 mol of O₂, and 3.0 × 24 = 72 dm³.

questions.q: In the equation 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, what is the Mr of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆? (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
Which row correctly shows the reaction type and energy change in photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis takes in energy from light, so it is endothermic.

questions.q: Why do plants and trees not remove all of the extra carbon dioxide produced by burning fossil fuels?
options: Carbon dioxide is produced faster than plants can absorb it, and forests are being cleared.
Plants absorb carbon dioxide only in the dark.
questions.explain: Deforestation and large emissions mean more carbon dioxide is released than photosynthesis removes.

questions.q: Which row correctly shows a reactant and a product of photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide is a reactant and oxygen is a product; glucose is a product, not a reactant.

questions.q: A fossil fuel contains 2.0% sulfur by mass. What mass of sulfur dioxide forms when 1000 kg of the fuel burns completely? (Ar: O = 16, S = 32; S + O₂ → SO₂)
questions.explain: Sulfur = 0.020 × 1000 = 20 kg. Each 32 g S gives 64 g SO₂, so 20 kg gives 40 kg.

questions.q: Which of these changes would reduce both carbon dioxide and methane levels in the atmosphere?
options: decreasing the use of fossil fuels and reducing livestock farming
questions.explain: Less fossil fuel burning cuts carbon dioxide and fewer livestock cuts methane; low-sulfur fuels and converters tackle other pollutants.

questions.q: Which of these correctly describes incomplete combustion of methane that produces carbon monoxide?
questions.explain: 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O has 2 C, 8 H and 6 O on both sides; the last option is the complete combustion.

questions.q: Complete combustion of 1 mole of methane, CH₄, produces how many moles of carbon dioxide?
questions.explain: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, so 1 mol of CH₄ gives 1 mol of CO₂.

questions.q: Which is the general formula of the alcohol homologous series?
questions.explain: Alcohols have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH, for example CH₃OH (n = 1) and C₂H₅OH (n = 2).

questions.q: An alkane molecule contains five carbon atoms. What is its molecular formula?
questions.explain: Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. For n = 5 this gives C₅H₁₂.

questions.q: What is a functional group?
options: the carbon chain that gives a compound its boiling point
the number of carbon atoms in each molecule of a compound
a group of atoms that is the same in every organic compound
an atom or group of atoms that determines the chemical properties of a homologous series
questions.explain: The functional group (such as C=C or –OH) is the part of the molecule that decides how the compounds react, so it determines the chemical properties.

questions.q: Which statement describes a saturated compound?
options: Its molecules contain at least one carbon–carbon double bond.
Its molecules contain no hydrogen atoms.
Its molecules contain the maximum number of carbon atoms.
Its molecules contain only single carbon–carbon bonds.
questions.explain: In a saturated compound all the carbon–carbon bonds are single bonds. Compounds with C=C bonds are unsaturated.

questions.q: Which pair of compounds are structural isomers of each other?
questions.explain: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula (here C₄H₁₀O) but different structural formulae. The other pairs have different molecular formulae.

questions.q: Which statement about the members of a homologous series is correct?
options: Each member has the same relative molecular mass.
Each member has identical physical properties.
Each member has the same number of carbon atoms.
Each member differs from the next by a –CH₂– unit.
questions.explain: Successive members differ by –CH₂–, so their relative molecular masses and physical properties change gradually along the series.

questions.q: What is the formula of the carboxylic acid with four carbon atoms in each molecule, using the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH?
questions.explain: The –COOH group contains one carbon atom, so the four-carbon acid has n = 3, giving C₃H₇COOH.

questions.q: Why is the molecular formula C₂H₆O not an unambiguous description of ethanol?
options: It does not show how the atoms are arranged, so it could also be CH₃OCH₃.
It does not show the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.
It does not show which elements are present in the molecule.
It shows the compound as an ionic substance.
questions.explain: A molecular formula gives only the atoms present. CH₃CH₂OH and CH₃OCH₃ share the formula C₂H₆O, so the structural formula is needed to be unambiguous.

questions.q: The displayed formula of ethene shows every atom and bond. How many covalent bonds does it show, counting the double bond as two bonds?
questions.explain: Ethene (C₂H₄) has four C–H bonds and one C=C double bond, which counts as two bonds, giving 4 + 2 = 6.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes ethene?
options: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ | contains a C=C double bond | unsaturated
CₙH₂ₙ | contains only single C–C bonds | saturated
CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ | contains only single C–C bonds | unsaturated
CₙH₂ₙ | contains a C=C double bond | unsaturated
questions.explain: Ethene is an alkene (CₙH₂ₙ) with a C=C double bond, so it is unsaturated.

questions.q: Which compound is a structural isomer of but-1-ene, CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂?
questions.explain: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ (but-2-ene) is C₄H₈ like but-1-ene but has the double bond in a different position. The others have different molecular formulae.

questions.q: Why do members of the same homologous series have similar chemical properties?
options: They have the same relative molecular mass.
They have the same functional group.
They have the same number of carbon atoms.
They have the same physical state at room temperature.
questions.explain: The functional group determines how a compound reacts, and every member of a series has the same one.

questions.q: How do the boiling points of the alkanes change as the number of carbon atoms increases?
options: They increase for odd numbers of carbon atoms only.
questions.explain: Physical properties show a trend along a homologous series. Longer molecules have stronger forces between them, so boiling points rise.

questions.q: How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of propanol, C₃H₇OH?
questions.explain: Seven hydrogen atoms are in the C₃H₇ group and one is in the –OH group, giving 8.

questions.q: A compound has a name ending in -ene. What type of compound is it?
questions.explain: The ending -ene shows a C=C double bond, so the compound is an alkene.

questions.q: Which of these names is that of an alcohol?
questions.explain: The ending -ol shows the –OH group of an alcohol. -ane is an alkane, -ene an alkene and -oic acid a carboxylic acid.

questions.q: What is the structural formula of ethanoic acid?
questions.explain: Ethanoic acid has two carbon atoms and the –COOH group, so it is CH₃COOH.

questions.q: A compound has the molecular formula C₄H₁₀. To which homologous series does it belong?
questions.explain: For n = 4 the alkane formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ gives C₄H₁₀. An alkene with four carbons would be C₄H₈.

questions.q: What is the name of the compound CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH?
questions.explain: The chain has four carbon atoms, including the carbon in –COOH, and the –COOH group, so the name is butanoic acid.

questions.q: What is the name of the compound with the structural formula CH₃CH(OH)CH₃?
questions.explain: It has three carbons with the –OH group on the second carbon atom, so it is propan-2-ol.

questions.q: What is the name of CH₃CH=CHCH₃?
questions.explain: The chain has four carbons and the double bond starts at carbon 2, giving but-2-ene.

questions.q: An ester is made from ethanol and propanoic acid. What is its name?
questions.explain: The alcohol provides the first part of the name (ethyl) and the acid provides the second part (propanoate), so the ester is ethyl propanoate.

questions.q: What is the name of the ester with the formula CH₃COOCH₃?
questions.explain: The acid part has two carbons (ethanoate) and the alcohol part has one (methyl), so it is methyl ethanoate.

questions.q: Ethene reacts with steam in the presence of an acid catalyst. What is the name of the product?
questions.explain: Steam adds across the C=C bond of ethene to form ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH.

questions.q: Which structural formula represents butan-2-ol?
questions.explain: Butan-2-ol has four carbons in a chain with the –OH group on carbon 2. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH is butan-1-ol.

questions.q: Which pair of compounds reacts to form the ester propyl methanoate?
questions.explain: The first part of the name (propyl) comes from the unbranched alcohol propan-1-ol, and the second part (methanoate) comes from methanoic acid.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes ethanol?
questions.explain: Ethanol (name ending -ol) is an alcohol with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH and the –OH functional group.

questions.q: Which compound is named ethane?
questions.explain: Ethane is the alkane with two carbon atoms joined by a single bond, CH₃CH₃. CH₂=CH₂ is ethene.

questions.q: Which list contains only fossil fuels?
questions.explain: The three fossil fuels are coal, natural gas and petroleum. Hydrogen, wood and ethanol are not fossil fuels.

questions.q: What is the main constituent of natural gas?
questions.explain: Natural gas is mainly methane, CH₄.

questions.q: Which compound is a hydrocarbon?
questions.explain: A hydrocarbon contains hydrogen and carbon only. The other compounds also contain oxygen or chlorine.

questions.q: Which statement about petroleum is correct?
options: It is a single compound of carbon and hydrogen.
It is a mixture of carbon and hydrogen elements.
It is a mixture of hydrocarbons.
It is a mixture of alcohols and carboxylic acids.
questions.explain: Petroleum is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons, which are separated into fractions.

questions.q: The fractions in petroleum are separated by fractional distillation. Which property allows this separation?
options: The fractions have different solubilities in water.
The fractions have different electrical conductivities.
The fractions have different boiling points.
questions.explain: Hydrocarbons of different chain length have different boiling points, so they condense at different heights in the fractionating column.

questions.q: Which row correctly compares a fraction collected at the top of the fractionating column with a fraction collected at the bottom?
options: shorter chains | higher boiling point | less viscous
longer chains | lower boiling point | more viscous
shorter chains | lower boiling point | more viscous
shorter chains | lower boiling point | less viscous
questions.explain: Fractions at the top have shorter hydrocarbon chains, lower boiling points, higher volatility and lower viscosity.

questions.q: Which fraction from petroleum is used to make roads?
questions.explain: Bitumen is the thick residue at the bottom of the column and is used for road surfaces.

questions.q: Which fraction of petroleum is used as jet fuel?
questions.explain: Kerosene is used as aircraft fuel. Gasoline is the fuel for cars and diesel oil is for diesel engines.

questions.q: Which fraction of petroleum is used as a chemical feedstock?
questions.explain: Naphtha is used as a feedstock for making many other chemicals. Refinery gas is used for heating and cooking.

questions.q: Which fraction of petroleum is used as a fuel for ships and for home heating systems?
questions.explain: Fuel oil is burned in ships and in home heating systems. Lubricating oil is used for lubricants, waxes and polishes.

questions.q: Which fraction from the fractionating column has the lowest boiling points?
questions.explain: Refinery gas contains the smallest molecules, so it has the lowest boiling points and is collected at the top.

questions.q: Which fraction is used for lubricants, waxes and polishes?
questions.explain: Lubricating oil has long, viscous molecules suitable for lubricants, waxes and polishes.

questions.q: Which fraction contains the molecules with the longest hydrocarbon chains?
questions.explain: Bitumen has the longest chains, the highest boiling point and the highest viscosity, so it condenses at the bottom of the column.

questions.q: Going down the fractionating column, how do the volatility and viscosity of the fractions change?
questions.explain: Lower down, the chains are longer, so the fractions are less volatile and flow less easily (higher viscosity).

questions.q: Which statement describes the bonding in alkanes?
options: All the bonds are single covalent bonds.
There is one C=C double bond in each molecule.
They contain ionic bonds between carbon and hydrogen.
They contain delocalised electrons between the carbon atoms.
questions.explain: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons that contain only single covalent bonds.

questions.q: What are the products of the complete combustion of methane?
questions.explain: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.q: Which equation represents the complete combustion of methane?
questions.explain: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O has 1 C, 4 H and 4 O on each side. The others are not balanced or do not give CO₂.

questions.q: What is the role of ultraviolet light in the reaction of methane with chlorine?
options: It removes the hydrogen chloride formed.
questions.explain: The reaction is photochemical: ultraviolet light provides the activation energy, Ea, needed to start the reaction.

questions.q: Methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight. Which pair of products forms in a monosubstitution?
questions.explain: One H atom is replaced by one Cl atom: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.

questions.q: Which equation represents the monosubstitution of ethane by chlorine in ultraviolet light?
questions.explain: In monosubstitution one hydrogen atom is replaced by one chlorine atom, and the displaced hydrogen forms HCl. The other equations are not balanced or show other products.

questions.q: A student bubbles ethane through aqueous bromine. What is observed?
questions.explain: Ethane is a saturated alkane and does not react with aqueous bromine under these conditions, so there is no colour change.

questions.q: What is a substitution reaction?
options: One atom or group of atoms is replaced by another atom or group of atoms.
Two molecules combine to form one product.
One large molecule breaks into smaller molecules.
Atoms are added across a carbon–carbon double bond.
questions.explain: In substitution an atom or group is replaced, such as H replaced by Cl in an alkane. Addition reactions join two molecules into one product.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the reaction of methane with chlorine to form chloromethane?
options: substitution | no light needed | two products
addition | no light needed | two products
questions.explain: Methane and chlorine undergo a photochemical substitution reaction that forms CH₃Cl and HCl.

questions.q: Which compound is a saturated hydrocarbon?
questions.explain: C₄H₁₀ is butane, an alkane with only single bonds. C₄H₈ and C₃H₆ are alkenes and C₂H₅OH is not a hydrocarbon.

questions.q: Which poisonous gas can form when an alkane burns in a limited supply of oxygen?
questions.explain: Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide, which is toxic, and sometimes carbon (soot).

questions.q: Propane reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light. Which formula is that of a monosubstitution product?
questions.explain: A monosubstitution product has one H replaced by one Cl: C₃H₇Cl. CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl is 1-chloropropane. The others have a double bond or more than one Cl.

questions.q: Which statement about alkenes is correct?
options: They are saturated hydrocarbons that contain only single bonds.
They are unsaturated hydrocarbons that contain a C=C double bond.
They are unsaturated compounds that contain oxygen.
They are saturated compounds that contain a C=C double bond.
questions.explain: Alkenes are hydrocarbons that contain a C=C double bond, so they are unsaturated.

questions.q: What conditions are used to crack large alkane molecules?
options: high temperature and an inert atmosphere only
questions.explain: Cracking breaks long alkane molecules into smaller ones using a high temperature and a catalyst.

questions.q: Why are large alkane molecules cracked in oil refineries?
options: to make longer molecules that are more viscous
to make shorter, more useful molecules, including alkenes
to make the molecules less volatile
to remove carbon and hydrogen from the molecules
questions.explain: There is more demand for short-chain fuels and alkenes than for long-chain molecules, so cracking turns the surplus long chains into more useful products.

questions.q: Which equation shows a possible cracking reaction of decane?
questions.explain: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ balances: 10 C and 22 H on each side. The other equations have unequal numbers of C or H atoms.

questions.q: What is observed when ethene is bubbled through aqueous bromine?
questions.explain: Ethene is unsaturated and reacts with bromine by addition, so the colour of the aqueous bromine disappears.

questions.q: What is true of every addition reaction?
options: A small molecule is always lost.
questions.explain: In an addition reaction two reactants join to give a single product.

questions.q: What is the product when ethene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst?
questions.explain: Hydrogen adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃.

questions.q: Which structural formula represents the product of the reaction of ethene with bromine?
questions.explain: Bromine adds across the double bond, so each carbon atom gets one bromine atom. The product is 1,2-dibromoethane.

questions.q: Ethene reacts with steam at 300 °C and 60 atm. What is the structural formula of the product?
questions.explain: Steam adds across the C=C bond in the presence of an acid catalyst to make ethanol.

questions.q: Which equation shows propene reacting with hydrogen?
questions.explain: Hydrogen adds across the double bond to form the saturated alkane propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃. The other formulae are incorrect.

questions.q: But-2-ene reacts with bromine. What is the structural formula of the product?
questions.explain: One Br atom adds to each carbon of the C=C bond, giving CH₃CHBrCHBrCH₃ (2,3-dibromobutane).

questions.q: Which substances can be manufactured by the cracking of larger alkane molecules?
questions.explain: Cracking breaks alkanes into shorter alkanes, alkenes and hydrogen.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the reaction of ethane and ethene with aqueous bromine?
questions.explain: Only the unsaturated alkene, ethene, decolourises aqueous bromine. Ethane is saturated and causes no change.

questions.q: Which reaction is an addition reaction?
questions.explain: In C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ two molecules join to form one product. The other reactions are substitution, combustion and cracking.

questions.q: A colourless gas is bubbled through aqueous bromine and the solution stays orange. Which could be the gas?
questions.explain: Only unsaturated compounds decolourise aqueous bromine. Ethane is saturated, so there is no reaction.

questions.q: Ethene reacts with steam to make ethanol: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH. What mass of ethanol forms from 14 g of ethene, assuming all the ethene reacts?
questions.explain: Mᵣ of C₂H₄ = 28 and of C₂H₅OH = 46. 14 g is 0.50 mol, which forms 0.50 mol of ethanol: 0.50 × 46 = 23 g.

questions.q: Which conditions are used to make ethanol by fermentation of aqueous glucose?
options: an acid catalyst, 25–35 °C and plenty of oxygen
questions.explain: Fermentation uses yeast at 25–35 °C in the absence of oxygen. Air is excluded so the ethanol is not oxidised.

questions.q: Which equation represents the fermentation of glucose?
questions.explain: Glucose gives two molecules of ethanol and two of carbon dioxide, which balances: 6 C, 12 H and 6 O on each side.

questions.q: Which conditions are used to make ethanol from ethene and steam?
questions.explain: Ethene and steam react at 300 °C and 6000 kPa (60 atm) with an acid catalyst.

questions.q: What are the products of the complete combustion of ethanol?
questions.explain: Ethanol burns in excess oxygen: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.

questions.q: Which two uses of ethanol are correct?
options: a fuel and a feedstock for making bitumen
questions.explain: Ethanol is used as a solvent, for example in perfumes and paints, and as a fuel.

questions.q: What is an advantage of making ethanol by hydration of ethene instead of by fermentation?
options: It uses a renewable raw material.
It works at a lower temperature.
It is faster and gives purer ethanol.
questions.explain: Hydration is a fast continuous process that gives pure ethanol. Fermentation is slow, uses lower temperature and gives an impure product.

questions.q: What is a disadvantage of making ethanol by hydration of ethene?
options: It produces a mixture of ethanol and carbon dioxide.
It needs yeast, which dies easily.
The ethene comes from petroleum, which is non-renewable.
questions.explain: Ethene is made from petroleum, a finite resource. Fermentation uses sugar from plants, which is renewable.

questions.q: What is a disadvantage of making ethanol by fermentation?
options: It is a slow batch process that gives a dilute, impure product.
It needs a very high pressure.
It uses a non-renewable raw material.
It produces a pure product that needs no further processing.
questions.explain: Fermentation gives a dilute mixture, so the ethanol must be separated by distillation, and each batch takes days.

questions.q: Why is air kept out during the fermentation of glucose to make ethanol?
options: Oxygen would make the yeast produce carbon dioxide.
Oxygen would make the glucose insoluble.
Oxygen would raise the temperature to 300 °C.
Oxygen would oxidise the ethanol to ethanoic acid.
questions.explain: In air the ethanol is oxidised by bacteria to ethanoic acid, so the mixture would turn into vinegar.

questions.q: Which gas is also produced during the fermentation of aqueous glucose by yeast?
questions.explain: Fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the manufacture of ethanol by the addition of steam to ethene?
options: hydration of ethene | glucose | acid catalyst
hydration of ethene | ethene and steam | acid catalyst
questions.explain: Hydration uses ethene and steam with an acid catalyst. Fermentation uses aqueous glucose with yeast.

questions.q: 4.6 g of ethanol, C₂H₅OH, burns completely. What volume of carbon dioxide is formed at room temperature and pressure? (Mᵣ of ethanol = 46; 1 mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.)
questions.explain: 4.6 ÷ 46 = 0.10 mol ethanol. C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O gives 0.20 mol CO₂, and 0.20 × 24 = 4.8 dm³.

questions.q: Why is ethanol made by fermentation of sugar cane used as a fuel in some countries?
options: The sugar cane can be regrown, so the raw material is renewable.
It burns to form no carbon dioxide.
questions.explain: Sugar cane is a plant raw material that can be regrown each year, unlike petroleum.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid reacts with magnesium. What are the products?
questions.explain: Like other acids, ethanoic acid reacts with a reactive metal to give a salt and hydrogen. The salt is magnesium ethanoate.

questions.q: What is the formula of sodium ethanoate?
questions.explain: Ethanoate is CH₃COO⁻ and sodium is Na⁺, so the salt is CH₃COONa.

questions.q: Solid sodium carbonate is added to ethanoic acid. What is observed?
options: A gas forms that relights a glowing splint.
A gas forms that burns with a squeaky pop.
Bubbles of gas form that turn limewater milky.
questions.explain: Carbonates react with acids to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.

questions.q: Which equation represents the reaction of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide?
questions.explain: A base and an acid give a salt and water. The equation CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O is balanced.

questions.q: What is the formula of calcium ethanoate?
questions.explain: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ and ethanoate is CH₃COO⁻, so two ethanoate ions are needed: (CH₃COO)₂Ca.

questions.q: Ethanol is oxidised by warming it with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII). What colour change is seen?
questions.explain: Acidified manganate(VII) is purple and is reduced to a colourless solution as it oxidises the ethanol to ethanoic acid.

questions.q: How is ethanoic acid made in vinegar production?
options: Ethene is hydrated using steam and an acid catalyst.
Bacteria oxidise ethanol using oxygen from the air.
Ethanol is cracked at high temperature.
questions.explain: In vinegar production bacteria oxidise ethanol in dilute alcoholic drinks such as wine to ethanoic acid.

questions.q: What is formed when ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst?
questions.explain: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol react to form an ester and water: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.

questions.q: Which structural formula represents the ester formed from ethanoic acid and methanol?
questions.explain: The ester link –COO– joins the two parts: CH₃CO– from the acid and –OCH₃ from methanol, giving CH₃COOCH₃ (methyl ethanoate).

questions.q: Which gas is produced when ethanoic acid reacts with zinc?
questions.explain: Acids react with reactive metals to produce hydrogen, which gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

questions.q: Which compound is a carboxylic acid?
questions.explain: Carboxylic acids contain the –COOH functional group. CH₃CH₂COOH is propanoic acid.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide of concentration 0.200 mol/dm³ is exactly neutralised by ethanoic acid. How many moles of ethanoic acid react?
questions.explain: Moles of NaOH = 0.0250 dm³ × 0.200 mol/dm³ = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol. The reaction is 1 : 1, so 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol of acid reacts.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the reaction of ethanoic acid with magnesium?
questions.explain: Magnesium releases hydrogen from ethanoic acid and forms magnesium ethanoate. Carbon dioxide is released only by carbonates.

questions.q: What is a polymer?
options: a small molecule made by breaking up a larger molecule
a large molecule built up from many small molecules called monomers
a molecule that contains only one repeating atom
questions.explain: Polymers are long molecules formed by joining many monomer molecules together.

questions.q: How is poly(ethene) formed?
options: Ethanol molecules join together by condensation polymerisation.
Ethane molecules are cracked and then joined.
Many ethene molecules join together by addition polymerisation.
Ethene molecules are oxidised and then joined.
questions.explain: Ethene monomers contain C=C. The double bonds open and the molecules join in long chains to form poly(ethene).

questions.q: Which substances are made from polymers?
questions.explain: Plastics are made from polymers.

questions.q: Why do plastics sent to landfill sites cause a problem?
options: Plastics dissolve in rain water and pollute rivers.
Plastics react with soil to form fuels.
Many plastics are not biodegradable, so they remain for a very long time.
Plastics decompose quickly and release oxygen.
questions.explain: Most plastics are unreactive and not broken down by microorganisms, so they persist in landfill sites and take up space.

questions.q: What is an environmental problem caused by burning plastics?
questions.explain: Burning plastics can release toxic gases, such as carbon monoxide, so disposal by burning causes pollution.

questions.q: What is an environmental problem caused by plastics being dumped in the sea?
options: They dissolve and make the sea more acidic.
They quickly rot and use up dissolved oxygen.
They accumulate in the oceans and can harm marine animals.
They form alkenes that kill fish.
questions.explain: Plastics do not rot, so they build up in oceans and can be swallowed or entangle marine animals.

questions.q: Which monomer can form an addition polymer?
questions.explain: Addition polymerisation needs a monomer with a C=C double bond. Propene has one but propane does not.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the formation of poly(ethene)?
questions.explain: Ethene molecules join by addition polymerisation, so the polymer is the only product.

questions.q: What is the repeat unit of poly(propene)?
questions.explain: Propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, opens its double bond to give –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–, with the CH₃ group as a side group.

questions.q: The repeat unit of poly(chloroethene) is –CH₂–CHCl–. What is the monomer?
questions.explain: For an addition polymer, replace the single bond in the chain by a double bond: CH₂=CHCl is chloroethene.

questions.q: What small molecule is lost when nylon forms from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine?
questions.explain: Nylon forms by condensation polymerisation: each amide link is formed with the loss of one molecule of water.

questions.q: Which link joins the monomer units in nylon?
questions.explain: Nylon is a polyamide, so its monomer units are joined by amide links, –CONH–.

questions.q: Which pair of monomers forms a polyester?
options: a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine
a dicarboxylic acid and a diol
questions.explain: A polyester forms when a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diol. The ester links form with loss of water.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes condensation polymerisation?
options: one C=C per monomer | polymer only
two functional groups per monomer | polymer and a small molecule
two functional groups per monomer | polymer only
one C=C per monomer | polymer and a small molecule
questions.explain: Condensation monomers have two functional groups, and a small molecule such as water is lost as each link forms. Addition polymerisation needs C=C and gives only the polymer.

questions.q: What can be done with PET plastic?
options: It can be cracked to form crude oil.
It can be converted back into monomers and re-polymerised.
It can be fermented to form ethanol.
It can be dissolved to form alkenes.
questions.explain: PET can be broken down to its monomers and the monomers re-polymerised to make new PET.

questions.q: What are proteins?
options: natural polyesters made from sugar monomers
addition polymers made from alkene monomers
natural polyamides made from amino acid monomers
questions.explain: Proteins are natural polymers with amide links, formed from amino acid monomers.

questions.q: Which two functional groups does every amino acid molecule contain?
options: an amino group, –NH₂, and a carboxylic acid group, –COOH
a hydroxyl group, –OH, and an ester group, –COO–
questions.explain: Amino acids have an –NH₂ group at one end and a –COOH group at the other. They link through these groups to make the amide bonds in a protein.

questions.q: Which statement about nylon and protein is correct?
options: Both are made by addition polymerisation.
Both are made from alkene monomers.
questions.explain: Nylon and proteins are polyamides made by condensation polymerisation and both have –CONH– links.

questions.q: A sample of poly(ethene) has a relative molecular mass of 28 000. How many ethene units, C₂H₄, are in each molecule?
questions.explain: The relative molecular mass of C₂H₄ is 28, so the number of units is 28 000 ÷ 28 = 1000.

questions.q: A chain in a protein is made from 5 amino acid molecules joined together. How many water molecules are formed?
questions.explain: Joining n monomers in a chain makes n – 1 links, and each link forms with the loss of one water molecule. For 5 amino acids that is 4 water molecules.

questions.q: Which pair of monomers could form a polyamide?
questions.explain: A polyamide needs a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine. A diol with a dicarboxylic acid would give a polyester.

questions.q: Why is it a problem to burn waste plastics to avoid using landfill sites?
options: The burning can produce toxic gases.
The plastics burn to make metal.
The plastics melt to form fuels.
questions.explain: Burning avoids landfill but some plastics release toxic gases, so it can cause air pollution.

questions.q: A plastic is not biodegradable. Which statement about its disposal is correct?
options: It rots in landfill within a few weeks.
It is broken down by bacteria in the soil.
It stays in landfill for a very long time.
questions.explain: Microorganisms cannot break it down, so a non-biodegradable plastic stays unchanged in landfill for a very long time.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes PET?
options: polyamide | amide link | dicarboxylic acid and diol
