polyester | ester link | dicarboxylic acid and diol
polyester | ester link | dicarboxylic acid and diamine
polyamide | amide link | dicarboxylic acid and diamine
questions.explain: PET is a polyester, so it has ester links and forms from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol.

questions.q: Which piece of apparatus is best for measuring exactly 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide into a conical flask?
questions.explain: A volumetric pipette delivers one fixed volume very accurately. A measuring cylinder is less accurate, a gas syringe measures gases and a beaker is only roughly graduated.

questions.q: Which apparatus is used to measure the volume of a gas given off during a reaction?
questions.explain: A gas syringe collects the gas and the plunger moves out so the volume can be read from the scale. The other items measure liquid volume, mass or temperature.

questions.q: Which row correctly pairs the apparatus with the quantity it measures?
questions.explain: A balance measures mass. A stop-watch measures time, a burette measures volume of liquid and a thermometer measures temperature.

questions.q: Sugar is stirred into water until all of it dissolves. Which row correctly names the solute and the solvent?
questions.explain: The solute is the substance that dissolves (sugar) and the solvent is the substance it dissolves in (water). The mixture of the two is the solution.

questions.q: Which statement describes a saturated solution?
options: It contains more solute than solvent.
It contains no dissolved solute at all.
It contains the maximum concentration of solute that can dissolve in the solvent at a given temperature.
It contains the maximum mass of solute that can dissolve at any temperature.
questions.explain: A saturated solution holds as much dissolved solute as it can at a stated temperature, so any extra solute stays undissolved. The amount that can dissolve changes with temperature.

questions.q: A mixture of chalk powder and water is poured through filter paper. Which statement is correct?
options: The chalk is the residue and the water is the filtrate.
The chalk is the filtrate and the water is the residue.
The chalk and the water are both the filtrate.
The water is the residue and the chalk is the solvent.
questions.explain: The solid that stays on the filter paper is the residue; the liquid that passes through is the filtrate.

questions.q: Which of these is a solution?
questions.explain: A solution is a solute completely dissolved in a solvent. Sand, oil and chalk do not dissolve in water, so they do not form solutions.

questions.q: A student adds acid to an alkali in a titration. What is one advantage of using a burette rather than a measuring cylinder to add the acid?
options: It can measure the volume of a gas as well.
The volume added can be controlled drop by drop and read more precisely.
It measures the mass of acid added.
It is quicker to fill and read.
questions.explain: A burette has a tap and a fine scale so small volumes can be added slowly and read accurately, which is needed to find an end-point.

questions.q: Which apparatus would be used to measure the mass of a solid to the nearest 0.01 g?
questions.explain: A balance measures mass. A measuring cylinder measures volume, a thermometer measures temperature and a stop-watch measures time.

questions.q: Which gas cannot be collected over water because it is very soluble in water?
questions.explain: Ammonia dissolves very readily in water, so collecting it over water would lose the gas. Hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen are only slightly soluble.

questions.q: A student follows the rate of a reaction that produces a gas. Which pair of apparatus is most suitable?
options: a volumetric pipette and a balance
a gas syringe and a stop-watch
a measuring cylinder and a thermometer
questions.explain: The volume of gas must be measured at regular times, so a gas syringe and a stop-watch are needed. The other pairs cannot measure gas volume against time.

questions.q: Zinc reacts with excess dilute acid to give hydrogen gas. Why is measuring the loss in mass of the flask a poor way to follow this reaction?
options: Hydrogen dissolves in the acid so no mass is lost.
A balance cannot be used with an acid.
The mass of hydrogen lost is so small that it is difficult to measure accurately.
Hydrogen is denser than air so it stays in the flask.
questions.explain: Hydrogen has a very low relative molecular mass, so the mass lost is tiny compared with the sensitivity of a typical balance.

questions.q: Extra solid is added to a saturated solution at constant temperature and stirred. What happens?
options: The extra solid dissolves and the solution stays saturated.
The extra solid stays undissolved because the maximum concentration has already been reached.
The extra solid dissolves and the solution becomes unsaturated.
The solid reacts with the solvent.
questions.explain: A saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute at that temperature, so the added solid remains as a residue at the bottom.

questions.q: In an experiment to measure a temperature change, a student uses a polystyrene cup instead of a glass beaker. What is the advantage?
options: Polystyrene is a better insulator so less heat is lost to the surroundings.
Polystyrene conducts heat better so the temperature changes faster.
Polystyrene reacts with the solution so the change is bigger.
Polystyrene is transparent so the solution can be seen.
questions.explain: Polystyrene is a poor conductor of heat, so less energy escapes and the measured temperature change is closer to the true value.

questions.q: Which description of an acid–base titration is correct?
options: A measuring cylinder puts exactly 25.0 cm³ of acid into a burette and alkali is added from a conical flask.
Indicator is placed in the burette and acid is poured into the conical flask all at once.
A volumetric pipette puts a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask, indicator is added and acid is run in from a burette until the colour changes.
Alkali is run from a burette into a volumetric pipette until the indicator changes colour.
questions.explain: The pipette measures one accurate volume into the flask. The burette adds the other solution gradually until the indicator shows the end-point.

questions.q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added slowly to aqueous sodium hydroxide containing methyl orange. What colour change shows the end-point?
questions.explain: Methyl orange is yellow in alkali and red in acid, so the end-point is the first permanent change from yellow to orange when acid is added to alkali.

questions.q: Dilute acid is added to aqueous sodium hydroxide containing thymolphthalein. What colour change shows the end-point?
questions.explain: Thymolphthalein is blue in alkali and colourless in acid, so adding acid to alkali causes a change from blue to colourless.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the indicator in a titration?
options: to speed up the neutralisation reaction
to measure the volume of acid added
to show the point at which the acid and alkali have exactly reacted
questions.explain: An indicator changes colour at the end-point, showing when exactly enough acid has been added to neutralise the alkali.

questions.q: Why is a burette rinsed with a little of the acid it is going to contain before it is filled?
options: Acid cleans the tap so it can be turned more easily.
Acid in the burette speeds up the reaction in the flask.
Water left in the burette would dilute the acid and make the titre wrong.
Rinsing with acid makes the end-point easier to see.
questions.explain: Any water left in the burette would lower the concentration of the acid, so the volume needed would not match the stated concentration.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?
questions.explain: Moles HCl = 0.0200 × 0.100 = 0.00200 mol. HCl and NaOH react 1 : 1, so concentration of NaOH = 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol/dm³.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?
questions.explain: Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.0250 × 0.200 = 0.00500 mol. Moles NaOH = 2 × 0.00500 = 0.0100 mol. Concentration = 0.0100 ÷ 0.0200 = 0.500 mol/dm³.

questions.q: Why is a titration repeated until two results agree closely?
options: so that the results are reliable and a mean titre can be calculated
so that all the acid is used up
to make the indicator change colour faster
to increase the concentration of the alkali
questions.explain: Titres that agree closely (concordant results) show that the measurements are reliable, so they can be averaged to give an accurate value.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes the use of the apparatus in a titration?
options: volumetric pipette | adds a variable volume of solution drop by drop
burette | adds a variable volume of solution drop by drop
conical flask | measures an exact volume of solution
burette | measures exactly 25.0 cm³ each time
questions.explain: The burette delivers any volume needed and can be controlled drop by drop. The pipette delivers one fixed volume and the conical flask only holds the mixture.

questions.q: A student titrates an acid with an alkali to prepare pure crystals of a salt. Why is the titration repeated without indicator using the same volumes?
options: The indicator would react with the acid to form a gas.
The reaction only works if no indicator is present.
The indicator would make the solution more acidic.
The indicator would contaminate the salt crystals.
questions.explain: The indicator is needed only to find the volumes that neutralise each other. Repeating without it gives a salt solution that is not contaminated by the dye.

questions.q: Which row gives the correct colours of the indicator in acid and in alkali?
questions.explain: Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali. Thymolphthalein is colourless in acid and blue in alkali, and litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali.

questions.q: In a titration the burette reading at the start is 3.10 cm³ and at the end-point is 23.30 cm³. What is the volume of acid added?
questions.explain: The volume added is the final reading minus the initial reading: 23.30 − 3.10 = 20.20 cm³.

questions.q: In paper chromatography the starting line is drawn in pencil rather than ink. Why?
options: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent, so it will not move up the paper.
Pencil is a better solvent than ink.
Ink would react with the paper.
Pencil lines make the spots move faster.
questions.explain: Ink contains dyes that would dissolve and run with the solvent. Pencil (graphite) is insoluble, so the line stays put and does not interfere.

questions.q: A student places the spot of ink below the level of the solvent in the beaker. What is the most likely result?
options: The solvent runs faster up the paper.
The coloured substances dissolve into the solvent and no chromatogram forms.
questions.explain: The solvent level must be below the starting line so that the spot is carried up the paper rather than washed away into the solvent.

questions.q: What does a single spot on a chromatogram suggest about a coloured substance?
options: It could be pure because it has not separated into more than one substance.
It is insoluble in the solvent.
questions.explain: A pure substance gives one spot, but one spot is only evidence of purity: it is also useful to run it in more than one solvent.

questions.q: A chromatogram of an unknown dye X shows two spots. Pure dyes A, B and C each give one spot. The spots from X match the heights of the spots from A and C. What does this show?
options: X is a mixture of three of the dyes.
X is a mixture of dye A and dye C.
questions.explain: Spots that travel the same distance in the same solvent are the same substance. X has two spots that match A and C, so it is a mixture of those two.

questions.q: In paper chromatography, which substance in a mixture travels the furthest up the paper?
options: the one most soluble in the solvent and least attracted to the paper
the one least soluble in the solvent and most attracted to the paper
the one with the darkest colour
the one that is the most dense
questions.explain: A substance that dissolves well in the solvent and sticks weakly to the paper is carried further by the moving solvent.

questions.q: A black ink is tested by chromatography and gives four separate coloured spots. What does this show?
options: The ink is a single pure substance.
The ink contains at least four different coloured substances.
The ink contains exactly one dye in four forms.
The ink is insoluble in the solvent.
questions.explain: Each separate spot is a different substance, so there are at least four. Two substances with identical movement would overlap into one spot.

questions.q: The beaker used for chromatography is often covered with a lid. Why?
options: to make the solvent move faster up the paper
to stop the solvent evaporating from the beaker
to stop the dyes being seen
questions.explain: The lid keeps the air saturated with solvent vapour, so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper and the run is more reliable.

questions.q: Some coloured dyes are insoluble in water. What can be done to separate them by paper chromatography?
options: Use a thicker piece of paper.
Heat the paper until the dyes dissolve.
Use a different suitable solvent, such as ethanol.
Use ink instead of the dyes.
questions.explain: The solvent must dissolve the substances to be separated, so if water does not dissolve them another solvent such as ethanol is chosen.

questions.q: Which observation on a chromatogram is evidence that a substance is impure?
options: It forms more than one spot.
It forms one spot that is not at the solvent front.
It forms a single coloured spot.
It stays on the starting line.
questions.explain: A pure substance produces one spot. More than one spot means more than one substance is present.

questions.q: Which method can be used to show that a green ink is a mixture of dyes?
options: paper chromatography with a suitable solvent
questions.explain: Chromatography separates soluble coloured substances so each dye appears as a separate spot. The other methods do not separate dyes.

questions.q: What is a chromatogram?
options: the solvent that moves up the paper
the paper showing the positions of the separated substances after the run
the line on which the mixture is first placed
the substance that does not move
questions.explain: A chromatogram is the paper record of the separation: the spots show where each substance finished.

questions.q: Amino acids are colourless. What must be done to see their positions on a chromatogram?
options: Run the chromatogram in the dark.
Use a thicker piece of paper.
Add more of the amino acids to the starting line.
Spray the paper with a locating agent that reacts with them to form coloured spots.
questions.explain: Colourless substances cannot be seen on the paper, so a locating agent that reacts with them to give a colour is applied after the run.

questions.q: On a chromatogram a spot travels 3.6 cm while the solvent travels 7.2 cm. What is the Rf value?
questions.explain: Rf = distance travelled by the substance ÷ distance travelled by the solvent = 3.6 ÷ 7.2 = 0.50.

questions.q: The solvent front moves 8.0 cm up the paper. A substance has an Rf value of 0.35. How far does the substance travel?
questions.explain: Distance = Rf × solvent distance = 0.35 × 8.0 = 2.8 cm.

questions.q: Which statement about Rf values is correct?
options: An Rf value is measured in cm and can be larger than 1.
An Rf value is larger when the substance is less soluble in the solvent.
An Rf value is the distance moved by the solvent divided by that moved by the substance.
An Rf value has no units and cannot be greater than 1.
questions.explain: Rf is a ratio of two distances, so it has no units. The substance can never travel further than the solvent, so Rf is never greater than 1.

questions.q: In one solvent, substances W, X, Y and Z have Rf values 0.25, 0.40, 0.55 and 0.80. In the same solvent an unknown spot travels 2.2 cm while the solvent front travels 5.5 cm. Which substance is it?
questions.explain: Rf of the unknown = 2.2 ÷ 5.5 = 0.40, which matches substance X.

questions.q: A student stops a chromatography run earlier than planned, with the same paper and solvent. What happens to the Rf value of a substance?
options: It decreases because the substance has moved a shorter distance.
It stays the same because both distances change in the same proportion.
It increases because the solvent has moved a shorter distance.
questions.explain: Rf is the ratio of the two distances. Stopping earlier shortens both distances proportionally, so the ratio is unchanged.

questions.q: In the same solvent, substance P has an Rf value of 0.72 and substance Q has an Rf value of 0.31. Which statement is correct?
options: P is more soluble in the solvent or less attracted to the paper than Q.
P is less soluble in the solvent than Q.
P and Q must be the same substance.
questions.explain: The higher Rf value means P travelled further relative to the solvent. That occurs when it dissolves better in the solvent or sticks less to the paper.

questions.q: Which technique separates undissolved chalk powder from water?
questions.explain: The chalk is insoluble, so it stays on the filter paper as the residue while the water passes through as the filtrate.

questions.q: Which method is used to obtain crystals of copper(II) sulfate from a solution of copper(II) sulfate?
options: Heat the solution until all the water has evaporated.
Heat the solution to evaporate some of the water, then leave it to cool so that crystals form.
Filter the solution and keep the filtrate.
Distil the solution and collect the distillate.
questions.explain: Partly evaporating the water gives a hot saturated solution; on cooling the solubility falls, so crystals form. Distilling would collect water, not crystals.

questions.q: In a simple distillation apparatus, how should cooling water pass through the condenser?
options: in at the top and out at the bottom, so that the jacket drains quickly
in and out at the same level
in at the bottom and out at the top, so that the jacket stays full of water
in at the bottom and out through the flask
questions.explain: Water entering at the bottom rises and fills the jacket, so the condenser stays cold along its whole length.

questions.q: A mixture of ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (boiling point 100 °C) is heated in fractional distillation apparatus. Which liquid is collected first?
options: ethanol, because it has the lower boiling point
water, because it has the higher boiling point
water, because it has the lower relative molecular mass
questions.explain: The liquid with the lower boiling point evaporates and reaches the top of the column first, so ethanol is collected first.

questions.q: A mixture contains sand and sodium chloride. Which sequence of steps separates both substances?
options: Add water and stir, filter, then evaporate the filtrate to obtain the salt.
Heat the mixture strongly and collect the vapour.
Filter the dry mixture and then add water to the filtrate.
Add water, evaporate the mixture, then filter the residue.
questions.explain: Salt dissolves and sand does not. Filtering removes the sand as the residue, and evaporating the salt solution leaves solid sodium chloride.

questions.q: A student heats an unknown solid and it melts completely between 120 °C and 126 °C. The pure compound melts at 130 °C. What can be concluded?
options: The sample is a different pure substance.
questions.explain: A pure substance melts sharply at its fixed melting point. Impurities lower the melting point and make the solid melt over a range of temperatures.

questions.q: A colourless liquid boils over the range 78–84 °C. What does this suggest?
options: The liquid is a pure substance.
The liquid is a solid dissolved in water.
questions.explain: A pure liquid boils at one fixed temperature. A range of boiling temperatures shows that more than one substance is present.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes how a pure solid and an impure solid melt?
options: melts over a range of temperatures | melts at one sharp temperature
melts at one sharp temperature | melts over a range of temperatures
melts at one sharp temperature | melts at a higher sharp temperature
melts over a range of temperatures | melts over a range at a higher temperature
questions.explain: A pure solid has a sharp melting point. Impurities usually lower the melting point and spread the melting over a range.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the glass beads or rings in a fractionating column?
options: They stop the liquid from boiling.
They keep the column hot at the top.
They provide a large surface area for repeated condensing and evaporating.
questions.explain: Vapour condenses on the large surface and re-evaporates repeatedly, so the vapour that reaches the top is richer in the more volatile liquid.

questions.q: A mixture of three miscible liquids X (boiling point 65 °C), Y (82 °C) and Z (118 °C) is separated by fractional distillation. In which order are they collected?
options: X, Y and Z all together
questions.explain: Liquids distil in order of increasing boiling point, so the one with the lowest boiling point (X) is collected first.

questions.q: Why is crystallisation by cooling a hot saturated solution preferred to evaporating all the water from copper(II) sulfate solution to obtain hydrated crystals?
options: Cooling makes the crystals dissolve in the solvent.
Evaporating to dryness makes the crystals blue.
Evaporating to dryness would drive off the water of crystallisation and could leave impurities mixed in the solid.
Evaporating to dryness is not possible with water.
questions.explain: Heating strongly removes the water that is part of the hydrated crystals. Crystallising from a saturated solution gives larger, purer crystals.

questions.q: A mixture of sodium chloride and sand is separated by adding water. Which property difference makes this possible?
options: Sand has a lower melting point than sodium chloride.
Sodium chloride is soluble in water but sand is not.
Sodium chloride is magnetic but sand is not.
Sand is denser than water but sodium chloride is not.
questions.explain: Adding a suitable solvent dissolves only the soluble substance, which allows the insoluble substance to be removed by filtration.

questions.q: Aqueous sodium chloride boils at 103 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. What does this show?
options: It is pure water, because boiling points vary.
It is pure water at higher pressure.
It is not pure water, because the dissolved salt raises the boiling point.
questions.explain: Pure water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure. Dissolved impurities raise the boiling point, so 103 °C shows the liquid is a solution.

questions.q: Seawater is separated by simple distillation. What collects in the receiving flask?
options: a mixture of salt and water vapour
questions.explain: Water evaporates and condenses in the condenser, so it is collected as the distillate. The salt stays in the distillation flask.

questions.q: In a simple distillation, where should the bulb of the thermometer be placed?
options: in the liquid at the bottom of the flask
level with the side arm of the flask, in the vapour
questions.explain: The thermometer is meant to read the temperature of the vapour that is about to leave the flask, which is the boiling point of the liquid.

questions.q: Four pure solids melt at these temperatures: P 41 °C, Q 80 °C, R 114 °C, S 135 °C. An unknown pure solid melts sharply at 80 °C. Which is it most likely to be?
questions.explain: A pure substance has a specific melting point, so an unknown that melts sharply at 80 °C is most likely to be Q.

questions.q: Which mixture needs fractional distillation rather than simple distillation to separate it?
options: two miscible liquids with similar boiling points
an insoluble solid in a liquid
questions.explain: Fractional distillation is used for liquids that mix and whose boiling points are close, so one distillation does not separate them. The other mixtures need filtration, simple distillation or chromatography.

questions.q: During the fractional distillation of a mixture of two miscible liquids, what happens to the thermometer reading at the top of the column?
options: It rises steadily all the time.
It stays steady at the boiling point of the lower boiling liquid, then rises.
It falls as the first liquid distils.
It stays at the boiling point of the higher boiling liquid.
questions.explain: While the more volatile liquid distils the temperature stays near its boiling point. When it has gone, the temperature rises towards the boiling point of the other liquid.

questions.q: Crystals are filtered from a solution and washed with a small amount of cold distilled water. Why is only a small amount of cold water used?
options: to remove soluble impurities without dissolving much of the crystals
questions.explain: The washing water removes solution clinging to the crystals. Using little and cold water means that only a small amount of the crystals dissolve.

questions.q: A saturated solution of a salt is cooled from 80 °C to 20 °C and crystals form. Why?
options: The salt reacts with the water at 20 °C.
Water evaporates when the solution is cooled.
The solubility of the salt is lower at the lower temperature, so the excess solute comes out of solution.
questions.explain: Most salts are less soluble when cold. The solution holds too much solute at 20 °C, so the excess crystallises.

questions.q: A fermented mixture contains yeast cells (insoluble), ethanol and water. Which sequence best obtains ethanol?
options: filtration to remove the yeast, then fractional distillation
questions.explain: Filtration removes the insoluble yeast. The ethanol and water are miscible liquids with different boiling points, so fractional distillation separates them.

questions.q: While a liquid is boiling, the thermometer reading stays constant at 78 °C. What does this suggest about the liquid?
options: It is a mixture of two liquids.
It is a solid dissolved in water.
It is probably a single pure substance.
questions.explain: A pure liquid boils at one fixed temperature. In a mixture the boiling temperature would rise as the more volatile component is lost.

questions.q: Which method gives pure water from seawater?
questions.explain: Simple distillation evaporates the water and condenses it again, leaving the dissolved salts behind.

questions.q: A pure liquid boils sharply at 56 °C. Boiling points: ethanol 78 °C, water 100 °C, propanone 56 °C, hexane 69 °C. Which liquid is it most likely to be?
questions.explain: A pure liquid has a fixed boiling point. The sample matches the boiling point of propanone.

questions.q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a solid. It fizzes, and the gas turns limewater milky. Which ion is most likely to be present in the solid?
questions.explain: Carbonates react with acid to give carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky. Sulfates, chlorides and nitrates do not give this gas.

questions.q: Which row gives the colour of the precipitate formed when acidified aqueous silver nitrate is added?
questions.explain: Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.

questions.q: Why is dilute nitric acid added before aqueous silver nitrate when testing for halide ions?
options: to make silver nitrate more soluble
to react with carbonate ions that would also form a precipitate with silver ions
questions.explain: Silver carbonate is also an insoluble precipitate. Adding nitric acid first destroys any carbonate so that only a halide gives a precipitate.

questions.q: A colourless solution is acidified with dilute nitric acid and aqueous barium nitrate is added. A white precipitate forms. Which ion is present?
questions.explain: Barium ions form insoluble white barium sulfate. Carbonate would have been destroyed by the acid and chloride and nitrate give no precipitate with barium ions.

questions.q: Why must dilute sulfuric acid not be used to acidify the solution in the test for sulfate ions?
options: It contains sulfate ions, which would give a precipitate with barium ions.
It would react with the barium nitrate to form a gas.
It is too weak an acid to remove carbonate ions.
It would turn the barium nitrate solution acidic.
questions.explain: Sulfuric acid supplies sulfate ions, so a white precipitate would form whether or not the sample contained sulfate. Nitric acid is used instead.

questions.q: Which procedure and observation are correct for the test for nitrate ions?
options: Add dilute acid; carbon dioxide is given off and turns limewater milky.
Add acidified silver nitrate; a white precipitate forms.
Add aluminium foil and dilute acid; hydrogen is given off and burns with a squeaky pop.
Add aqueous sodium hydroxide and aluminium foil and warm; ammonia is given off and turns damp red litmus paper blue.
questions.explain: In alkaline solution, aluminium reduces nitrate ions to ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus paper blue.

questions.q: What happens to the nitrate ions in the test with aluminium foil and aqueous sodium hydroxide?
options: They are oxidised to nitrogen dioxide.
They are unchanged; the ammonia comes from the sodium hydroxide.
questions.explain: Aluminium reduces nitrate (nitrogen oxidation state +5) to ammonia (−3). Sodium hydroxide contains no nitrogen, so it cannot be the source of ammonia.

questions.q: A colourless solution decolourises acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII), changing from purple to colourless. Which ion could be present?
questions.explain: Sulfite ions reduce the manganate(VII) ions, so the purple colour disappears. Sulfate, carbonate and nitrate do not.

questions.q: A sodium compound fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid and the gas turns limewater milky. Which compound could it be?
questions.explain: The gas is carbon dioxide, which comes from the reaction of acid with a carbonate. Sulfates, chlorides and nitrates do not give carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents the formation of the precipitate in the test for chloride ions?
questions.explain: Silver ions and chloride ions combine in a 1 : 1 ratio to give insoluble silver chloride. Silver nitrate and barium chloride are both soluble.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents the formation of the precipitate in the test for sulfate ions?
questions.explain: One Ba²⁺ ion combines with one SO₄²⁻ ion to give solid BaSO₄, which is insoluble. The charges must balance: +2 and −2.

questions.q: What is seen when aqueous silver nitrate is added to an acidified solution of potassium iodide?
questions.explain: Iodide ions form yellow silver iodide. White is for chloride and cream is for bromide.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents the reaction between carbonate ions and dilute acid?
questions.explain: Carbonate ions react with hydrogen ions to give carbon dioxide and water. Only this equation balances in both atoms and charge.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes a test for an ion?
options: SO₄²⁻ | acidified aqueous silver nitrate | white precipitate
SO₄²⁻ | acidified aqueous barium nitrate | white precipitate
Cl⁻ | acidified aqueous barium nitrate | white precipitate
CO₃²⁻ | dilute acid | no visible change
questions.explain: Sulfate ions are tested with acidified barium nitrate. Chloride ions need acidified silver nitrate, and carbonates fizz with dilute acid.

questions.q: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to a solution until in excess. A light blue precipitate forms which does not dissolve. Which cation is present?
questions.explain: Copper(II) hydroxide is light blue and insoluble in excess alkali. Iron(II) is green, iron(III) is red-brown and chromium(III) is green.

questions.q: Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a red-brown precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. Which cation is present?
questions.explain: Fe³⁺ forms red-brown iron(III) hydroxide which is insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide.

questions.q: Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a green precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. Which cation is present?
questions.explain: Fe²⁺ forms a green precipitate that is insoluble in excess. The green precipitate from chromium(III) dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide.

questions.q: A solution is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. A gas is given off that turns damp red litmus paper blue. Which cation is present?
questions.explain: Ammonium ions react with alkali on warming to release ammonia, the only common alkaline gas, which turns damp red litmus blue.

questions.q: Aqueous aluminium ions and aqueous zinc ions both give a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess. How can the two be distinguished?
options: Add more aqueous sodium hydroxide: only the zinc precipitate dissolves.
Add aqueous ammonia in excess: the aluminium precipitate dissolves but the zinc precipitate does not.
Add dilute nitric acid: only the aluminium precipitate dissolves.
Add aqueous ammonia in excess: the zinc precipitate dissolves but the aluminium precipitate does not.
questions.explain: Zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia to give a colourless solution, but aluminium hydroxide stays as a white precipitate.

questions.q: Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. With aqueous ammonia there is no precipitate or only a very slight one. Which cation is present?
questions.explain: Calcium hydroxide is a white precipitate that is insoluble in excess alkali. Aluminium and zinc precipitates dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide, and ammonium gives no precipitate.

questions.q: Excess aqueous ammonia is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate. What is seen?
options: A light blue precipitate forms and does not dissolve.
A light blue precipitate forms and then dissolves to give a dark blue solution.
A green precipitate forms and does not dissolve.
questions.explain: Copper(II) hydroxide first forms as a light blue precipitate, which dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep blue solution.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes what happens when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added slowly to excess?
options: Al³⁺ | white precipitate that dissolves in excess
Ca²⁺ | white precipitate that dissolves in excess
Cu²⁺ | blue precipitate that dissolves in excess
Fe³⁺ | green precipitate that does not dissolve in excess
questions.explain: Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, so its white precipitate dissolves in excess. Calcium hydroxide does not dissolve, copper(II) hydroxide does not dissolve and iron(III) gives a red-brown precipitate.

questions.q: A green precipitate forms when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to a solution. The precipitate dissolves in excess to give a green solution. Which cation is present?
questions.explain: Chromium(III) hydroxide is green and dissolves in excess alkali. Fe²⁺ gives a green precipitate that stays, and zinc gives a white precipitate.

questions.q: A pale green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide turns brown at the surface when left in air. What is the explanation?
options: Iron(III) ions are reduced to iron(II) ions by the air.
Iron(II) ions are oxidised to iron(III) ions by oxygen in the air.
Carbon dioxide in the air reacts with the precipitate.
questions.explain: Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺ by oxygen, forming red-brown iron(III) hydroxide on the surface.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents the formation of the precipitate when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate?
questions.explain: Each Cu²⁺ ion needs two OH⁻ ions to balance the charge, and the hydroxide is insoluble, so (s) is shown.

questions.q: What is the formula of the red-brown precipitate formed when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to aqueous iron(III) chloride?
questions.explain: Fe³⁺ combines with three OH⁻ ions to give iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₃. Fe(OH)₂ is the green iron(II) hydroxide.

questions.q: A solution gives a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess. With aqueous ammonia it gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. Which cation is present?
questions.explain: Both Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide, but only the zinc precipitate dissolves in excess ammonia. So the cation is aluminium.

questions.q: A solution gives a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that does not dissolve in excess. A flame test gives a brick-red flame. Which cation is present?
questions.explain: A white precipitate insoluble in excess alkali and a brick-red flame are both characteristic of calcium. Barium gives a green flame and aluminium and zinc precipitates dissolve in excess.

questions.q: Why is aqueous sodium hydroxide added to a solution a little at a time and then in excess?
options: to find the volume of alkali needed
to see whether any precipitate that forms dissolves in excess
questions.explain: Whether the precipitate redissolves in excess alkali is part of identifying the cation, for example aluminium and zinc compared with calcium.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents the release of ammonia when an ammonium salt is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
questions.explain: Ammonium ions give up a hydrogen ion to hydroxide ions, forming ammonia and water. This is the only equation that balances and shows ammonia escaping as a gas.

questions.q: Excess aqueous ammonia is added to a solution of zinc sulfate. What is seen?
options: A white precipitate forms and does not dissolve.
A blue precipitate forms and dissolves to give a dark blue solution.
A white precipitate forms and then dissolves to give a colourless solution.
questions.explain: Zinc hydroxide is a white precipitate that dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia to give a colourless solution.

questions.q: Which test is used to identify hydrogen?
options: A lighted splint makes a squeaky pop.
Damp red litmus paper turns blue.
questions.explain: Hydrogen burns explosively with oxygen, giving a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

questions.q: Which test and result identify oxygen?
options: A lighted splint makes a squeaky pop.
questions.explain: Oxygen supports combustion, so a glowing splint bursts into flame.

questions.q: Which gas turns limewater milky?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which makes the limewater milky.

questions.q: A gas turns damp blue litmus paper red and then bleaches it white. Which gas is it?
questions.explain: Chlorine forms an acidic solution in the damp paper, which turns the litmus red, and then bleaches it.

questions.q: A gas turns damp red litmus paper blue. Which gas is it?
questions.explain: Ammonia is the common alkaline gas. It dissolves in the water on the paper to form an alkaline solution.

questions.q: Which gas turns acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless?
questions.explain: Sulfur dioxide is a reducing agent and reduces the purple manganate(VII) ions to colourless Mn²⁺ ions.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives a gas, its test and the positive result?
questions.explain: Oxygen relights a glowing splint. Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint, carbon dioxide turns limewater milky and chlorine bleaches damp litmus.

questions.q: A white precipitate forms when carbon dioxide is bubbled into limewater. What is the precipitate?
questions.explain: Limewater is aqueous calcium hydroxide. It reacts with carbon dioxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

questions.q: A green solid is heated and turns black. The gas produced turns limewater milky. Which solid was heated?
questions.explain: Copper(II) carbonate is green. It decomposes to black copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.

questions.q: A colourless gas does not change the colour of acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) but turns limewater milky. Which gas is it?
questions.explain: Both sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide can give a milky limewater, but only sulfur dioxide decolourises acidified manganate(VII). The gas is therefore carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Why must the litmus paper be damp when testing for ammonia?
options: Water cools the ammonia so it can be detected.
Water acts as a catalyst for the colour change.
Water removes carbon dioxide from the gas.
Ammonia dissolves in the water to form an alkaline solution that changes the colour of the litmus.
questions.explain: Dry ammonia gas does not change the colour of litmus. It must dissolve in water on the paper to form alkaline hydroxide ions.

questions.q: Which cation gives a red flame in a flame test?
questions.explain: Lithium compounds give a red flame. Potassium is lilac, sodium is yellow and barium is light green.

questions.q: Which colour does a sodium compound give in a flame test?
questions.explain: Sodium ions give an intense yellow flame.

questions.q: A compound burns in a flame test with a lilac flame. Which cation is present?
questions.explain: Potassium compounds give a lilac flame. Lithium gives red, sodium yellow and copper(II) blue-green.

questions.q: Which cation gives an orange-red flame in a flame test?
questions.explain: Calcium compounds give an orange-red (brick-red) flame. Barium gives a light green flame and copper(II) gives a blue-green flame.

questions.q: Which cation gives a light green flame in a flame test?
questions.explain: Barium compounds give a light green flame.

questions.q: A flame test gives a blue-green flame. Which cation is present?
questions.explain: Copper(II) compounds give a blue-green flame.

questions.q: Which row correctly gives the flame colour for the cation?
questions.explain: Copper(II) is blue-green. Lithium is red, potassium is lilac and sodium is yellow.

questions.q: A white solid gives a lilac flame in a flame test. Its aqueous solution gives a white precipitate with acidified aqueous silver nitrate. What is the solid?
questions.explain: The lilac flame shows potassium, and a white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate shows chloride. Iodide would give a yellow precipitate.

questions.q: Why is the wire for a flame test cleaned with dilute hydrochloric acid and heated before use?
options: to remove traces of other substances that could colour the flame
to give the flame a green colour
questions.explain: Contamination on the wire, especially sodium, would give flame colours that mask the colour of the sample being tested.

questions.q: A solid dissolves in water to form a colourless solution. A flame test gives a lilac flame. Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives no precipitate. After acidifying with dilute nitric acid, aqueous barium nitrate gives a white precipitate. What is the solid?
questions.explain: Lilac means potassium. The precipitate with acidified barium nitrate means sulfate. A calcium salt would have given a precipitate with sodium hydroxide.
